question: Hume said a trained critic and a careless one don't just disagree about a poem — one is RIGHT, the way a tuned ear hears a sour note. Which view is Hume defending?
answer: Realism — real features, like craft, make a work better.
choices: Realism — real features, like craft, make a work better.
Subjectivism — 'better' just means it pleases me more.
Relativism — each culture sets what counts as good.
Expressionism — it is better if it carries stronger feeling.
context: Aesthetic realism says artworks carry real qualities — craft, structure, originality — beyond personal taste. David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) is the classic defense: trained 'true judges' converge on real merit, so a sour note really is a flaw, not just a feeling.

question: Ben shrugs off a fight over a song: 'If I call it great and you don't, neither of us is wrong — there's just nothing to argue about.' Which view of art is Ben using?
answer: Subjectivism — 'great' only reports your own taste.
choices: Subjectivism — 'great' only reports your own taste.
Realism — real features, like skill, make a work better.
Relativism — each culture sets what counts as good.
Formalism — only line, color, and shape decide it.
context: Aesthetic subjectivism turns 'great' or 'better' into a report on the viewer's own response — so there's no fact to dispute. Critics note we argue about taste as if more than feelings were at stake: calling a song great looks like a claim, not a confession.

question: A mask judged ugly here is treasured there. Priya shrugs: 'There's no asking who's right — each tradition just measures by its own yardstick.' Which view of art is she using?
answer: Relativism — each culture sets what counts as good.
choices: Relativism — each culture sets what counts as good.
Realism — real features, like craft, make a work better.
Subjectivism — 'good' just means it pleases me more.
Formalism — only line, color, and shape decide it.
context: Cultural relativism in aesthetics holds that beauty standards are products of a tradition, not universal facts. Critics ask: if standards never cross cultures, how does a 30,000-year-old cave painting still stop a modern viewer cold?

question: Tolstoy argued a song is art only if the singer's exact feeling LEAPS into you — a polished but hollow piece fails, a rough one that makes you feel it succeeds. Which view is that?
answer: Expressionism — art works when feeling carries across.
choices: Expressionism — art works when feeling carries across.
Formalism — only line, color, and shape decide it.
Imitation — it is good if it depicts something well.
Subjectivism — 'good' just means it pleases me more.
context: Expressionism (Leo Tolstoy, What Is Art?, 1897; later Collingwood) makes shared feeling the heart of art — a work counts when the artist's emotion genuinely crosses to the audience. Critics ask whether sincere feeling alone is ever enough.

question: Clive Bell claimed it makes NO difference whether a painting shows a saint or a soup can — only the lines, shapes, and colors decide if it's art. Which view is that?
answer: Formalism — only the arrangement of parts counts.
choices: Formalism — only the arrangement of parts counts.
Expressionism — it is good if it carries real feeling.
Imitation — it is good if it depicts something well.
Relativism — each culture sets what counts as good.
context: Formalism (Clive Bell, Art, 1914) argues that 'significant form' — relations of line and color — is what makes anything art, whatever its subject. Critics say it leaves out the content and meaning that clearly matter to viewers.

question: Show a sunset to a thousand strangers and nearly all call it beautiful — yet a rock's weight is the same unseen. Sara says beauty lives in that wide agreement. Which view is that?
answer: Shared-response — beauty rests on reactions most people share.
choices: Shared-response — beauty rests on reactions most people share.
Realism — beauty sits in the object, no viewer needed.
Subjectivism — 'beautiful' only means it pleases me alone.
Relativism — only your own culture's rules decide it.
context: The response-dependent view is a middle path: beauty is neither in objects alone nor in lone viewers, but in where shared human sensibilities meet the world. Building on Hume, it fits modern cognitive science, which finds wide agreement on basic responses.

question: Aristotle said our oldest delight in art is RECOGNITION — we point at a drawing and cry 'that's a dog!', the fur so sharp you could almost touch it. Which view of art is that?
answer: Imitation — it is good if it depicts reality skillfully.
choices: Imitation — it is good if it depicts reality skillfully.
Formalism — only line, color, and shape decide it.
Expressionism — it is good if it carries real feeling.
Convention — it counts because people long agreed it does.
context: The imitative (mimetic) theory goes back to Plato and Aristotle; Aristotle's Poetics treats skillful likeness — and the recognition it sparks — as a real, natural human pleasure tied to learning. Critics ask how abstract or non-representational art could ever count as good under it.

question: In 1917 a urinal signed 'R. Mutt' was entered in an art show as sculpture. The committee split — some said it was art simply because the art world chose to treat it so. Which view is that?
answer: Convention view — art is whatever shared practice treats as art.
choices: Convention view — art is whatever shared practice treats as art.
Realist view — real craft makes a work art, agree or not.
Subjectivist view — 'art' just means 'I happen to like it.'
Feeling view — art is whatever carries deep emotion.
context: The piece was Marcel Duchamp's 'Fountain.' Convention (institutional) theory, sharpened by George Dickie, grounds the standard in what the 'artworld' settles on. Realists answer that conventions can drift far from real craft; subjectivists deny any shared standard at all.

question: A teacher shows the Beethoven stacks four melodies while the pop tune loops one chord. 'The structure is really on the page,' she says, 'not just in your mood.' Which view is that?
answer: Realist view — real structure in the writing makes it better.
choices: Realist view — real structure in the writing makes it better.
Subjectivist view — 'deeper' just means 'it impressed me.'
Feeling view — deeper means it stirs stronger emotion in you.
Convention view — deep is whatever people came to call deep.
context: Aesthetic realists hold that complexity and structure are real, tractable features of the work itself — countable on the page — not merely the listener's impression. The standing objection: the same listener can hear depth one year and shallowness the next.

question: Two friends argue an hour over whether a painting is a masterpiece. Nora shrugs: 'There's no fact to settle — calling it great just announces our own taste.' Which view is that?
answer: Subjectivist view — 'masterpiece' only reports what I like.
choices: Subjectivist view — 'masterpiece' only reports what I like.
Realist view — real craft makes it great, noticed or not.
Form view — great means its shapes are balanced and whole.
Likeness view — great means it depicts its subject truly.
context: Strict subjectivism collapses an art claim into a report on the speaker. The puzzle it leaves sits right there in the scene: the two argued for an hour, which is strange behavior if there is truly nothing being argued about beyond private feeling.

question: Late in life Tolstoy dismissed even his own great novels: art counts, he argued, only when real feeling passes from maker to audience — the way a sad song makes you cry. Which view is that?
answer: Feeling view — art works by passing real emotion to you.
choices: Feeling view — art works by passing real emotion to you.
Form view — what matters is how the parts fit, not feeling.
Likeness view — art is good when it depicts something well.
Subjectivist view — 'good' just means 'I happen to like it.'
context: In What Is Art? (1897), Tolstoy made shared feeling the heart of art — a work counts only when genuine emotion 'infects' the audience, passing from artist to viewer (Collingwood later refined the view). Critics ask whether a beautiful but cold piece can still be great.

question: Before a sculpture that depicts nothing at all, the critic Clive Bell calls its power pure 'significant form' — the curves and lines simply balance and stir us. Which view is Bell using?
answer: Form view — balanced shape is beautiful on its own.
choices: Form view — balanced shape is beautiful on its own.
Likeness view — art is good when it depicts a real thing.
Feeling view — art is good when it carries real emotion.
Subjectivist view — 'beautiful' only reports what I like.
context: Clive Bell coined 'significant form' (Art, 1914) for the arrangement of line and shape that gives art its power, regardless of subject. Formalists prize abstract sculpture; critics ask whether form alone can carry meaning with no tie to content.

question: Hume argues: beauty is no weight you can measure in a thing, yet no private dream either — humans share eyes and brains, so we mostly agree on what moves us. Which view is this?
answer: Shared-response view — beauty tracks how humans react alike.
choices: Shared-response view — beauty tracks how humans react alike.
Realist view — beauty sits in the object, viewer or not.
Form view — beauty is just shapes and lines fitting well.
Likeness view — beauty means it depicts a real thing truly.
context: In 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), Hume treats beauty like color: real and shareable, but only because creatures like us perceive a certain way. Some cognitive research finds wide cross-cultural agreement on many basic aesthetic responses, fitting the picture.

question: Before a Roman bust that keeps every wart and wrinkle, a senator tells his nephew: 'The sculptor caught his face truly — that skill at real likeness is what makes art good.' Which view is that?
answer: Likeness view — art is good when it depicts reality well.
choices: Likeness view — art is good when it depicts reality well.
Form view — balanced shape is good, likeness or not.
Feeling view — art is good when it carries real emotion.
Culture view — each tradition decides what good art is.
context: Aristotle's Poetics treated mimesis (imitation) as a deep human pleasure: we delight in a skilled likeness even of unpleasant things. Roman verist busts are this view at its most committed — every wart preserved. Modern philosophers ask whether photography threatens the theory.

question: Hannah travels widely: a scale that sounds gorgeous in one land sounds strange in the next. She decides beauty has no single right answer. Which view fits her?
answer: Cultural standard — beauty is whatever a tradition counts as beauty.
choices: Cultural standard — beauty is whatever a tradition counts as beauty.
Real quality — craft and structure make a work beautiful for anyone.
Personal taste — 'beautiful' just reports what one listener likes.
Shared human ear — people everywhere hear beauty much the same.
context: Cultural relativism in aesthetics points to musical scales, color values, and bodily ideals that differ widely by tradition. The counter: people often come to love foreign art deeply, which suggests standards may not be wholly sealed off from one another.

question: Wes hears his friend's rough homemade song. 'It's not slick, but you can hear he really MEANT it — that honest feeling is what makes music count.' Which view fits him?
answer: Felt expression — what counts is the genuine feeling the work conveys.
choices: Felt expression — what counts is the genuine feeling the work conveys.
Polished craft — skilled structure and technique make music good.
Pure form — the pattern of melody and rhythm alone makes music good.
Group agreement — good is what musicians settle on over time.
context: This is expressionism: R.G. Collingwood (Principles of Art, 1938) argued real art clarifies an emotion the artist genuinely had and passes it to the audience. Critics ask whether a polished work with little feeling can still be great — most listeners think it plainly can.

question: Jordan's brother loves silly cartoons others mock. 'Whatever YOU like is good,' she tells him — 'that's all 'good' really means in art.' Which view fits her?
answer: Personal taste — 'good art' just means the art you happen to enjoy.
choices: Personal taste — 'good art' just means the art you happen to enjoy.
Real quality — craft and structure make some works better than others.
Cultural standard — good is whatever your tradition counts as good.
Shared response — beauty tracks what humans feel, not one person.
context: Subjectivism is the most permissive view, but the hardest to square with how we actually argue about art. If 'good' meant only 'I like it,' two friends would have nothing to disagree about — yet they plainly do, and treat the dispute as real.

question: Eli stands under a stained-glass window. 'Forget what it shows,' he says. 'The way the colors and shapes balance — THAT makes it gorgeous.' Which view fits him?
answer: Pure form — the arrangement of color and shape is what makes it good.
choices: Pure form — the arrangement of color and shape is what makes it good.
True likeness — art is good when it skillfully depicts something real.
Felt expression — art is good for the feeling it stirs, not design.
Group agreement — good is what people settled on over time.
context: This is formalism: Clive Bell (Art, 1914) coined 'significant form' for the arrangement of line and color that gives art its power, regardless of subject. It explains abstract and decorative art well; critics say it leaves out meaning that clearly matters to viewers.

question: Marcus says the Homer lines that gripped readers 2,500 years ago still grip us. 'The pacing, the word choice — those are really better, not just opinion.' Which view fits him?
answer: Real quality — craft like pacing and word choice makes a story better.
choices: Real quality — craft like pacing and word choice makes a story better.
Personal taste — 'better written' just reports what a reader enjoys.
Cultural standard — good writing is whatever a tradition counts good.
Shared response — good writing is what readers everywhere feel.
context: Aesthetic realists about writing point to broadly stable judgments — readers across centuries still find Homer powerful. Skeptics note that conventions of 'good prose' have shifted enormously; today's plain style would have shocked a Victorian reader.

question: Dad explains why nearly every kid hums the same nursery tune: 'It isn't random, and it isn't in the notes alone — we just hear a few intervals the same way.' Which view fits him?
answer: Shared human ear — beauty tracks how people hear, not the notes alone.
choices: Shared human ear — beauty tracks how people hear, not the notes alone.
In the sound — beauty sits in the notes, listener or not.
Personal taste — 'catchy' just reports what one listener likes.
Cultural standard — catchy is whatever a tradition counts catchy.
context: The response-dependent view fits music psychology well: octave equivalence, consonance preferences, and basic rhythmic responses are broadly cross-cultural, even where scales differ. Realists (beauty is in the sound) and relativists each push back.

question: At the guild meeting Maya defends her favorite song: 'It's not just that I like it more — the writing, the structure, the way the bridge builds, those are real reasons it's better.' Which view fits her?
answer: Real quality — craft and structure make a work genuinely better, beyond taste.
choices: Real quality — craft and structure make a work genuinely better, beyond taste.
Personal taste — 'better' just means it pleases her; no fact beyond that.
Cultural standard — quality is whatever her community happens to prize.
Felt expression — what counts is the honest feeling it conveys, not the craft.
context: Aesthetic realism holds that artworks have real qualities — craft, structure, originality — beyond personal taste. Critics press: how do we settle disagreements? Hume's 1757 essay 'Of the Standard of Taste' offers a middle path: trained judges converge on real merit even as taste varies.

question: Devon hates his friends' favourite band and shrugs: 'There's no fact about whether a band is good. "Better" just means it pleases YOU more.' If Devon is right, what follows?
answer: Then nobody is ever mistaken about a band - each person's liking settles it.
choices: Then nobody is ever mistaken about a band - each person's liking settles it.
Then the band's real skill makes it good, whatever Devon happens to feel.
Then whatever the local music scene praises is what counts as good.
Then trained reviewers, who've heard thousands of records, can prove him wrong.
context: Devon's view is aesthetic subjectivism: a 'better' claim only reports the speaker's reaction, not a feature of the music. Its sharpest cost is the one the answer names - if liking is all there is, no one can be wrong, and a beginner's verdict weighs as much as an expert's. Hume ('Of the Standard of Taste,' 1757) pressed exactly that worry.

question: Her cousin laughs at last decade's fashion photos. Priya says: 'Cool isn't a fact about the jacket - it's a fact about the crowd. Whatever the people around you call good-looking just IS.' If she's right?
answer: Then the jacket was cool then and uncool now - both true, each for its crowd.
choices: Then the jacket was cool then and uncool now - both true, each for its crowd.
Then the jacket's cut and stitching never changed, so its quality can't flip.
Then it only ever mattered whether Priya herself liked wearing the jacket.
Then a trained eye could overrule the whole crowd and rank the jacket fairly.
context: Priya holds cultural relativism about taste: the standard lives inside a community, not in the object or the lone viewer - so a verdict can flip when the crowd changes. Critics (Hume, 1757) note that trained judges from very different cultures sometimes land on the same works, which pure relativism struggles to explain.

question: In 'Of the Standard of Taste,' Hume tells of two wine-tasters mocked for swearing a cask tasted of leather and iron - then a key on a leather thong turned up at the bottom. Hume's point about taste?
answer: Trained judges, with wide experience, land on real merit as casual taste varies.
choices: Trained judges, with wide experience, land on real merit as casual taste varies.
'Good' only reports your own reaction; no merit beyond what pleases you.
Whatever the local crowd happens to praise is exactly what counts as good.
No verdict can be settled, since every standard rests on an untested one.
context: Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) borrows the wine-and-key tale from Cervantes' Don Quixote: a delicate palate detects something genuinely in the cask. So with art - individual taste varies, but 'true judges' (wide experience, fine discrimination, fair temperament) converge on works of real merit, sidestepping both flat subjectivism and pure realism.

question: Late in life Tolstoy wrote 'What Is Art?': a work is art only if real FEELING passes from maker to audience - and on that test he dismissed even his own Anna Karenina as mere craft. Where is art's value?
answer: In the feeling the work transmits - skilled technique with no emotion isn't art.
choices: In the feeling the work transmits - skilled technique with no emotion isn't art.
In the arrangement of its parts - how shape, balance and pattern fit together.
In plain craftsmanship - a work is art if it's skilfully made, feelings aside.
In your own reaction - 'good' just reports what happens to please you.
context: This is expressionism (Tolstoy, 'What Is Art?', 1897-98; also Collingwood): art succeeds when felt experience 'infects' the audience, so technique without that transmission falls short. After his late conversion Tolstoy really did renounce Anna Karenina and War and Peace as bad art. Formalists (Bell, 1914) disagree - structure alone can carry the value.

question: Clive Bell pointed at a Persian carpet with a bold claim: its pure pattern of lines and colours can move you MORE than a sentimental portrait - subject matter is beside the point. Where is beauty?
answer: In the arrangement of parts - the shape and pattern, seen for how they fit.
choices: In the arrangement of parts - the shape and pattern, seen for how they fit.
In the feeling it stirs - value comes from emotion passing to the viewer.
In its plain craftsmanship - the skill it took to make, beauty aside.
In your own reaction - 'good' just reports what happens to please you.
context: This is formalism - Clive Bell's 'significant form' (Art, 1914): aesthetic value lives in structure (shape, balance, pattern) and the satisfaction of seeing how the parts fit, with representation irrelevant. Bell really did rank a patterned carpet above a sentimental portrait. Expressionists object that form with no felt content is empty.

question: Reading the art-show winners, Owen rolls his eyes: 'You can't settle which painting is best. Every reason leans on an earlier idea of good - and that on another, with no bottom.' Which view is Owen taking?
answer: No verdict can be settled - each standard just leans on another, no bottom.
choices: No verdict can be settled - each standard just leans on another, no bottom.
'Best' only reports what YOU like most; no fact beyond your reaction.
'Best' is whatever the local crowd crowns - the standard lives in the scene.
Some paintings really are better-made, full stop - the merit is there to find.
context: Owen's view is aesthetic skepticism: no aesthetic claim can be settled, because any standard you appeal to needs its own defense, and so on without end. Critics reply that the same regress would threaten all reasoning. Hume (1757) offers a practical, defeasible answer instead: the convergence of trained judges.

question: Gazing up at his rival Brunelleschi's vast Florence dome, a master mason concedes: 'Not what I'd have built. But the proportions, the spring of the ribs - real strengths, noticed or not.' Where is the value?
answer: In the work's real qualities - strengths it has whether or not anyone notices.
choices: In the work's real qualities - strengths it has whether or not anyone notices.
In the mason's response - 'strong' just reports what pleases the one looking.
In whatever the builders' guild votes best this year - the standard is theirs.
In how long it stands - good building just means whatever lasts the longest.
context: The mason's view is aesthetic realism: a work carries real merits (craft, structure, proportion) independent of any viewer's response. Critics press how a merit could be 'there' unperceived. Brunelleschi's dome (Florence, finished 1436) is the real marvel here - raised without external scaffolding, its proportions admired ever since.

question: Two scholars stand over a flawless ruby sealed in a tomb no eye will ever open. One says: 'Its fire, its symmetry — the beauty is IN the stone. It stays beautiful even sealed here unseen forever.' Which view fits her reasoning?
answer: Beauty is in the object — its features, viewer or not.
choices: Beauty is in the object — its features, viewer or not.
Beauty is a feeling in the viewer — no viewer, none.
Beauty is the fit between object and a trained eye.
Beauty is whatever a crowd agrees to praise.
context: The first scholar takes beauty to be a real property of the ruby itself. The rival view (Hume, Kant) reads beauty as a response in the viewer; relational views split the difference, calling beauty the fit between an object's features and a prepared eye.

question: The second scholar shakes her head: 'A ruby walled in a tomb where no one will ever stand isn't beautiful. Beauty needs someone to FEEL it. Sealed away unseen, it's only cold stone.' Which view fits her reasoning?
answer: Beauty is a feeling in the viewer — no viewer, none.
choices: Beauty is a feeling in the viewer — no viewer, none.
Beauty is in the object — its features, viewer or not.
Beauty is the fit between object and a trained eye.
Beauty is whatever a crowd agrees to praise.
context: This scholar makes beauty a response in the viewer — the modern line from Hume's 'Standard of Taste' (1757) through Kant's 'Critique of Judgement' (1790). On this view beauty isn't free-standing; it arises only when an object meets a perceiver.

question: An abbot praises the bare geometry of his Norman chapter house: 'It pictures nothing — yet the rhythm of the columns and balance of the bays is where the beauty lives. The arrangement IS the point.' Which view fits his reasoning?
answer: Formalism — the value is in how the parts are arranged.
choices: Formalism — the value is in how the parts are arranged.
Expressionism — the value is in the feeling it carries.
Realism — the value is in how truly it pictures the world.
Subjectivism — 'beautiful' just reports what pleases you.
context: Formalism (Clive Bell's 'significant form,' 1914) locates value in the arrangement of parts — shape, balance, proportion. Romanesque architecture is a textbook case: austere, rhythmic, regularly proportioned. Expressionists object that form without felt content is hollow.

question: Tolstoy stunned his friends by ranking a simple peasant song above Beethoven: 'When it lands, you FEEL exactly what the singer felt. Carrying that feeling between people is what makes real art.' Which view fits his reasoning?
answer: Expressionism — the value is in the feeling it carries.
choices: Expressionism — the value is in the feeling it carries.
Formalism — the value is in how the parts are arranged.
Realism — the value is in how truly it pictures the world.
Subjectivism — 'better' just reports what pleases you.
context: In 'What Is Art?' (1897) Tolstoy held art succeeds when felt experience passes from artist to audience — and really did rank a sincere peasant song above a Beethoven sonata on that test. Collingwood later built on the expression tradition. Formalists reply that structure, not feeling, carries the value.

question: A Mongol envoy calls a Florentine fresco 'flat and pious.' The host replies: 'You weren't raised in the tradition that taught us to see it. Great painting is judged from inside a tradition — and yours isn't ours.' Which view fits his reasoning?
answer: Relativism — each tradition sets its own standard.
choices: Relativism — each tradition sets its own standard.
Subjectivism — quality is just what pleases one viewer.
Realism — real craft makes a work good in any tradition.
Skepticism — no judgment of quality can be settled.
context: Cultural relativism in aesthetics holds standards live inside communities and traditions, capturing real variation in what cultures prize. Critics (Hume, 1757) reply that some convergence DOES happen across cultures over time, suggesting the standards aren't purely local.

question: An apprentice illuminator finds her abbey's prized Book of Hours dull. Her teacher answers: 'Generations of careful eyes rank it among the greatest. Maybe trained vision sees what yours misses.' Which view is the teacher using?
answer: Trained judges converge on merit, though raw taste varies.
choices: Trained judges converge on merit, though raw taste varies.
Quality is just whatever pleases an individual viewer.
Each tradition picks its own favorites — no shared standard.
No judgment of quality can ever be settled at all.
context: This is Hume's 'Standard of Taste' (1757): trained, attentive observers across time are the practical standard. Personal taste varies widely; trained taste varies far less. It explains why some works survive critically for centuries without collapsing into pure objectivism.

question: Defending Dante, an apprentice scribe insists: 'It is not just MY enthusiasm. The Comedy's plotting, the precision of every line — these are real strengths the poem has, whether a reader notices or not.' Which view fits his reasoning?
answer: Realism — the strengths are real whether anyone sees them or not.
choices: Realism — the strengths are real whether anyone sees them or not.
Subjectivism — 'better' just reports what pleases you.
Conventionalism — trained judges converge, raw taste varies.
Skepticism — no judgment of quality can ever be settled.
context: Aesthetic realism holds works carry real merits and demerits independent of any reader's response. Critics ask how a merit could be 'there' if no one perceived it. Hume (1757) routes around the worry: convergent trained judgment is the practical mark of real quality.

question: Settling a fashion debate, Sara says: 'Beauty isn't purely in the outfit, and not purely how I feel. It's the FIT - between real features of the outfit and an eye trained to see them.' Which view is Sara using?
answer: Relational - beauty is the fit between an object and a prepared viewer.
choices: Relational - beauty is the fit between an object and a prepared viewer.
In the object - beauty is a real feature, viewer or no viewer.
In the viewer - beauty is just the feeling it stirs in you.
In the crowd - beauty is whatever the people around you praise.
context: Relational views of beauty (developing the response-side theories of Hume and Kant) locate beauty in the meeting of an object's features with a viewer prepared to perceive them - neither in the thing alone nor in the lone observer. Serious philosophers split between these camps, so the bank attributes the view to Sara rather than crowning a winner.

question: Two herald-painters argue over a banner. One shrugs: 'Striking to me, garish to you - end of story. No fact underneath makes either of us right or wrong. Only our two reactions.' Which view is the herald using?
answer: Subjectivism - 'beautiful' just reports how it strikes you.
choices: Subjectivism - 'beautiful' just reports how it strikes you.
Relativism - beauty is whatever your community happens to prize.
Realism - real qualities make the banner good or bad.
Trained-taste - skilled judges converge on what's truly good.
context: Subjectivism reduces 'beautiful' or 'ugly' to a report on the speaker's own response - no shared fact lies beneath. It is simple and dodges hard metaphysics. Critics (Hume, 1757) ask why we then argue about art at all, and why a trained reviewer's verdict seems to count for more. The bank attributes the view rather than declaring it correct.

question: Her brother calls the Bach fugue 'dry math.' The apprentice answers: 'Hear how the voices weave - answer against subject, each entry shifting the texture. Arrangement IS the point.' Which view is she using?
answer: Formalism - value lives in how the parts are arranged.
choices: Formalism - value lives in how the parts are arranged.
Expressionism - value lives in the feeling it carries.
Realism - value lives in how truly it depicts the world.
Subjectivism - value is just whatever pleases the listener.
context: Formalism (Clive Bell, 'significant form,' 1914) locates value in the arrangement of parts - shape, balance, the play of voices. Counterpoint like Bach's is a natural fit. Expressionists object that fugues carry an emotional weight Bell undervalues. The bank attributes the view to the apprentice rather than settling the dispute.

question: A tutor calls an eastern caliphate song 'not real music.' The minstrel answers: 'This is how our people have always heard it - our scale, our tradition, our standard.' Which view is the minstrel using?
answer: Relativism - the standard is set inside each tradition.
choices: Relativism - the standard is set inside each tradition.
Subjectivism - 'good' just reports one listener's taste.
Realism - real qualities make the song good or bad.
Trained-taste - skilled judges converge across traditions.
context: Cultural relativism treats aesthetic standards as community-relative - set by 'our people,' not one listener. Music is a strong test case: tunings, scales, and rhythms vary widely between traditions. Critics still ask whether trained cross-cultural ears converge on quality more than naive ones - a Humean pressure on the relativist. The bank attributes the view rather than endorsing it.

question: The captain of the lists rules on a banner: 'Heralds who have judged thousands agree which banners are strong. Their agreement isn't proof, but it's the surest sign of merit.' Which view is the captain using?
answer: Trained-taste - expert agreement is our best evidence of merit.
choices: Trained-taste - expert agreement is our best evidence of merit.
Realism - merit sits in the banner, judges or no judges.
Subjectivism - 'strong' just reports one herald's own taste.
Relativism - merit is whatever a tradition happens to prize.
context: Hume's 'Standard of Taste' (1757) treats convergent skilled judgment as the practical mark of merit. The senior heralds play the role Hume gives skilled critics: wide exposure, careful attention, fair temperament. The view sits between subjectivism and pure realism - agreement is evidence, not proof, and not what makes the banner good. The bank attributes it rather than crowning it.

question: A reviewer compares two films: the first masterful but emotionally hollow, the second rough but deeply moving. She rules: 'The second is better - technique with no feeling behind it is just empty craft.' Which view of art's value is she using?
answer: Expressionism - value is the feeling carried from artist to audience.
choices: Expressionism - value is the feeling carried from artist to audience.
Formalism - value is the pattern, and feeling is beside the point.
Realism - value is how truly the film depicts the real world.
Institutional - value is whatever the artworld decides to honor.
context: Expressionism (Tolstoy, What Is Art? 1897; Croce 1902; Collingwood 1938) holds that art transmits feeling from artist to audience; without that transmission, only craft remains. Formalism - value is in the pattern - is its main twentieth-century rival. Both are live positions, so the bank attributes the view to the reviewer rather than declaring a winner.

question: A monastery chronicler reviews an abstract painting: 'Forget what it represents, or what the painter felt. The arrangement of line and color does the work - that pattern is what makes it valuable.' Which view of art's value is she using?
answer: Formalism - value is the arrangement of line, color, and shape.
choices: Formalism - value is the arrangement of line, color, and shape.
Expressionism - value is the feeling the work transmits to you.
Realism - value is how truly the work depicts the real world.
Cognitivism - value is the knowledge the work gives about life.
context: Formalism is most associated with Clive Bell (Art, 1914), who coined 'significant form,' and Roger Fry. The view emerged partly to defend abstract and non-representational art from the charge of emptiness: pattern itself, attended to, is what matters. Rivals insist feeling or knowledge must come in too - so the bank attributes the view rather than settling it.

question: By the 1800s the camera could copy a face or a valley more exactly than any painter's hand. Yet painters did not quit. For the view that art's whole worth is faithful copying, what did the camera expose?
answer: That copying can't be the whole point, since the better copier did not replace painters.
choices: That copying can't be the whole point, since the better copier did not replace painters.
That a photograph is simply a newer, higher kind of painting we now prefer.
That all the centuries of painting before it had been wasted skilled effort.
That a picture counts as real art only once a machine has produced it.
context: The view that art's value is mimesis (faithful imitation) traces to Plato and Aristotle's Poetics (~335 BC) and ruled Western aesthetics for centuries. Photography and, later, abstract art forced its revision: if a camera copies better, copying cannot be what painting was for.

question: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp bought a plain factory urinal, signed it 'R. Mutt', titled it 'Fountain', and submitted it to an art show. No carving, no painting, no skill. On what does its claim to be ART actually rest?
answer: On the artworld choosing to exhibit and discuss it as a work worth appreciating.
choices: On the artworld choosing to exhibit and discuss it as a work worth appreciating.
On the years of craft and skill the maker put into shaping the object.
On the genuine beauty of the object's smooth curves and porcelain surface.
On the deep private feelings the maker poured into the act of making it.
context: Duchamp's 'Fountain' is the textbook case for the institutional theory of art (George Dickie, 1974): nothing visible in the object makes it art -- its status is conferred when galleries, critics, and the artworld treat it as a candidate for appreciation.

question: Two friends stand before Michelangelo's David. One calls it truly beautiful. The other answers: 'It only SEEMS so to you -- there's no beauty in the marble itself, only the feeling it stirs in whoever looks.' Which view is the second friend using?
answer: Beauty lives in the viewer -- 'beautiful' just names the feeling a thing stirs.
choices: Beauty lives in the viewer -- 'beautiful' just names the feeling a thing stirs.
Beauty lives in the marble -- a real feature the statue has on its very own.
Beauty is simply whatever one's own culture has been raised up to praise.
Beauty is the sculptor's own feeling carried over into the shaped stone.
context: The second friend defends subjectivism about beauty -- 'in the eye of the beholder' -- which locates aesthetic value in the viewer's response, not in the object. Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) is the classic middle path: response-based, yet trained judges converge on merit.

question: A critic notes that across four centuries, trained judges keep returning to the same masters -- Shakespeare, Bach, Rembrandt -- while passing fads fade. That lasting agreement, she says, is our best sign of real merit. Which view is she using?
answer: Trained judges converge -- their lasting agreement is the best evidence of merit.
choices: Trained judges converge -- their lasting agreement is the best evidence of merit.
Beauty is in the viewer -- an expert's reaction counts no more than a novice's.
Merit is nothing more than whatever a culture happens to keep on praising.
Merit is a plain feature sitting in the work, needing no judges at all to see.
context: This is Hume's standard of taste ('Of the Standard of Taste', 1757). Hume grants that taste varies, yet argues that qualified critics -- practiced, comparative, free of prejudice -- converge over time, and their lasting consensus is the working standard of beauty.

question: A reader argues that Crime and Punishment hands you what no report could: what it truly feels like to carry a murderer's guilt. Its worth, she says, is the real understanding of a life unlike your own. Which view of art's value is she using?
answer: Its worth is the real knowledge of human experience it gives that nothing else can.
choices: Its worth is the real knowledge of human experience it gives that nothing else can.
Its worth is the strong feeling it manages to pass from the maker across to you.
Its worth is the pleasing pattern and structure formed by its arranged parts.
Its worth is nothing more than whatever raw reaction it happens to stir in you.
context: She defends cognitivism about art (Nelson Goodman, 1968; Martha Nussbaum, Love's Knowledge, 1990): art is a serious source of knowledge. Dostoevsky's novel can teach the texture of a life you could never live -- an understanding the sciences, by their nature, cannot supply.

question: A classmate shrugs that a scribble is 'as good as a Vermeer if you like it.' The reviewer objects: its brush control and composition are real qualities -- liking cannot make them appear, nor disliking erase them. Which view is the reviewer using?
answer: Quality is real in the work itself -- the craft is there whether or not you like it.
choices: Quality is real in the work itself -- the craft is there whether or not you like it.
'Better' only ever means 'pleases me more' -- there is no quality past liking.
Quality is nothing more than what a given culture has agreed to call quality.
Quality gets settled only by trained expert judges slowly agreeing over time.
context: The reviewer takes the aesthetic realist line: works have mind-independent, value-relevant qualities -- craft, structure, control -- that liking neither creates nor destroys. Subjectivism reduces 'better' to 'more pleasing to me'; Hume carves a middle path through converging trained judges.

question: Ridley Scott says his Blade Runner hero Deckard is secretly a replicant; many fans insist the film stays open. Scott argues: 'I BUILT the meaning in -- what the maker intended is part of what the work says.' Which view is he using?
answer: The maker's intention helps fix the meaning -- ignore it and you misread the work.
choices: The maker's intention helps fix the meaning -- ignore it and you misread the work.
Only the finished film on the screen counts -- the maker's aims are just biography.
Meaning is whatever each single viewer makes of it -- every reading is equally valid.
Meaning is simply whatever the critics and the wider artworld agree to accept.
context: This is the author-intent view (Richard Wollheim, 1987; Jerrold Levinson): the maker's intention partly constitutes a work's meaning. The opposing classic is Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'intentional fallacy' (1946) -- that only the work itself, never the author's aim, is the proper object of reading.

question: A gallery hangs two identical-looking paintings: one a painter's months of labor, one a machine's random output. A critic shrugs: 'If your eyes can't tell them apart, they're equally good art. Who made it is just backstory.' Which view is he using?
answer: Empiricism — only what you can see in the work counts; the rest is backstory.
choices: Empiricism — only what you can see in the work counts; the rest is backstory.
Intentionalism — what the maker meant is part of what the work actually is.
Institutional theory — art is whatever the gallery and critics crown as art.
Cognitivism — a work's worth is the real insight it manages to teach you.
context: Aesthetic empiricism (Monroe Beardsley, 1958) holds the work just is what the viewer perceives; the maker's intention is biography, not part of the art. The AI-art debate sharpens it: if two images look identical, does it matter that one was made on purpose? Intentionalists (Wollheim, Levinson) say yes.

question: In 1917 a gallery rejected Duchamp's signed urinal 'Fountain'; a museum now enshrines it. A critic shrugs: 'Same object, different verdict. Art has no fixed essence — just the customs a society builds, and customs change.' Which view is he using?
answer: Convention — art is a social custom, so it shifts as the customs shift.
choices: Convention — art is a social custom, so it shifts as the customs shift.
Realism (mimesis) — art is a faithful copy of how the world really looks.
Expressionism — art is one person's feeling passed on to another.
Formalism — art is shape and color that please the eye on their own.
context: Convention theory holds art is a rule-governed practice with no fixed essence — what counts shifts culture to culture. Duchamp's 'Fountain' (1917), spurned then canonized, is the stock case. The view overlaps Dickie's institutional theory but stresses the custom itself over any act of conferral; Wittgenstein's 'family resemblance' (1953) lies behind both.

question: A wartime propaganda poster makes a debate captain reflect, argue, and rethink her values. She says: 'It did everything art does. Don't ask what a thing is made of — if it does art's job, that's what makes it art.' Which view is she using?
answer: Functionalism — art is whatever does art's job, not what it's made of.
choices: Functionalism — art is whatever does art's job, not what it's made of.
Institutional theory — art is whatever the galleries and critics crown.
Intentionalism — art is fixed by what the maker meant to do.
Formalism — art is shape and color arranged to please the eye.
context: Functionalism defines art by what it does (provoking reflection, refining taste, passing on culture) rather than by any built-in trait or stamp of approval. The standard worry is exactly this scene: advertising and propaganda do those jobs too, yet we hesitate to call them art.

question: Leni Riefenstahl's 'Triumph of the Will' is dazzling filmmaking — and a worshipful advertisement for the Nazi party. A critic argues: 'The cruelty it glorifies isn't only a moral stain. It makes the film worse AS art.' Which view is she using?
answer: Moralism — a moral flaw in a work is also a flaw in it as art.
choices: Moralism — a moral flaw in a work is also a flaw in it as art.
Autonomism — art and morality are judged on wholly separate scales.
Formalism — only craft and form decide a work's worth as art.
Empiricism — only what the viewer perceives fixes the work's value.
context: Ethical criticism of art holds a moral defect can be an aesthetic defect — a work that wins you to cruelty fails partly as art. Berys Gaut's ethicism (1998) makes the strong, universal claim; Noel Carroll's moderate moralism the weaker, sometimes-claim. Riefenstahl's 'Triumph of the Will' (1935) is the standard test case; autonomists reply that craft and morality never touch.

question: A second critic, watching Riefenstahl's 'Triumph of the Will,' disagrees: 'It can be vile and still be a masterpiece. Framing, pacing, performance settle whether it's GREAT film. Whether it's wicked is a separate question.' Which view is he using?
answer: Autonomism — a work's art and its morals sit on separate scales.
choices: Autonomism — a work's art and its morals sit on separate scales.
Moralism — a moral flaw in a work is also a flaw in it as art.
Cognitivism — a work's worth is the true insight it gives you.
Institutional theory — art is whatever the artworld crowns as art.
context: Autonomism holds the aesthetic and the moral are judged on separate scales — a film can be wicked yet brilliant. Strong autonomism (Beardsley) keeps them fully apart; moderate moralism (Carroll) and ethicism (Gaut) deny it. Propaganda masterpieces like 'Triumph of the Will' are the battleground.

question: A Banksy stencil appears overnight on a wall, then draws curated tours, reviews, and a gallery show. A debate captain says it's now real art: 'A serious art community took it up — that recognition is what makes a thing art.' Which view is she using?
answer: Institutional theory — recognition by the artworld is what makes it art.
choices: Institutional theory — recognition by the artworld is what makes it art.
Realism (mimesis) — art is a faithful copy of how the world looks.
Expressionism — art is one person's feeling carried to another.
Formalism — real skill and form, not applause, make a thing art.
context: Whether street art is art is a live test for the institutional theory (George Dickie, 1974): art is what qualified artworld members put forward for appreciation. As critics and galleries take a Banksy piece up, the theory predicts it becomes art — recognition does the work, not any built-in quality.

question: A critic stares at a blazing red sunset and says: "Strip away every viewer and you're left with just photons -- nothing beautiful. The beauty only happens when a trained eye meets these colors." Which view of beauty is she using?
answer: Response-dependent: beauty is a real relation between the colors and a trained eye.
choices: Response-dependent: beauty is a real relation between the colors and a trained eye.
Realist: the beauty sits in the sunset itself, there to be noticed or missed.
Subjectivist: beauty is just whatever any single person happens to like.
Formalist: beauty is pure pattern, the same with or without any viewer.
context: Response-dependent views (Hume; later John McDowell) place beauty neither purely 'in the object' (realism) nor merely 'in the eye' (subjectivism), but in a real relation between the work and a qualified observer. The critic's 'only when a trained eye meets it' line is the response-dependent move.

question: A slow, quiet Ozu drama bores a Hollywood action crowd, yet another culture reveres it as a peak of cinema. A critic argues: 'There's no neutral yardstick to rank them. Each culture's standards only hold inside its own frame.' Which view is he using?
answer: Cultural relativism — film standards only hold inside the culture that sets them.
choices: Cultural relativism — film standards only hold inside the culture that sets them.
Hume's standard — trained judges everywhere slowly converge on real merit.
Subjectivism — a film is good if it happens to please you, and that's all.
Institutional theory — art is whatever each culture's critics crown as art.
context: Cultural relativism about taste holds aesthetic standards are frame-relative — there's no view from nowhere to rank cultures by. Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) is the classic rival: trained judges across cultures converging is itself evidence that merit is real, not merely local.

question: A reader says Tolstoy's tale of Ivan Ilyich's slow dying taught her what death feels like from the inside, something no statistic about mortality could ever convey. Her friend asks what she thinks art is FOR. Which view of art's value is she using?
answer: Cognitivism — art hands you real knowledge of experience that facts cannot.
choices: Cognitivism — art hands you real knowledge of experience that facts cannot.
Expressionism — art passes feeling from maker to viewer, not knowledge.
Formalism — what matters is shape and structure, not what art teaches.
Subjectivism — art is worth just the reaction it happens to stir in you.
context: Cognitivism (Nelson Goodman, Languages of Art, 1968; Martha Nussbaum, Love's Knowledge, 1990) holds art is a real source of knowledge — especially the texture of lives a reader could never live, as Tolstoy's The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) hands you the inside of dying. Expressionism, its closest rival, says art transmits feeling rather than delivering knowledge.

question: In 1999 Tracey Emin showed My Bed at the Tate: her own unmade bed, stained sheets and floor litter, no craft applied. Critics debated it for the Turner Prize as art. A student says THAT debate is what makes it art. Which view of art is she using?
answer: Institutional theory — the artworld's recognition is what confers art-status.
choices: Institutional theory — the artworld's recognition is what confers art-status.
Aesthetic realism — only real craft and quality can make a thing art.
Expressionism — with no feeling to transmit, it isn't art at all.
Formalism — no striking form means no art, whatever a gallery says.
context: Institutional theory (George Dickie, Art and the Aesthetic, 1974) was built to handle readymades and found objects in the line Duchamp opened: artworld conferral, not any intrinsic property, makes art art. Emin's My Bed (Turner Prize shortlist, 1999) is a real test case. The three rivals here each DENY the object is art, demanding a different intrinsic quality — craft, expressed feeling, or significant form.

question: At a Jackson Pollock drip painting, a sibling says: 'Calling this great is not reporting a fact about it. It is just voicing your approval. Aesthetic talk does not describe a work; it cheers for one.' Which view of aesthetic judgment is she using?
answer: Non-cognitivism — aesthetic words voice attitudes, not facts.
choices: Non-cognitivism — aesthetic words voice attitudes, not facts.
Aesthetic realism — 'great' reports a real quality, true or false.
Ideal-critic view — 'great' means trained judges would agree.
Cognitivism — 'great' tracks the knowledge the work delivers.
context: Aesthetic non-cognitivism parallels ethical emotivism (A.J. Ayer, C.L. Stevenson): a judgment like 'great' expresses approval rather than stating a fact, so disagreement is a clash of attitude, not of accuracy. The ideal-critic rival descends from Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste,' where true judges converge. Critics note how hard non-cognitivism makes it to explain genuine aesthetic reasoning and argument.

question: In 1757 David Hume asked why critics across the centuries keep crowning the same masterpieces -- if beauty were private taste, why the agreement? His answer: beauty is what qualified judges converge on -- real, yet no trait you could measure on the canvas. Which view is that?
answer: Response-dependent: beauty is what qualified judges converge on, not a measurable trait.
choices: Response-dependent: beauty is what qualified judges converge on, not a measurable trait.
Realist: beauty is a fixed trait of the canvas, the same for every eye that looks.
Subjectivist: beauty is whatever each viewer privately likes, agreement or not.
Formalist: beauty is shared response to pure form, the judges set entirely aside.
context: Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) argues beauty is no quality in the object, yet not arbitrary either: it tracks the verdicts of qualified judges (delicate sense, practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice). Their convergence over time is evidence of a standard, not of a mind-independent property.

question: In 1790 Kant noticed something strange: a painting can move you with no stake in owning it, eating it, or using it -- yet you still expect everyone else to feel its pull too. He called that 'disinterested' pleasure that speaks with a universal voice. Which view fits that odd pair?
answer: Kantian: pleasure with no personal stake that still speaks with a universal voice.
choices: Kantian: pleasure with no personal stake that still speaks with a universal voice.
Hedonist: art is simply pleasure, like good food or owning fine things.
Subjectivist: the demand that others agree just masks your private taste.
Moralist: the real pull is the work's moral content, not any detachment.
context: Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) calls aesthetic judgment 'disinterested' pleasure (no stake in whether the thing exists) that still claims subjective universality -- the judge speaking 'with a universal voice.' That structure sets beauty apart from the merely agreeable (private) and the good (interested).

question: The Tate quietly bought a tidy stack of 120 firebricks as sculpture in 1972; when the press got wind in 1976, headlines howled "they're just bricks!" The curator's reply: an artworld figure presented them for appreciation, and that is what makes them art. Which view is that?
answer: Institutional: the artworld confers art status by presenting the object.
choices: Institutional: the artworld confers art status by presenting the object.
Aesthetic-experience: art is whatever rewards close, careful looking.
Imitative: art must skillfully represent some real thing in the world.
Expression: art must carry a genuine feeling pressed in by its maker.
context: George Dickie's institutional theory (Art and the Aesthetic, 1974) says a work is art when someone acting for the artworld confers candidate-for-appreciation status on it. Carl Andre's 'Equivalent VIII' (1966), the Tate firebricks, is the real test case; the public furor broke in 1976, four years after the quiet purchase. Critics call the account circular; defenders deny it.

question: In 1964 the philosopher Arthur Danto saw Warhol's 'Brillo Box' -- a plywood sculpture you could not tell apart from the grocery carton beside it. One was art, one was a shipping box. That puzzle launched his whole theory. Where did Danto say the difference lies?
answer: In theory and art history that interpret it, not in anything the eye can see.
choices: In theory and art history that interpret it, not in anything the eye can see.
In significant form, so two identical objects must rank equally as art.
In the experience it affords, which identical objects would supply alike.
In what it represents, and both depict Brillo, so neither counts as art.
context: Arthur Danto's 'The Artworld' (1964) and The Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981) argue art requires an 'atmosphere of theory' -- an interpretation placing the work in art history. The Brillo Box case shows two visually identical objects can hold different art statuses, so the eye alone cannot settle it.

question: In 1958 Monroe Beardsley pointed at a viewer who forgets the time before a canvas, feels its scattered parts suddenly lock into one, and is swept up whole. THAT, he said -- not its price or its pedigree -- is where a work's worth lives. Where does Beardsley locate the value of art?
answer: In the viewer's experience: how it absorbs, unifies, and grips attention.
choices: In the viewer's experience: how it absorbs, unifies, and grips attention.
In the artworld's say-so: status handed down by critics and curators.
In the artist's feeling: an emotion pressed into the finished work.
In the object's pure form: line, color, and composition alone.
context: Beardsley (Aesthetics, 1958) locates art's value in its power to produce experiences marked by unity, intensity, and complexity. Rivals (Dickie, Danto) object that some conceptual and minimalist art doesn't aim at experience in this sense at all, which is why the view is contested rather than settled.

question: Late in life Tolstoy -- author of War and Peace -- declared: "Art is the conscious passing of a feeling I already have on to you, through words or paint, so that you come to feel the very same thing." Which view of art is that?
answer: Transmission: handing an already-felt emotion across to the audience.
choices: Transmission: handing an already-felt emotion across to the audience.
Discovery: the artist finds out a murky feeling by making the work.
Formalism: value lies in the form; the feeling passed on is beside the point.
Institutional: art is whatever the artworld presents, feeling or not.
context: Tolstoy's What Is Art? (1897) defines art as the transmission of feeling: the artist evokes an emotion in herself, then expresses it so others feel the same. The rival 'discovery' view is R. G. Collingwood's (Principles of Art, 1938), where the artist clarifies a feeling she did not yet understand by making the work.

question: A composer says: 'I started with only a vague unease. The piece wasn't me sending a feeling I already had — it was how I FOUND OUT what I felt. The feeling became clear only as the work took shape.' Which view of art best fits how he describes it?
answer: Art clarifies a hazy feeling — the work is how the artist finds it.
choices: Art clarifies a hazy feeling — the work is how the artist finds it.
Art transmits a feeling the artist already knows to the audience.
Art exists to give the viewer a rich, intense experience.
Art is pure form — line and color — and feeling is beside it.
context: R. G. Collingwood (The Principles of Art, 1938) called this expressing emotion: clarifying a vague feeling into a clear one through the act of making. He set it against Tolstoy's view that art transmits an already-known feeling. On Collingwood's view the artist often doesn't know what she feels until the work exists.

question: The critic Clive Bell claimed a Byzantine icon and a Cezanne still life move us by the very same thing — and it is NOT their subjects. A painting of a saint and a painting of apples can share it. What did Bell say this shared source of art's power was?
answer: The arrangement of its lines, shapes, and colors — its form.
choices: The arrangement of its lines, shapes, and colors — its form.
The depth of feeling the artist poured into the work.
How skillfully the work imitates a real subject in the world.
The rich experience it stirs in an attentive viewer.
context: Clive Bell (Art, 1914) coined 'significant form' — the arrangement of lines and colors that stirs a special 'aesthetic emotion,' independent of subject. He held it cuts across all cultures and eras, which is why an icon and a still life can share it. Critics call the idea circular; modernists embraced it.

question: Edmund Burke noted something strange: a storm under a thousand-foot cliff fills you with awe, dread, AND a thrill all at once — he called this the sublime, not mere beauty. On Burke's account, which single condition turns that terror into delight rather than panic?
answer: You're safe — distance removes the real danger.
choices: You're safe — distance removes the real danger.
The scene is genuinely beautiful underneath the fear.
You fully understand the storm and how it works.
You believe a higher power is protecting you.
context: Edmund Burke (A Philosophical Enquiry, 1757) treated the sublime as a bodily response: vast power or magnitude is thrilling — 'delightful' — only when safety or distance removes the actual threat. Remove the safety and you get plain terror. He held the sublime is a category sharply distinct from beauty.

question: Kant gazes up at the night sky and says: 'I can't grasp the number of stars — my imagination fails. Yet that very failure summons in me the idea of the infinite. The awe is in THAT movement, not in the stars.' Where does Kant locate the sublime?
answer: In the mind — reason's idea of the infinite when imagination fails.
choices: In the mind — reason's idea of the infinite when imagination fails.
In the object — the stars truly carry the quality out there.
In safe terror — vast power felt from a secure distance.
In great writing — language that lifts and transports the reader.
context: In the Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790), Kant placed the sublime not in the object but in the mind: when imagination can't take in sheer magnitude, reason supplies the idea of the infinite, and the awe lives in that gap. This 'mathematical sublime' contrasts with Burke, who placed it in safely-felt terror.

question: A novel is praised for its gorgeous prose, but a critic objects: 'Its sneering contempt for its women is a flaw in the BOOK AS ART, not a separate moral gripe — the same callousness that shapes its sentences shapes its whole world.' Which view of art and morality is the critic taking?
answer: A moral flaw in a work can itself be an artistic flaw.
choices: A moral flaw in a work can itself be an artistic flaw.
A moral flaw never bears on a work's artistic worth.
A moral flaw can sometimes make a work better as art.
A work's worth is just the true understanding it gives us.
context: This is aesthetic moralism (Berys Gaut's 'ethicism,' 1998; Noel Carroll, 1996): because the attitudes shaping a work's morals also shape its imaginative texture, a moral defect can be an aesthetic defect. It opposes autonomism (morals and art are independent) and immoralism (a moral flaw can be an artistic merit).

question: A panelist argues: 'Whether a film GLORIFIES violence is a moral question. Whether it SUCCEEDS as cinema is a separate one. Mix them up and you praise bad films that preach well and trash good ones whose politics annoy you.' Which view of art and morality is the panelist taking?
answer: A work's moral message and its artistic worth are independent.
choices: A work's moral message and its artistic worth are independent.
A moral flaw in a work is itself an artistic flaw.
A moral flaw can sometimes make a work better as art.
A work's worth is just the true understanding it gives us.
context: This is strict autonomism, echoing Oscar Wilde ('There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book'); modern defenders include Richard Posner (1997). Moral and artistic value are judged separately. It opposes moralism (Gaut, Carroll), on which a moral defect can count as an artistic one.

question: A flawless forgery hangs beside the real Vermeer, and no eye can tell them apart YET. A collector says that settles it — identical-looking means equal as art. The philosopher Nelson Goodman disagreed. What was his reason they need NOT be equal?
answer: Knowing which is real can train the eye to spot differences not yet seen.
choices: Knowing which is real can train the eye to spot differences not yet seen.
The forgery is a lie, and a moral wrong drags down its art.
No gallery would call a known fake art, so it loses its status.
The real one is older, and age alone makes a painting worth more.
context: Nelson Goodman (Languages of Art, 1968) argued that knowing one painting is the original can teach a viewer to perceive differences not visible yet — so 'they look identical now' doesn't settle that they're equal as art. His point turns on perceptual learning, not on the forgery's dishonesty or its gallery status.

question: In 1946 two New Critics, William Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley, named a famous mistake: judging a poem by what its author meant to do rather than by what the words on the page actually achieve. On their view, what fixes a poem's meaning?
answer: The poem itself — its words on the page, not the poet's private aim.
choices: The poem itself — its words on the page, not the poet's private aim.
The poet — the meaning just is whatever she meant to say.
An ideal reader — what the words would mean to a perfect audience.
Each reader — the meaning forms fresh in whoever happens to read it.
context: Wimsatt and Beardsley called this 'the intentional fallacy': a poet's intention is neither reliably recoverable nor decisive — meaning lives in the words on the page. Rivals defend a role for intention: E. D. Hirsch (the author's actual aim) and Jerrold Levinson (what an ideal reader would credit the author with).

question: A conceptual artist exhibits only a signed certificate describing an idea — no object at all. 'Nothing to see!' a visitor scoffs. Curator Lila answers: 'The work is the proposal, placed inside art's ongoing story; the certificate is just its medium.' Which view is Lila using?
answer: Art's story decides — a thing is art if the art world's theory frames it so, object or not.
choices: Art's story decides — a thing is art if the art world's theory frames it so, object or not.
The eye decides — with no object to perceive, there is nothing here to call art.
Form decides — art needs lines and colors to arrange, which a certificate lacks.
Likeness decides — art must skillfully picture something, and this pictures nothing.
context: Arthur Danto ('The Artworld,' 1964) argued that what makes something art is an 'atmosphere of theory' and art-historical context, not how it looks — so a non-visual proposal can be art. Sol LeWitt's 'Paragraphs on Conceptual Art' (1967) and Lawrence Weiner's word-only Statements (1968) are real cases of art reduced to an idea.

question: Plato wanted poets thrown out of his ideal city: drama, he warned, just stirs up emotions that reason should rule. His pupil Aristotle answered in the Poetics, arguing the stage is exactly where such feelings can safely run their course. How did Aristotle say tragedy benefits its audience?
answer: It stirs up pity and fear, then works them through to a cleansing release.
choices: It stirs up pity and fear, then works them through to a cleansing release.
It copies real life so exactly the audience mistakes the play for reality.
It spells out morals plainly, the way a sermon or fable states its lesson.
It puts emotion aside and persuades the audience by cool reason alone.
context: In the Poetics (c. 335 BC) Aristotle calls this release katharsis — tragedy lets an audience feel pity and fear within safe bounds and come out steadier. It was his direct reply to his teacher Plato, who in Republic Book X wanted poets banished for feeding the passions. Their quarrel is the founding debate of Western aesthetics.

question: A critic argues: 'Milton's Satan is magnificent precisely because he is wicked — the menace a reader must push through is itself an achievement no tame, wholesome work could reach.' Which view of art and morality is the critic defending?
answer: A moral flaw can sometimes raise a work as art, not only lower it.
choices: A moral flaw can sometimes raise a work as art, not only lower it.
A moral flaw can only lower a work as art; it never raises it.
Moral worth and artistic worth stand apart; a flaw does neither.
Art's worth is the truth it teaches; a flaw just muddies that.
context: This is aesthetic immoralism, defended by A. W. Eaton ('Robust Immoralism,' 2012) and Matthew Kieran ('Forbidden Knowledge,' 2003): a work's moral defect can sometimes be the source of its power. It is the mirror image of Berys Gaut's ethicism, which holds that a moral flaw always counts against a work as art. Milton's grand, seductive Satan in Paradise Lost is the classic test case.

question: Two trained listeners clash over a Bach fugue — one calls the harmony glorious, the other cold — and Rinaldo says only one can be RIGHT: 'It's not a fact ABOUT us. The harmony is in the music, like a color in a wall — ears catch it or miss it.' Which view of beauty is Rinaldo defending?
answer: Beauty is in the work — a real feature our reactions try to track, and can get wrong.
choices: Beauty is in the work — a real feature our reactions try to track, and can get wrong.
Beauty is in our shared reaction — it holds only where trained viewers agree.
Beauty is just personal taste — no fact in the music, only what each ear likes.
Beauty is a feeling we demand others share — not a property of the work at all.
context: Aesthetic realism (Nick Zangwill, The Metaphysics of Beauty, 2001) holds beauty is a real feature of the work itself, which a competent response can catch or miss — so two trained listeners can disagree and at most one be right. The rivals deny that: response-dependent views (Hume) ground beauty in qualified observers' agreement, and Kant treats it as a felt judgment we expect others to share, not a property out there.

question: For fifty years a recluse filled notebooks with extraordinary drawings and showed no one. They are found only after her death. Critic Wim insists: 'These were art the whole time — the depth is in the works, whether or not anyone ever noticed.' Which view is Wim using?
answer: Art all along — the depth in the works decides, with or without an audience.
choices: Art all along — the depth in the works decides, with or without an audience.
Art only once the art world takes them up — the status is conferred, not built in.
Never art — art must pass a feeling to an audience, and these reached no one.
Art only if they skillfully copy the real world — which private sketches need not.
context: Outsider-art cases like Henry Darger's discovered notebooks and the Vivian Maier photographs test this split. Beardsley-style theorists say a work is art by the experience it can give a viewer, so it was art all along; Dickie-style institutionalists say art-status is conferred by the art world, so the real question becomes exactly when that happened.

question: Asked what novels do that essays can't, a writer points to George Eliot's Middlemarch: 'It lets you live inside another person's life and learn, from within, what that life is actually like. THAT knowledge is what literature is for.' Which view of art is the writer defending?
answer: Art's value is the real understanding it gives — here, a life known from inside.
choices: Art's value is the real understanding it gives — here, a life known from inside.
Art's value is the rich experience it gives the senses; any lesson is a side effect.
Art's value is the feeling it passes from maker to audience, not what it teaches.
Art's value is its form alone; what it tells you about life is beside the point.
context: Cognitivism about art (Martha Nussbaum, Love's Knowledge, 1990) holds that literature delivers a real, particular understanding — what a life feels like from inside — that no argument can; Nussbaum draws her own examples from novels like George Eliot's. Critics such as Jerome Stolnitz and Peter Lamarque deny art gives any special knowledge, treating its value as experience or form instead.

question: On a panel, a defender of AI art argues: 'Cover the labels. If a viewer would judge an AI image and a hand-painted one identically on what is actually visible, the line, the color, the rhythm, then they have identical artistic value. Who or what made it is beside the point.' Which view is she using?
answer: Aesthetic empiricism — once the visible features match, the value matches; origin is irrelevant.
choices: Aesthetic empiricism — once the visible features match, the value matches; origin is irrelevant.
Intentionalism — a maker's intention is part of the work, so a mindless process only mimics art.
Institutional theory — art-status comes from the artworld's recognition, not from visible features.
Historical theory — a thing is art only if meant to be viewed as past art was viewed.
context: Aesthetic empiricism (Monroe Beardsley, Aesthetics, 1958; 'The Intentional Fallacy,' with W.K. Wimsatt, 1946) holds the work itself — its perceptible features — is the whole aesthetic object; the maker's biography and intention drop out. The AI-art debate sharpens it: intentionalists like Richard Wollheim reply that how a thing came to exist is part of what it IS.

question: An art critic argues: 'Picture two canvases that look exactly alike, one painted by a Renaissance master, one made by paint spilled at random. They are NOT the same artwork. What the maker did, meant, and answered to is part of what the work IS.' Which view is she using?
answer: Intentionalism — the maker's intent is part of the work, so look-alikes can be different works.
choices: Intentionalism — the maker's intent is part of the work, so look-alikes can be different works.
Aesthetic empiricism — identical visible features mean identical value; how each arose can't matter.
Institutional theory — whether the spill is art turns on the artworld's recognition, not intent.
Cluster theory — art has no single mark; intent is just one trait among many that may be present.
context: Intentionalism (Richard Wollheim, Art and Its Objects, 1968; Jerrold Levinson, 'Defining Art Historically,' 1979) makes the maker's intentional activity partly constitutive of a work, so two indiscernible objects can be different artworks. Beardsley's anti-intentionalist empiricism is the classic opposing view; Danto's Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981) presses the indiscernibles puzzle too.

question: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp bought an ordinary urinal, signed it 'R. Mutt,' titled it Fountain, and submitted it to a New York show that had vowed to accept ANY entry. The jury hid it. By picking a mass-made object he hadn't even crafted, Duchamp meant to force which question?
answer: Whether art-status can come from an artist's choice and context, not from skill or beauty.
choices: Whether art-status can come from an artist's choice and context, not from skill or beauty.
Whether a sculpture can ever be as beautiful as a painting of the same subject.
Whether mass-produced goods were cheapening the craft of traditional sculptors.
Whether a hidden artwork can still count as having been publicly exhibited.
context: Duchamp submitted Fountain to the 1917 Society of Independent Artists, whose rules promised to show any work whose fee was paid; the board suppressed it and he resigned in protest. The readymade became the standard test case for George Dickie's institutional theory (Art and the Aesthetic, 1974): art-status as something conferred by choice and context rather than craft.

question: In 1964 the philosopher Arthur Danto walked into a New York gallery and saw Andy Warhol's Brillo Boxes: plywood boxes printed to look EXACTLY like the soap-pad cartons stacked in any grocery store. The puzzle that seized him: why is Warhol's box art when the grocer's identical box is not? What was Danto's answer?
answer: The difference is nothing you can see — it's the theory and art-history around the gesture.
choices: The difference is nothing you can see — it's the theory and art-history around the gesture.
Warhol's boxes were built from finer materials than the cardboard grocery cartons.
Warhol's boxes were beautiful in a way ordinary soap cartons simply are not.
There is no real difference — Warhol's boxes are not actually art either.
context: Seeing the Brillo Boxes at the Stable Gallery prompted Arthur Danto's essay 'The Artworld' (Journal of Philosophy, 1964), later The Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981): the art/non-art line cannot be perceptual — it lies in 'an atmosphere of theory' and art-history. Danto's idea shaped Dickie's institutional theory, though the two split over whether the artworld is interpretive (Danto) or institutional (Dickie).

question: Borrowing Wittgenstein's image that games share no single trait—just a family of overlapping ones—Berys Gaut argues: 'Stop hunting for the ONE thing that makes art art. There isn't one. Art has a bundle of typical marks—skill, expression, imagination, form—and a work qualifies when enough show up.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Cluster view — no single feature is required; enough of a bundle of typical art-marks suffices.
choices: Cluster view — no single feature is required; enough of a bundle of typical art-marks suffices.
Institutional view — one thing settles it: the artworld conferring the status of art.
Intentionalist view — one thing settles it: the maker intending the object as art.
Formalist view — one thing settles it: significant form, the arrangement of line and color.
context: Berys Gaut's 'Art as a Cluster Concept' (2000, in Carroll's Theories of Art Today) adapts Wittgenstein's family-resemblance idea and abandons the hunt for necessary-and-sufficient conditions. Each rival here stakes everything on a single criterion; the cluster view's whole point is that none of them is required on its own.

question: Jerrold Levinson argues art is defined by an unbroken chain reaching back: 'A new thing counts as art when its maker means it to be approached the way earlier artworks were approached. Art is its link backward to the tradition of regard—not any timeless trait like beauty or expression.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Historical view — art is whatever is meant to be regarded as past artworks were regarded.
choices: Historical view — art is whatever is meant to be regarded as past artworks were regarded.
Institutional view — art is whatever the artworld today confers the status of art upon.
Formalist view — art is whatever has significant form, regardless of any past tradition.
Expressionist view — art is whatever expresses and transmits the maker's felt emotion.
context: Jerrold Levinson's 'Defining Art Historically' (1979) defines art recursively, anchoring each new work to the tradition of how earlier art was regarded. The three rivals fix art in something non-historical—present institutions, intrinsic form, or transmitted feeling—which is exactly what the backward-looking view rejects.

question: David Hume retells a tale: two kinsmen swore a wine had a faint taste of iron and of leather, and were mocked—until a key on a leather thong turned up at the cask's bottom. Beauty isn't simply in the object, Hume argues, nor is taste merely whatever pleases you. So where is its standard?
answer: Qualified-judges view — beauty's standard is the converging verdict of practiced, unbiased judges.
choices: Qualified-judges view — beauty's standard is the converging verdict of practiced, unbiased judges.
Realist view — beauty is a feature in the object; judges discover it but do not set the standard.
Subjectivist view — beauty is just what pleases each person; no judge ranks above any other.
Disinterested-pleasure view — beauty is whatever pleases apart from any interest in the thing.
