context: David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) uses the wine-cask tale from Don Quixote to steer between pure subjectivism and realism: objectivity rests in the agreement of qualified judges—delicate, practiced, comparing widely, free of prejudice. The disinterested-pleasure rival is Kant's; the realist locates beauty in the object; the subjectivist denies any standard at all.

question: Immanuel Kant argues: 'Calling something beautiful claims everyone should agree—yet it tracks no property in the object. You can call a painting beautiful while wanting nothing from it, caring nothing for its use; that pleasure is free of all interest, so anyone with the same mind would feel it too.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Disinterested-pleasure view — beauty's universal claim rests on a pleasure free of all interest.
choices: Disinterested-pleasure view — beauty's universal claim rests on a pleasure free of all interest.
Qualified-judges view — beauty's standard is the agreement of practiced, unprejudiced critics.
Realist view — beauty is a feature in the object that the judgment simply reports.
Subjectivist view — beauty is just private response; the claim that all should agree is a mistake.
context: Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) grounds beauty's claim to universal agreement not in a property of the object but in disinterested pleasure—delight that wants nothing from the thing's existence or use, and so is shareable by all. Hume's route runs through the convergence of trained judges instead; the realist and subjectivist take the two extremes Kant rejects.

question: Frank Sibley notes that an expert spots a painting's GRACE at a glance—yet hand them its every line, color, and measurement and no rule lets them DEDUCE that it is graceful. The aesthetic rides on those plain facts but follows from no rule. Which claim is he defending?
answer: Rides-on-but-no-rule — aesthetic qualities depend on the plain features yet follow by no rule.
choices: Rides-on-but-no-rule — aesthetic qualities depend on the plain features yet follow by no rule.
Rule-derivable — the right measurements simply entail that a work is graceful or balanced.
Pure projection — 'graceful' reports only the viewer's feeling, not anything in the work.
Form-only — just the formal structure matters; talk of grace adds nothing to that structure.
context: Frank Sibley's 'Aesthetic Concepts' (1959) argues aesthetic terms depend on non-aesthetic features without being condition-governed by them: spotting grace takes trained sensitivity, and no inference carries you from the bare facts to the verdict. The rule-derivable and pure-projection options are the two views Sibley is denying at once.

question: Kendall Walton points to a cubist painting: judge it as a normal portrait and it looks like a botched mess; judge it as cubist and it is a triumph. Whether a work is bold or clumsy depends on the CATEGORY you view it through—and the right category is set by its history, not your whim. Which view is he defending?
answer: Category-relative view — a work's aesthetic qualities depend on the historically right category.
choices: Category-relative view — a work's aesthetic qualities depend on the historically right category.
Visible-features view — only what the eye plainly sees counts; no category enters the judgment.
In-the-work view — boldness or clumsiness sits in the work itself, the same under any category.
Artworld-status view — what categories decide is whether a thing is art at all, not its merit.
context: Kendall Walton's 'Categories of Art' (1970) argues aesthetic properties are perceived relative to a category—cubism, impressionism, sonata-form—and the correct category is fixed by the artist's intention and historical context, not the viewer's choice. The rivals deny categories any role in perception, or confuse a question about merit with one about art-status.

question: Clive Bell insists every great work—a Persian carpet, a Giotto fresco, a Cezanne—shares one thing he calls SIGNIFICANT FORM: an arrangement of lines, colors, and masses that stirs a special aesthetic emotion. Subject, biography, history: none of it counts. Only the form, for its own sake. Which view is he defending?
answer: Form-only view — significant form alone makes art; subject, biography, and context are irrelevant.
choices: Form-only view — significant form alone makes art; subject, biography, and context are irrelevant.
Expression view — what makes art is the artist clarifying a felt emotion by giving it outward form.
Knowledge view — what makes art is the genuine understanding of life that the work delivers.
Artworld view — what makes art is the status the artworld confers on it, whatever its form.
context: Clive Bell's Art (1914) names 'significant form'—the combination of perceptual elements that stirs the aesthetic emotion—as the one essence shared by all art, with representation, subject, and context set aside. Each rival locates art's essence elsewhere: clarified feeling (Collingwood, who denied art merely transmits emotion to an audience), knowledge (the cognitivists), or institutional conferral (Dickie).

question: A urinal in a gallery and the same urinal in a restroom look identical. Nelson Goodman says only the gallery one can be art — because there it does a JOB the restroom one doesn't. What is that job?
answer: It works as a symbol — it points beyond itself, representing or expressing something.
choices: It works as a symbol — it points beyond itself, representing or expressing something.
It has been granted the status of art by the artworld that displays it.
It pleases the eye with a clean, well-shaped surface and nothing more.
It arranges line and form into a balance that stirs aesthetic emotion.
context: Nelson Goodman (Languages of Art, 1968; 'When Is Art?', 1978) shifted the question from 'what is art' to 'when does a thing function as art', analyzing works as symbols within structured systems — representation, expression, exemplification. The rivals answer with a different job: institutional status (Dickie), surface pleasure (the empiricist Beardsley), formal arrangement (Bell).

question: Plato warned that storytelling only breeds ignorance — pretty lies, two steps from the truth. A modern theorist fires back: great novels give REAL knowledge, moral and psychological, a sense of what other lives are like — and that knowing is PART of what makes them good art. Which view is this?
answer: Cognitivism — the knowledge a work delivers is part of its value as art.
choices: Cognitivism — the knowledge a work delivers is part of its value as art.
Autonomism — any truths are a bonus; they add nothing to its art-value.
Formalism — only the arrangement of parts matters; content is irrelevant.
Expressionism — art transmits the maker's feeling, not real knowledge.
context: Noel Carroll ('Art, Narrative, and Moral Understanding', 1998) and Gregory Currie (Narratives and Narrators, 2010) argue art's cognitive yield — moral, psychological, modal knowledge — is partly constitutive of its value, answering Plato's old charge in Republic X that mimesis only breeds ignorance. Autonomists (Lamarque, Stolnitz) reply that incidental truth is not art-value.

question: A reader gives Crime and Punishment five stars FOR teaching him real psychology. A philosopher of literature objects: even granting the psychology is true, that's the wrong reason to rate it as literature — true facts and art-merit are different kinds of value, and mixing them confuses the two. Which view is this?
answer: Autonomism — a work's art-value is separate from any knowledge it delivers.
choices: Autonomism — a work's art-value is separate from any knowledge it delivers.
Moralism — a work's moral failings count directly against it as art.
Institutional view — the artworld's verdict, not its content, makes it art.
Expressionism — a work's value is the feeling it transmits to the reader.
context: Peter Lamarque and Stein Haugom Olsen (Truth, Fiction, and Literature, 1994) defend the autonomist 'no-truth thesis': fiction may contain truths, but those truths are not what makes it literature. The cognitivist opponents (Carroll, Currie) hold the reverse. The dispute runs back through Sidney and Shelley to Plato's Republic X.

question: A novel is built to make readers ENJOY the torture of innocents — engineering that delight on purpose. A film scholar says this makes it worse AS ART, not merely morally worse: a moral flaw of that kind is an artistic flaw. Which view of art and morality is this?
answer: Moralism — a moral flaw of the right kind counts directly against the work as art.
choices: Moralism — a moral flaw of the right kind counts directly against the work as art.
Autonomism — moral and artistic merit are separate; a vicious work can be great art.
Institutional view — the artworld's verdict, not the morality, settles its art-status.
Formalism — only form matters; what a work asks you to feel is beside the point.
context: Noel Carroll ('Moderate Moralism', 1996) and Berys Gaut ('The Ethical Criticism of Art', 1998; his own term is 'ethicism') hold that ethical defects in the response a work elicits can be aesthetic defects. Autonomists (Lamarque, Olsen) deny any link; immoralists (Eaton, Jacobson) argue moral transgression is sometimes an artistic asset. The test cases are propaganda films.

question: In 1945 Han van Meegeren confessed he had FORGED the Vermeers that fooled Europe's experts — to escape execution for selling a Dutch treasure to the Nazis. An art historian grants the forgery looks identical to a real Vermeer, yet says it is worth LESS, because value rides on what the maker actually achieved. Which view is this?
answer: Achievement view — the maker's real achievement is part of the value, so a forgery is worth less.
choices: Achievement view — the maker's real achievement is part of the value, so a forgery is worth less.
Empiricism — identical look means identical value; how it was made is outside the work.
Institutional view — the forgery's worth turns on what status the artworld grants it.
Functionalism — if both afford the very same experience, then both have the same value.
context: The forgery debate (Alfred Lessing, 'What Is Wrong with a Forgery?', 1965; Goodman's Languages of Art, 1968; Denis Dutton on authenticity) tests whether value rides on perceptible features alone. The achievement (intentionalist) view makes the maker's achievement-history constitutive of value; the empiricist (Beardsley) denies it. Van Meegeren confessed in 1945 to escape a Nazi-collaboration charge.

question: A gallery hangs a blank canvas and calls it art; over the sea a sunset blazes that no one curated. A philosopher says the gallery CAN'T make the canvas art, and nothing stops the sunset from being art — all that matters is whether you get a certain attentive, unified experience. Which view is this?
answer: Functionalism — art is whatever performs the job of affording aesthetic experience.
choices: Functionalism — art is whatever performs the job of affording aesthetic experience.
Institutional view — art is whatever the artworld grants the status of art.
Cluster view — art has no one defining feature, just a bundle of typical traits.
Intentionalism — a thing is art only if its maker intended it as art.
context: Monroe Beardsley (Aesthetics, 1958) defines art as anything meant to afford aesthetic experience marked by unity, intensity, and complexity. Berys Gaut pursued related functionalist lines before moving to his cluster account (2000). Critics object the definition is too broad (rainbows, sports plays) and too narrow (avant-garde works built to unsettle).

question: Two friends sincerely clash over whether a song is beautiful. A philosopher says NEITHER is mistaken about any feature of the song — each is just reporting how it strikes them. 'Beautiful' picks out no shared property in the song at all. Which view of beauty is this?
answer: Subjectivism — 'beautiful' reports the listener's own response, not a property of the song.
choices: Subjectivism — 'beautiful' reports the listener's own response, not a property of the song.
Realism — beauty is a real feature of the song; one side here must be mistaken.
Expressionism — beauty is the feeling the composer poured in, recoverable in the song.
Cultural view — the song is beautiful if the listener's culture counts it so.
context: Pure aesthetic subjectivism, defended in readings from Hutcheson through Ayer's emotivism, makes aesthetic predicates express individual response rather than track shared properties. The rivals: realism (Mary Mothersill, Beauty Restored, 1984), expression theory, and culture-relative response-dependence — versus Hume's qualified-judges standard ('Of the Standard of Taste', 1757). The puzzle of sincere disagreement drives each.

question: A gallery hangs a single typed certificate: no image, no craft, nothing to look at. The artist insists the real work is the idea it states; the paper is just a receipt for it. Treated on its own terms, which theory of art does this defend?
answer: Conceptualism — the idea IS the work; the object is mere documentation.
choices: Conceptualism — the idea IS the work; the object is mere documentation.
Expressionism — the work is felt emotion passed from maker to viewer.
Formalism — the work is its arrangement of line, color, and shape.
Mimeticism — the work succeeds by faithfully depicting the world.
context: Sol LeWitt's 'Paragraphs on Conceptual Art' (1967): 'The idea becomes a machine that makes the art.' Conceptualism makes the proposition primary and the physical object secondary — exactly inverting formalism (Bell) and expressionism (Collingwood), which locate the art in something perceptible or felt.

question: A flawless pianist leaves a hall cold; a second, no more skilled, works a real grief through the same piece and the room weeps. A critic says only the second made ART, not mere craft — because feeling was clarified and handed to the listener. Which theory of art is that?
answer: Expressionism — art clarifies a real emotion and hands it to the listener.
choices: Expressionism — art clarifies a real emotion and hands it to the listener.
Formalism — art is its arrangement of pattern, perceived for its own sake.
Cognitivism — art's worth is the genuine knowledge it can deliver to you.
Conceptualism — the work just is the bare idea behind the performance.
context: R.G. Collingwood's The Principles of Art (1938) and Tolstoy's What Is Art? (1898): art is the imaginative expression of emotion — the maker clarifies a feeling in the making, and a successful work transmits it. The view splits sharply from Bell's formalism, where transmitted feeling is incidental to perceived form.

question: At the tournament a squire calls 'heads!' as the marshal flips the toss-coin - just a hunch, no reason at all. It lands heads. Did the squire actually KNOW it would?
answer: No - a lucky hunch that lands right is not knowledge.
choices: No - a lucky hunch that lands right is not knowledge.
Yes - his call came true, and a true belief is knowing.
Yes - a strong gut feeling counts as real evidence here.
No - nobody could ever know how a flipped coin will land.
context: Knowledge is more than a true belief. A lucky hunch gets the answer right by accident - the reason doesn't connect to the truth. JTB (justified, true, belief) names the missing piece: justification.

question: In the keep a squire hears claws scrape under his cot and swears a beast is below. The torch shows a loose tapestry brushing the stone. Before the torch, was his belief REASONABLE?
answer: Yes - it fit what he heard; reasonable beliefs can still be wrong.
choices: Yes - it fit what he heard; reasonable beliefs can still be wrong.
No - beasts under cots aren't real, so it was never reasonable.
Yes - but only because the torch later showed no beast there.
No - no guess about what lurks below counts until you check.
context: A belief can be REASONABLE (well-supported by what someone knows) and still turn out wrong. Reasonableness is about the quality of the inference, not whether the conclusion lands true.

question: A seer says the eclipse comes at dawn because she 'always gets a dawn feeling' - that is her only reason. Dawn comes, and so does the eclipse. Did the seer actually KNOW it would?
answer: No - her 'dawn feeling' has no link to eclipses; she got lucky.
choices: No - her 'dawn feeling' has no link to eclipses; she got lucky.
Yes - she felt sure and was right, which is what knowing is.
Yes - a vivid feeling is its own kind of evidence here.
No - the hour of an eclipse can never be known by anyone.
context: For a reason to make a belief KNOWLEDGE, it must connect to what makes the belief true. A 'dawn feeling' has nothing to do with eclipses, so even a right answer from it is a lucky guess - the heart of the justification rule.

question: A ship's lookout sees black thunderheads piling over the bay and calls a storm before a single drop falls - he is going by the sky. At that moment, was his belief REASONABLE?
answer: Yes - skies like that reliably bring storms, so the call fits.
choices: Yes - skies like that reliably bring storms, so the call fits.
No - a belief turns reasonable only once it has come true.
Yes - any guess at all about the weather is reasonable.
No - only a trained navigator could reasonably call a storm.
context: Reasonable belief depends on how well evidence supports the inference - not on the result. The lookout is using a well-established pattern (black thunderheads bring storms), so the belief is reasonable now.

question: At the joust a man backs the red knight just for the color - the heralds had posted both champions' records, but he never read them. The red knight wins. Did the man KNOW he would?
answer: No - he ignored the records and chose on color; he got lucky.
choices: No - he ignored the records and chose on color; he got lucky.
Yes - his pick came true, and a true belief is knowing.
Yes - a confident backer at the joust counts as knowing.
No - the winner of a joust can never be known by anyone.
context: Knowledge needs reasons that connect to what decides the contest. Real evidence (the heralds' records) was available, but a favorite color has no link to who wins - so a right pick made that way is a lucky guess, not knowing.

question: A page hears a hound bay down the hall and says the lord's hound is loose. The bay was a neighbor's hound - but the lord's hound truly IS there, asleep. Did he KNOW it?
answer: No - the bay was the neighbor's hound; he got the hall right by luck.
choices: No - the bay was the neighbor's hound; he got the hall right by luck.
Yes - his belief was true, and a true belief is what knowing is.
Yes - he had a reason, the baying, and the hall turned out right.
No - only seeing the hound himself could ever count as knowing.
context: This is a Gettier-style case: true belief plus a reason - but the reason (the neighbor's hound) doesn't connect to what makes the belief true. The page got the hall right by accident, so it isn't real knowledge.

question: Leo is certain he ate roast venison at last winter's feast. The chronicler shows him the kitchen ledger: it was mutton that night. Before the ledger, was Leo's BELIEF reasonable?
answer: Yes - trusting your own memory is reasonable, but memory can slip.
choices: Yes - trusting your own memory is reasonable, but memory can slip.
No - a memory isn't reasonable unless someone else confirms it.
Yes - he felt sure, and being sure makes a belief reasonable.
No - memory is too unreliable to ground a reasonable belief.
context: Memory is a reasonable source of belief and knowledge - we rely on it daily - but it is not infallible. A reasonable belief from a normally reliable source can still turn out wrong on the facts.

question: A scout rides back from the ridge, where he watched the siege end, and tells the squire the castle has fallen. The squire believes him. Was the squire's belief REASONABLE?
answer: Yes — trusting a scout who actually saw it is a fair way to form it.
choices: Yes — trusting a scout who actually saw it is a fair way to form it.
No — you must witness a thing yourself before you may believe it.
Yes — any claim a scout makes is automatically reasonable.
No — only a great lord's word could make a belief reasonable.
context: Testimony from someone who was actually there is a normal, reasonable source of belief — we use it constantly. The scout is no lord, but he was a witness, which is what matters here.

question: At the well a squire tells Jamie: 'I heard from someone, who heard from someone, that we feast tomorrow.' Jamie tells the steward a feast is coming. Was Jamie's belief REASONABLE?
answer: No — a 'someone heard from someone' chain is too thin to trust.
choices: No — a 'someone heard from someone' chain is too thin to trust.
Yes — if a squire says it aloud, that settles it well enough.
Yes — exciting news is worth repeating whether or not it's true.
No — only the steward's own word in hall could ever count.
context: Testimony chains lose reliability at every step. A belief is reasonable only when the evidence can hold its weight — a third-hand rumor cannot carry a confident claim.

question: A hooded stranger rides to the gate. Before a word is spoken, the young squire says, 'I just KNOW he means no harm.' The stranger does turn out friendly. Did the squire KNOW?

context: Even when a hunch about people lands right, a hunch isn't knowledge — nothing connects the belief to the truth. Real knowing needs reasons that link up, not just a feeling.

question: A watchman reads the signal-fires on the hills — a pattern the realm has trusted for years — and reports the home banner still holds the wall. It does. Was his belief REASONABLE?

No — fires can be misread, so no belief from them is reasonable.

context: Signals can fail, but a normally reliable source still yields a reasonable belief. Reasonableness doesn't demand a source that NEVER errs — only one that works well in normal conditions.

question: The stablemaster's hound always bays when an armed rider nears the gate. An armed rider approaches, and the master says, 'He's about to bay.' Was the master's belief REASONABLE?

context: A pattern seen many times is good evidence for the next case — that's how we form most reasonable beliefs about the world. The master could still be wrong, but the reasoning itself is strong.

question: A squire reads the herald's tally: 56 knights returned. He's sure — the herald wrote it. But the herald only GUESSED, and by chance just 56 did return. Did the squire really KNOW?
answer: No — his reason was a lucky guess; being right by luck isn't knowing.

question: A boy finds a torn parchment with no seal and no signer. It claims the king will visit the village. The boy plans to announce it in the square. Was the boy's belief REASONABLE?
answer: No — an unsigned, unsealed scrap is too weak for a confident claim.

context: Reasonable belief depends on the quality of the source. An unsigned, unsealed scrap is too thin for a confident claim — feeling true and sounding exciting aren't the same as being supported.

question: Back from school, Jules sees fresh puddles on the dry driveway and tells her dad it rained while they were out. It really had. Was her belief REASONABLE?
answer: Yes — fresh puddles point to rain; the guess fits what she saw.
choices: Yes — fresh puddles point to rain; the guess fits what she saw.

context: Reasoning from what you see (fresh puddles) to the best cause (rain) is exactly how reasonable belief works. Other causes are possible, but rain is the best explanation here — reasonable beliefs can be overturned by new evidence yet still be reasonable now.

question: After her team loses, Ava says, 'I knew they'd lose all along.' But before the game she had told everyone they would WIN. Did she really KNOW they would lose?
answer: No — she believed they'd WIN; 'I knew it' now is just hindsight.
choices: No — she believed they'd WIN; 'I knew it' now is just hindsight.

context: 'Hindsight knowing' — claiming you knew once you find out — is a common but mistaken move. Real knowing needs the belief to have been there, with reasons, BEFORE the answer was visible. Ava's actual belief beforehand was the opposite.

question: Lila is wrong about lunch half the time but loudly says 'pizza!' Sam is right nine times in ten and quietly says 'salad.' Theo believes Lila. Was his belief REASONABLE?
answer: No — Sam's record beats Lila's volume; Theo trusted the worse witness.

context: Past reliability — track record — is one of the best clues for weighing testimony. Confidence and volume don't track truth. A reasonable belief weighs witnesses by how often they've been right, not by how loud they are.

question: Hana doesn't know the answer and circles B at random. B turns out correct. Asked later, did she really KNOW the answer before she circled it?
answer: No — a random pick isn't knowing, even when luck hits the answer.
choices: No — a random pick isn't knowing, even when luck hits the answer.

context: Random guessing is the clearest case of accidental truth — pure chance, no reason. Even when the guess hits, the answer is right but un-KNOWN. The missing piece is justification: a reason that connects the belief to the truth.

question: An older kid tells Marco the club is canceled today, and Marco repeats it as fact. The older kid was only guessing — but it really is canceled. Did Marco KNOW it was?
answer: No — the older kid was guessing, so Marco's reason was luck, not fact.
choices: No — the older kid was guessing, so Marco's reason was luck, not fact.

context: Trusting someone whose 'reason' is just their own guess passes the weakness right along. The belief lands true by accident — there is no real chain of reasons running from Marco's belief back to the fact.

question: Ben's older sister says their younger brother broke the lamp; the brother says he didn't. Ben sides with his sister just because she's older. Was his belief REASONABLE?
answer: No — being older doesn't track who's truthful; he ignored the clues.
choices: No — being older doesn't track who's truthful; he ignored the clues.

context: When two reports conflict, age alone doesn't track truth — outside evidence does. A reasonable belief here weighs the actual clues (broken pieces, who was nearby, motive), not which speaker happens to be older.

question: A fellow squire says, 'I just KNOW the captain's drill is tomorrow — I have a feeling.' She hasn't checked the duty roster. The drill DOES turn out to be tomorrow. Did she really KNOW?
answer: No — a feeling that lands right is a lucky guess; it never tracked the day.

context: Knowing takes more than a true belief: the reason has to TRACK the truth. A feeling that happens to be right is a lucky guess — she'd have had the very same feeling whether the drill was tomorrow or next week, so it never connected to the real day.

question: After one rude kid from the rival school is rude to him, Theo announces: 'I KNOW everyone over there is rude.' Did Theo really KNOW that?

context: Knowing needs a reason as big as the claim. One rude classmate supports 'I met a rude kid,' never 'everyone there is rude.' Leaping from a single case to all of them is the reasoning slip called hasty generalization.

question: Lila hears it fourth-hand — Sara told Devon who heard from Jess — that Mia hates her. She tells everyone: 'I KNOW Mia hates me.' Did Lila really KNOW that?
answer: No — a four-person rumor chain can twist on the way to her.

context: Testimony can give knowledge, but only when the chain stays reliable. Each retelling adds room to distort — a four-link chain needs every link both honest and accurate, with nothing here to suggest it. The message is doubtful before its truth is even tested.

question: Ben says the school was built in 1962, recalling a teacher who said so. He misremembers — she said 1972 — but the school WAS built in 1962. Did Ben KNOW the year?
answer: No — his memory was wrong, so landing on 1962 was luck.
choices: No — his memory was wrong, so landing on 1962 was luck.

context: A classic Gettier case: the belief is true (1962) and Ben has a reason (a teacher), but the reason is broken — she actually said 1972. He landed on the truth by accident. Justified true belief still fails when the justification doesn't connect to the fact.

question: Marcus says lightning never strikes the same spot twice — yet the Empire State Building is hit dozens of times a year. Asked how he knows, he shrugs: 'Everyone knows that.' Did Marcus really KNOW it?
answer: No — a saying being popular doesn't make it true, and this one isn't.

context: 'Everyone says so' doesn't transfer to knowledge. Wide repetition tracks how catchy a line is, not whether it's true — and this saying is plainly false. Knowing needs a reason that connects to how things actually are.

question: Before tryouts Riley insists: 'I just KNOW Coach will pick me — I can feel it.' Coach does pick her, but only because two other players got sick. Did Riley KNOW she'd be picked?
answer: No — the sickness picked her, not her feeling.

question: Owen's bus has come at 7:42 every Tuesday for months, so he plans around catching it next Tuesday. On Sunday the route changes and he misses it. BEFORE the change, was his belief REASONABLE?
answer: Yes — months of seeing it was good reason at the time.

context: Reasonableness is about the quality of your thinking, not how it turns out. A belief well-supported by repeated observation can still go false when the world changes on Sunday. The question is whether the reasons WERE good given what Owen knew — not whether he happened to be right.

question: Your little brother says: 'Mom said I don't have to do chores tonight.' You doubt he heard right. What's the most careful first question to ask?
answer: Did you hear Mom say it, or did someone else tell you?
choices: Did you hear Mom say it, or did someone else tell you?

Are you usually honest with me about this kind of thing?
Could Mom even change the chore rule for one night?
context: Knowledge from testimony hinges on the source. Hearing Mom directly is far stronger than a relayed message. 'Where did your information come from?' is the careful first move whenever someone reports a claim — it checks the chain before you check the content.

question: At the guild meeting a classmate flashes his phone: 'Did you know the lake by school has piranhas now?' Before you believe it, which question best traces whether the claim is TRUE and not just fun to repost?
answer: Where did the post he saw get this — a wildlife report, the news, an eyewitness?

context: Online posts circulate with no reliability check, so the careful move is to chase the SOURCE: a state wildlife report, a local news story, someone who actually saw one. Likes and reposts track shareability, not truth; the sharer's own confidence isn't evidence; and 'would people repost this?' measures how scary it looks, not whether it happened.

question: Jada is sure she returned the library book: 'I KNOW I did — I remember dropping it in the slot.' Three days later it turns up under her bed, never returned. Did Jada KNOW she had returned it?
answer: No — the belief is false (the book was never returned), so it isn't knowledge.
choices: No — the belief is false (the book was never returned), so it isn't knowledge.
Yes — her memory of the slot was vivid, and a vivid memory settles what you did.

context: Knowledge has three legs — justified, true, belief (JTB). Here the TRUTH leg snaps: the book under the bed proves Jada never returned it, so however vivid or sincere her memory, it cannot be knowledge. Vivid recollections can be wholly invented by the mind. You can BELIEVE something untrue; you can't KNOW it.

question: Before the midday meal Ana announces in the great hall: 'I KNOW it's venison day!' She has no list and no word from the kitchen — she just blurted a guess. The cooks carry out venison. Did Ana KNOW?

Ana's guess happened to match the menu, but a lucky hit isn't knowing: she had nothing to go on. Confidence isn't a reason either; you can feel certain about a pure guess. Being right by accident is not the same as knowing.

question: Tess's friend works in the school office and usually has the right info. The friend whispers that tomorrow is a surprise snow day — and it truly is. Going only on her friend's word, did Tess KNOW?
answer: Yes — reliable source, the news was true, and it reached Tess intact: knowledge.

All three legs hold: the office is the source (justification), the snow day really is on (truth), and the message reached Tess unbroken (belief). Most of what anyone knows about news, history, and science arrives this same way — through trustworthy testimony, not firsthand sight.

question: After one cup at the new tavern, Devon declares: 'I KNOW this place is amazing — the best ale of any tavern in the kingdom, better than all the rest.' Did Devon KNOW it was the best in the kingdom?
answer: No — one cup supports liking it, not ranking it best vs taverns he never tried.

context: The size of your evidence has to match the size of your claim. Devon could fairly say 'I liked that cup' — but 'best in the kingdom, better than all the rest' ranks every tavern, and he has visited exactly one. Reaching from a single sample to a sweeping comparison is the classic hasty leap, and it shows up here as a knowledge failure.

question: Your older brother says: 'You can't watch that movie — Mom said it's too violent.' You suspect he may be bending the rule. Which question best tests whether his report is straight?
answer: Did Mom actually say those words, or is 'too violent' your brother's addition?

Is the movie really that violent — bad enough that a parent would ban it anyway?
Has Mom banned other movies before, the way she'd probably ban this one too?
Does your brother dislike the movie, giving him a reason to keep you from it?
context: Testimony is filtered by the messenger, so the sharpest check is to separate what Mom actually SAID from what your brother is adding. The other questions probe related things — the film's content, Mom's past pattern, your brother's motive — but none gets at the heart of it: did this rule really come from Mom, in her words?

question: In 1963 Edmund Gettier set a famous trap: a belief that is justified AND true yet still not knowledge. Marco's pencil sits in the top drawer where he always puts it — but only because it rolled there yesterday. Did Marco KNOW where it was?
answer: No — his habit didn't put it there; it rolled there, so being right was luck.
choices: No — his habit didn't put it there; it rolled there, so being right was luck.

context: Gettier's 1963 paper broke the old formula 'knowledge = justified true belief': the belief is justified (his habit), true (the pencil is there), yet still not knowledge — because the justification and the truth are disconnected. The pencil rolled there; it isn't there BECAUSE Marco always puts it there. Justified true belief alone isn't enough.

question: Eva has barely spoken to the new kid, but tells a friend: 'I KNOW he doesn't like me — it's just a vibe.' Did Eva really KNOW the new kid disliked her?
answer: No — a vibe is her own feeling, not a sign of what he actually thinks.

A 'vibe' tracks Eva's own mood, not his opinion, so the belief has no justification that connects to the truth. (The 'only he can ever know' option overshoots: we read other minds from behavior all the time.)

question: By the gatehouse, Priya insists: 'I KNOW bats are blind — everyone says so.' In fact bats see fine; they just also use echolocation in the dark. Did Priya really KNOW bats were blind?
answer: No — the belief is simply false, and a false belief can't be knowledge.

context: 'Blind as a bat' is a popular saying that happens to be wrong — fruit bats see well, and echolocating bats still have working eyes. Hearing a line your whole life makes it feel certain, but familiarity tracks how often you've heard it, not whether it's true. Truth is one leg of knowledge (justified true belief), so a false belief never counts, however familiar it feels.

question: Sam warns you: 'Mr. Owen HATES it when students email him at night — he'll dock your grade for sure.' You're not sure Sam knows this. Which question best tests whether to believe him?
answer: Did Mr. Owen actually say it, or is Sam only guessing?

Are the other students in class nervous about it too?

context: The careful first move with any reported claim is to find its source: did it come from Mr. Owen (his words, a syllabus) or is Sam inventing the 'hates it' part? The other questions check Sam's habits, the crowd's mood, or the stakes — all beside the point of whether the testimony traces back to the teacher at all.

question: Zoe points at a photo: 'I KNOW that was our zoo day — I remember it clearly.' Her mom checks the date stamp: it was a different trip entirely. Did Zoe really KNOW it was the zoo day?

context: Memory feels certain from the inside but can be plain wrong. The date stamp is harder evidence and settles the truth: that wasn't the zoo day. A false belief is never knowledge — it fails the 'true' leg of justified true belief — no matter how vivid or sincere the memory.

question: After beating a new opponent once, Liam tells a friend: 'I KNOW I'm the better player — I won.' Did one win really let Liam KNOW he was better at chess?
answer: No — one game can be luck or an off day; ranking skill needs many games.
choices: No — one game can be luck or an off day; ranking skill needs many games.

context: A weaker player can beat a stronger one on any given day, so one result can't separate skill from chance. Trying harder doesn't fix that — effort isn't proof of being better. To know who's better you need enough games to see a pattern; the evidence has to match the size of the claim.

question: Bertrand Russell's famous puzzle: a man glances at a clock reading 3:00 — and it truly IS 3:00. But the clock froze at 3:00 weeks ago and is right only twice a day. Did he really KNOW the time?
answer: No — he was right only by luck; knowledge needs reasons that track the truth.
choices: No — he was right only by luck; knowledge needs reasons that track the truth.
Yes — his belief was true and he had no reason at all to doubt the clock.

context: Russell posed this stopped-clock case in 1948, fifteen years before Edmund Gettier's famous 1963 papers used the same trick to break the old 'knowledge = justified true belief' formula. The belief is true and reasonable, yet true purely by accident — the frozen clock would read 3:00 at any hour. The lesson: your reasons have to connect to the fact, not just happen to coincide with it.

question: Chisholm's sheep puzzle: a farmer sees a sheep-shaped white rock across a field and thinks 'there's a sheep out there.' There IS one — but it's hidden behind a hill, not the rock he saw. Did he really KNOW a sheep was there?
answer: No — true by luck; the rock he saw has no link to the real hidden sheep.
choices: No — true by luck; the rock he saw has no link to the real hidden sheep.
Yes — his belief was true and he had real visual evidence for it.

context: This echoes Roderick Chisholm's sheep-in-the-field case (1966), a textbook example of the Gettier problem. The belief is justified (he sees a sheep-shape) and true (a sheep is there), yet it isn't knowledge: the thing that justifies him — the look-alike object — is disconnected from the thing that makes it true, the hidden sheep. (Chisholm's original used a sheep-shaped figure; the rock is the common classroom retelling.)

question: A healer swears a berry cures fever. Asked her source, she names a traveling bard. The bard heard it from a tavern singer. The singer read it on a tattered notice. The notice names no one. Why should you doubt the whole chain?

context: A testimony chain is only as strong as its weakest link: when no one in it has actually inspected the original evidence, the whole chain collapses to a single unchecked source. David Hume (1748, 'Of Miracles') warned against credulity — accepting testimony beyond what experience justifies — especially once it has passed through many hands.

question: Two ship's surgeons aboard one vessel reach opposite verdicts on what is sickening the crew, each citing the ship's log. The captain wants to post one as settled fact. Since their training is equal, what is the most careful question to ask first?

choices: Which surgeon's case actually engages the evidence in the other's log?

context: When equally qualified experts disagree, credentials cancel and the careful reader asks whose case actually grapples with the rival evidence rather than talking past it. Expert disagreement is a studied problem in social epistemology (Goldman, 2001).

question: Even after a court ruling and three musicologists agree her favorite singer copied the lyrics, a fan insists: 'I just KNOW she'd never do that.' Her certainty has not budged an inch. Is her conviction knowledge?
answer: No — her certainty tracks how badly she wants the singer innocent, not the evidence.
choices: No — her certainty tracks how badly she wants the singer innocent, not the evidence.

context: Motivated reasoning (Kunda, 1990) is believing what you wish were true while feeling sure your reasoning is independent. The tell: evidence piles up against the belief and the believer's confidence still does not move.

question: A woman vividly remembers meeting a famous author at a signing as a child — the pen, the smile, all of it. Then her mother finds tickets proving the family was two states away on holiday that whole week. Did she KNOW she had met the author?
answer: No — a memory's vividness shows how clearly she recalls it, not whether it happened.
choices: No — a memory's vividness shows how clearly she recalls it, not whether it happened.
Yes — the memory was detailed and undisputed, and that clarity is what knowing the past means.

context: False-memory research (Loftus, 1997) shows that how vivid and confident a memory feels comes apart from whether it is accurate. A richly detailed memory can be entirely constructed; knowledge needs the memory to actually track the past.

question: A reporter sees smoke pouring from the cafeteria, concludes there is a kitchen fire, and warns the principal. In fact a smoke machine was being tested for the school play. To judge whether she KNEW there was a fire, what should you ask?
answer: Was her belief reasonable, given what she could see at the time?
choices: Was her belief reasonable, given what she could see at the time?
Was the principal annoyed by the false alarm she raised?
Do schools around here test smoke machines this often?
Did anyone else looking on also think it was a fire?
context: A belief can be reasonable — well-justified by what someone could see — and still turn out false. Reasonableness measures the quality of the belief; truth measures its match with the world. The two come apart, and that gap is basic to knowledge.

question: A brand calls its water 'scientifically proven' to boost focus. The study was paid for and run by the brand, never peer-reviewed, and tested 12 of its own staff — who were told what result it hoped to find. Why doubt the claim most?
answer: Three flaws stack — seller-run, no outside review, a primed sample — leaving almost nothing.
choices: Three flaws stack — seller-run, no outside review, a primed sample — leaving almost nothing.

Focus is hard to measure cleanly, so reasonable people could disagree on the result.
context: Three flaws each independently undermine warrant: the funder ran the study, no peer review caught its errors, and the primed sample knew the wanted answer. When all three converge, the claim has essentially no support left.

question: Sure his teammate will win, a boy points to the flawless practice score sheet the teammate proudly showed him. The teammate does win — but in a different event, and the sheet was actually his brother's. Did the boy KNOW his teammate would win?
answer: No — the sheet that convinced him was his brother's, so his reason never linked to the win.
choices: No — the sheet that convinced him was his brother's, so his reason never linked to the win.
Yes — he had solid evidence and his prediction came true, and that pairing is what knowing is.
Yes — trusting a teammate's practice scores usually works, so it counts as knowledge here too.
No — no one can ever really know who will win a contest before it is even played.
context: A classic Gettier case: the belief is justified (the impressive sheet) and true (the teammate wins), yet the justification and the truth never connect — the sheet was his brother's, and the win came in another event. Luck, not knowledge.

question: Priya overheard their teacher confirm the chemistry test is Friday, and tells Sam. Sam trusts her and now believes it too. The test really is Friday. Did Sam KNOW the test was Friday from Priya's word?
answer: Yes — she had real knowledge to pass on, and Sam had no reason to doubt her.
choices: Yes — she had real knowledge to pass on, and Sam had no reason to doubt her.
Yes — Sam believed a true claim, and any sincere true belief counts as knowing.
No — Priya only overheard a remark, so her word is too shaky to lean on.
No — Sam didn't hear it himself, and only firsthand experience can be knowledge.
context: Testimony is a real source of knowledge when the speaker knows and the listener has no reason to doubt (a 'defeater'). Most of what anyone knows about history, science, and the news arrives this way — secondhand but sound. The anti-reductionist view of testimony was defended by C. A. J. Coady (1992).

question: An online forecaster picks tomorrow's weather by flipping a coin: heads means rain, tails means sun. Tuesday she flips heads, predicts rain — and it rains. Did she KNOW it would rain on Tuesday?
answer: No — a coin flip isn't tied to the weather, so a correct call is just luck.
choices: No — a coin flip isn't tied to the weather, so a correct call is just luck.
Yes — she predicted Tuesday's rain and was right, and that is what knowing is.
Yes — a coin is right about half the time, and half-right is enough to count.
No — tomorrow's weather can never be known, however the guess is reached.
context: Reliabilism holds that knowing needs a belief-forming process reliably connected to the truth (Alvin Goldman, 1979). A coin lands right sometimes, but its link to the weather is random — so no flip, lucky or not, can deliver knowledge.

choices: A few personal stories can't outweigh careful trials built to screen out exactly that bias.
She hasn't actually read the trials herself, so her own view stays unproven until she does.
Migraines differ a lot between people, so the supplement may truly help a few of them.
Drug makers sometimes rig their trials, so every published trial result deserves doubt.
answer: A few personal stories can't outweigh careful trials built to screen out exactly that bias.
context: Anecdote-versus-data is a recurring fault line in reasoning. A few vivid stories feel heavier than a statistic, but claims about whether a treatment works need designs — control groups, blinding, large samples — built precisely to filter out wishful patterns.
question: An influencer says a supplement cures migraines — it helped her and three commenters. A reviewer points out that controlled trials on thousands of patients found no effect. What's the strongest reason to doubt her claim?
A debater quietly fears he isn't prepared. To kill the worry he repeats 'I'm ready' until he feels sure — but he still hasn't reviewed a single note. Did he KNOW he was ready?
answer: No — repeating a line until it feels true says nothing about whether he is ready.
choices: No — repeating a line until it feels true says nothing about whether he is ready.
Yes — by tournament time the belief was sincere, and sincere belief is knowing.
Yes — what you believe about yourself, held firmly, always rises to knowledge.
No — readiness can never be known by anyone except a coach who tests you.
context: Self-deception is the trick of manufacturing confidence by dodging the evidence against a belief (Alfred Mele, 2001). Feeling certain is not warrant; warrant comes from reasons that actually track the truth of the thing believed — here, the unreviewed notes.

question: A study in a real peer-reviewed journal is later exposed as built on fabricated data. Before the fraud surfaced, a science teacher taught it and said 'we KNOW this is true.' What's the most careful question to ask about that claim?
answer: Can peer review itself fail on hidden fraud, leaving the teacher careful but still wrong?
choices: Can peer review itself fail on hidden fraud, leaving the teacher careful but still wrong?
Should the teacher be personally blamed for repeating the faked study to the class?
Will the journal print a public retraction now that the fraud has been exposed?
Did any of the students happen to catch the fraud on their own by reading more?
context: Even our strongest social checks — peer review, reputable journals — can fail without the believer ever knowing. Justified-but-false belief is common; the lesson is fallibilism: good reasons are real and worth having, but they never guarantee being right.

question: A school paper cites ONE new study to declare 'students who eat breakfast score 20% higher' — and notes the result has never been repeated by any other lab. What's the strongest reason to doubt the claim?
answer: Single studies often fail to replicate, so one unconfirmed result isn't a settled fact yet.
choices: Single studies often fail to replicate, so one unconfirmed result isn't a settled fact yet.
Twenty percent is a suspiciously round number a reporter may have rounded up.
The finding sounds sensible, so it is probably safe to repeat as it stands.
The paper may have picked the one study matching what the reporter believed.
context: The replication crisis (Ioannidis, 2005; the Open Science Collaboration, 2015) showed that many headline findings vanish when other labs repeat them. Knowledge claims about effects should rest on results that converge across studies, not on a lone fresh paper.

question: A blogger believes a diet works after a video by a credentialed doctor — who sells that very plan and earns a cut of every sign-up. The diet does help some people. Did she KNOW the diet works?
answer: No — she never weighed the doctor's credentials against his stake in selling the plan.
choices: No — she never weighed the doctor's credentials against his stake in selling the plan.
Yes — a credentialed doctor said it works and it does for some, which is knowing.
Yes — the doctor has credentials and it helps some, so what he earns doesn't matter.
No — a video can never give knowledge; only a clinic visit in person could.
context: Judging a source means weighing credentials AGAINST conflicts of interest. A credentialed-but-paid source doesn't stand on the same footing as an independent one; ignoring the financial stake that pulls the other way lowers how much trust the testimony has earned.

question: A herald reads the crowd one fiery sentence from a rival lord's speech, lifted from a broadsheet. The full speech is nowhere to be found. Before repeating the line as the lord's view, what's the most careful question to ask?
answer: Does the full speech actually say it, and mean it the way the snippet sounds?
choices: Does the full speech actually say it, and mean it the way the snippet sounds?
Has the lord said harsh things in past speeches before this one?
Has the broadsheet's version been copied and shared by many readers?
Has the lord put out any public denial of the quoted line yet?
context: Context-collapse is the engine of viral misquotation: a snippet drops the qualifications around it and flips the meaning. The careful move is to read the whole original before treating the clipped line as known. Past harshness, wide sharing, and a denial all dodge the real question: what did he actually say?

question: A squire is sure he'll win the tourney because he tied on his lucky ribbon, 'and it always works.' He does win. Going by the ribbon, did he really KNOW he'd win before the lists opened?
answer: No - a ribbon can't shape sword-work, so his belief was a wish that happened to land.
choices: No - a ribbon can't shape sword-work, so his belief was a wish that happened to land.
Yes - he felt sure and the win matched, and that match is what knowing is.
Yes - the ribbon lifted his nerve, and that real boost made the win his to know.
No - no fighter can ever know a tourney's end until the final blow is struck.
context: A charm has no causal link to who wins, so belief built on it is wishful even when it lands right. Reasons that don't track the truth give coincidence, not knowledge - the win and the ribbon simply had nothing to do with each other.

question: A monk is certain a rumored plot is real: he's read a stack of scrolls backing it. Pressed, he admits he reads only scrolls from scribes who already agree, and burns the skeptical ones unread. What's STILL the strongest reason to doubt he KNOWS?
answer: Reading only what agrees makes your confidence climb with the page count, true or not.
choices: Reading only what agrees makes your confidence climb with the page count, true or not.
Plots are sometimes real, so his belief just might turn out correct anyway.
He feels certain, and that strong feeling of certainty is what knowing a thing is.
Belief in plots tends to fade once a person stops dwelling on the matter.
context: Confirmation bias (named by Peter Wason, 1960) inflates confidence: every agreeing scroll adds felt weight, but a diet filtered to agreement never once meets the evidence that could disprove the claim. The count of sources rises while the test of the belief never happens. Feeling certain is not the same as knowing.

question: A knight spots a familiar face waving across the great hall and concludes 'Lady Mira is at the feast.' Mira IS at the feast - seated at the far end. The waver was Mira's visiting twin. Going by that glimpse, did he really KNOW Mira was there?
answer: No - the belief was true, but he saw the twin; his glimpse had no link to where Mira sat.
choices: No - the belief was true, but he saw the twin; his glimpse had no link to where Mira sat.
Yes - he made a clear identification and it turned out true, and that is what knowing is.
Yes - the twins look alike, so the mix-up was fair, and a fair guess that lands is knowledge.
No - no one can know where another sits from a single glance across a crowded hall.
context: Twin and look-alike cases are textbook Gettier examples: justified, true, yet not knowledge, because the source of the justification (the twin) is not the source of the truth (Mira seated elsewhere). The belief lands right by luck, not by tracking the fact.

question: A watch officer glances at the tower clock - it reads three - and believes 'It is three.' It truly IS three. But the clock froze exactly twelve hours ago and has read three the whole time. Did the officer actually KNOW the time?
answer: No - it's true, but he'd read three at any hour; a stopped clock makes being right an accident.
choices: No - it's true, but he'd read three at any hour; a stopped clock makes being right an accident.
Yes - he had a justified true belief, and justified true belief just is what knowledge means.
Yes - he trusted a clock he had every reason to trust, and trusting reliable means is knowing.
No - he never checked the clock against a second source, and unverified belief is never knowledge.
context: Edmund Gettier (1963) showed justified true belief isn't enough for knowledge. Bertrand Russell's stopped-clock case is the textbook variant: the officer's reasons track only the clock's face, not the hour, so the truth of his belief is luck.

question: A scholar declares: 'Nothing about life before written records can truly be KNOWN - we have only broken fragments to infer from.' A sage replies: 'By that bar you can't know what you did in your own hall yesterday either - that's just memory.' What does the sage's reply show?
answer: The bar, applied evenly, erases ordinary memory too - so it proves too much and refutes itself.
choices: The bar, applied evenly, erases ordinary memory too - so it proves too much and refutes itself.
Only what you see right now survives the bar; everything past or ancient fails it.
Only pure logic and arithmetic survive; the bar bites just claims drawn from the world.
Yesterday survives but the ancient past does not, since recent memory is more reliable.
context: The sage's move is a 'tu quoque' turned into a reductio: set the bar for knowing the deep past high enough to exclude it, and the same bar excludes remembering yesterday. Either the standard is lowered or it collapses into near-total skepticism - which is why most readers reject the bar, not their own memories.

question: A herald hears from a trusted fellow: 'The mayor resigned this morning.' He believes it. Unknown to him, the fellow had taken a jester's parody bill for real news - yet the mayor truly HAD resigned earlier, over a different matter. Does the herald KNOW the mayor resigned?
answer: No - true, but his trust ran through a parody, so the belief never tracked the event.
choices: No - true, but his trust ran through a parody, so the belief never tracked the event.
Yes - he had a justified true belief, and that just is what knowing something is.
Yes - the news came through a normally reliable fellow, and reliable channels yield knowledge.
No - the resignation was not yet public record, and unrecorded events cannot be known.
context: A defeater is a fact that, once known, would undo your justification. Here the parody is a hidden 'undercutting' defeater: it doesn't argue the mayor stayed - it severs the reason the herald trusted. The fellow's channel was not reliable on this occasion, so the true belief lands by luck and falls short of knowledge.

question: A master chick-sexer sorts day-old chicks male or female at near-perfect rates, but cannot say what cues he uses — 'I just see it.' He sorts one chick correctly as male, unable to explain why. Does he KNOW it is male?
answer: Yes — a process this reliable yields knowledge, even with no reasons he can put into words.
choices: Yes — a process this reliable yields knowledge, even with no reasons he can put into words.
No — if he cannot put his reasons into words, his true verdict is not knowledge.
No — with no reason he can give, it is a lucky guess that happened to land.
Yes — any belief that turns out true is knowledge, reliable process or not.
context: Reliabilism (Alvin Goldman, 1979) says knowledge is true belief from a reliable process, with no need to access one's reasons. The chicken-sexer is the stock test case: internalists deny he KNOWS, reliabilists insist he does.

question: Two equally senior surgeons read the very same scan and clash at your bedside — one says operate NOW, the other says wait — each calling the other careful and sharp. If real equals who split on the same evidence should each pull toward the middle, what should you, listening, do?
answer: Grow LESS sure of either call — if the experts should ease off, so should the onlooker.
choices: Grow LESS sure of either call — if the experts should ease off, so should the onlooker.
Stay just as sure and simply pick one — the clash changes nothing for a bystander.
Trust whichever surgeon trained most recently and treat that as the safe anchor.
Ignore both of them and defer to whatever most surgeons elsewhere would say.
context: Peer disagreement (Christensen 2007, Elga 2007) splits into conciliationist and steadfast camps. Conciliationists hold that recognizing a real peer is in tension with keeping your prior confidence once they disagree on the same evidence; the steadfast camp resists that pull.

question: A town's records show 999 of every 1,000 drivers carry insurance, so by the numbers this one driver almost certainly does. A juror, seeing nothing else about him, believes 'this driver is insured.' He happens to be. Does the juror KNOW it?
answer: No — the 99.9% describes the whole town, not this one driver she singled out.
choices: No — the 99.9% describes the whole town, not this one driver she singled out.
Yes — odds that high on a belief that turns out true are plenty to count as knowing.
Yes — the town rate is 99.9%, and that rate carries straight to her one driver.
No — records are secondhand, and only seeing the policy herself could be knowledge.
context: The lottery and 'proof' paradoxes (Cohen 1977, Buchak 2014) press the intuition that statistics alone — however high the probability — don't deliver knowledge of an individual case. Courts track this too: a bare number rarely convicts THIS defendant.

question: A guru insists you can be sure of nothing outside your own mind — every sight could be a dream or a trick. A listener accepts the challenge and asks: granting all of that, is there ONE thing you would still be certain of at the very moment you doubt?
answer: That you are thinking right now — doubting is itself a thought, so the doubter cannot doubt it away.
choices: That you are thinking right now — doubting is itself a thought, so the doubter cannot doubt it away.
That an outside world exists, since your sensations must be coming from somewhere real.
Nothing at all — once every source is suspended, no certainty of any kind is left.
That math is true, since arithmetic holds even in a dream or a deceiver's world.
context: Descartes (Meditations, 1641) found the cogito as the one claim a radical doubter cannot coherently doubt: the act of doubting is itself a thought, so 'I think' stays certain. Critics like Lichtenberg pressed back on the 'I.'

question: A weather columnist trusts his rooftop barometer and tells viewers tomorrow will be sunny. It IS sunny. But a memo sitting on his own desk — which he never read — says the barometer jammed a week ago on one fixed reading. Did he KNOW it would be sunny?
answer: No — the memo he could easily have read would have killed his reason to trust the dial.
choices: No — the memo he could easily have read would have killed his reason to trust the dial.
Yes — his belief came out true, and not knowing about the memo lets him off the hook.
Yes — he has a good track record with the barometer, so today's reading is knowledge.
No — barometers are unreliable, so nobody trusting one can ever know the weather.
context: An undercutting defeater (John Pollock, 1986) removes your reason for a belief without showing the belief false. Epistemology's 'no defeaters' clause is usually qualified: defeaters you could easily have found must be checked.

question: An op-ed writer says he KNOWS his flight is at 6pm — he glanced at his calendar once. Told that missing it would sink a billion-dollar deal, he blinks: 'I'd better double-check.' One glance felt like enough at low stakes but not now. Did he KNOW the time before checking?
answer: No — once the stakes shot up, one quick calendar glance no longer clears the bar.
choices: No — once the stakes shot up, one quick calendar glance no longer clears the bar.
Yes — stakes change nothing; his evidence is the same, so he knew all along.
Yes — a calendar is reliable and his belief is true, which is all knowing needs.
No — one calendar glance never gives knowledge of your own schedule, stakes aside.
context: Epistemic contextualism (Cohen 1986, DeRose 1995, Lewis 1996) holds that what counts as 'knowing' shifts with the conversation: raise the stakes or a salient way of being wrong, and the bar for saying someone 'knows' goes up.

question: A traveler in strange country glances at a barn and thinks 'there's a barn.' There IS — but the whole roadside is lined with fake barn-fronts so convincing he could not have told them apart. He just happened to point at the one real barn. Did he KNOW it was a barn?
answer: No — surrounded by fakes he could not tell apart, he was right only by luck, and luck is not knowing.
choices: No — surrounded by fakes he could not tell apart, he was right only by luck, and luck is not knowing.
Yes — his eyes work and his belief came out true, and that is all knowing a barn takes.
Yes — true, believed, and seen with his own eyes: that ticks every box knowledge needs.
No — eyesight alone never gives knowledge of far-off things without other proof.
context: Goldman's fake-barn case (1976) showed reliable faculties producing a true belief can still miss knowledge when the area is full of fakes. The safety condition (Sosa 1999, Pritchard) captures it: the belief could too easily have been false.

question: A squire has never crossed the eastern mountains, but every royal cartographer agrees the great river lies beyond them. On their word alone he believes it does. The river truly is there. Does the squire KNOW the river is there?
answer: Yes — trusting a strong expert consensus is itself a reliable route, so his true belief is knowledge.
choices: Yes — trusting a strong expert consensus is itself a reliable route, so his true belief is knowledge.
No — only someone who has crossed the mountains himself could truly know what lies beyond them.
No — a belief passed along by people he has never once met can never rise to real knowledge.
Yes — any belief he sincerely holds that also happens to be true already counts as knowledge.
context: Testimony as a route to knowledge (C.A.J. Coady, Testimony, 1992; Jennifer Lackey 2008) is now broadly accepted; the live question is WHEN testimony is reliable. A strong professional consensus, backed by the field's track record, is a paradigm reliable case — you need not verify it firsthand to know.

question: Avi's lottery ticket is one of a hundred million — he is far likelier to be struck by lightning — so he believes he lost. He did lose. But had he WON and not yet heard, he would believe the very same thing. Does Avi KNOW he lost?
answer: No — he'd believe it even if it were false, so his belief doesn't track whether he won.
choices: No — he'd believe it even if it were false, so his belief doesn't track whether he won.
Yes — he is right and feels certain, and a confident true belief is all that knowing takes.
Yes — a reliable bit of reasoning gave him a true belief, which is all knowing requires.
No — no lottery result can be known by anyone until it is officially announced.
context: Robert Nozick's sensitivity condition (Philosophical Explanations, 1981): you know P only if you would NOT believe P were P false. Avi's belief is insensitive — he'd hold it whether or not he won — so it fails. Ernest Sosa (1999) offered the rival 'safety' condition; lottery cases sharpen the gap between the two.

question: Coen reads in a journal that a rare mineral lines deep-sea vents, and believes it — the claim is true. A week later that journal is credibly exposed for inventing sources in that very article. He hasn't checked whether his fact was a fake. Right now, does he KNOW it?
answer: No — once the source is exposed as unreliable, his reason for the belief is cut, though the belief is true.
choices: No — once the source is exposed as unreliable, his reason for the belief is cut, though the belief is true.
Yes — he learned it honestly back then, and a later scandal cannot reach back and remove knowledge.
Yes — journals are reliable enough overall that one exposed article leaves his belief untouched.
No — nothing merely read in print was ever real knowledge to begin with, scandal or no scandal.
context: Defeaters can arrive AFTER a belief forms. This is an undercutting defeater (John Pollock, 1986): it doesn't prove the belief false — the mineral may really be there — it just removes your warrant for holding it. Whether the belief counted as knowledge at some earlier moment is a separate question from whether it does now.

question: Two equally trained scholars publish opposite verdicts on a remedy, and the rule says when equals clash you should meet in the middle. Reporter Sela then learns one is quietly paid by the remedy's maker and the other has no such tie. Should she still treat them as equals?
answer: No — the hidden payment means they are no longer equals, so the rule to weigh them evenly drops away.
choices: No — the hidden payment means they are no longer equals, so the rule to weigh them evenly drops away.
Yes — equal training alone makes them equals, and who funds whom cannot change that.
Yes — any two credentialed experts who clash must always just split the difference.
No — she should simply trust the paid scholar, who likely sees the maker's private data.
context: When recognized 'epistemic peers' disagree on shared evidence, conciliationism (Christensen 2007, Elga 2007) says each should lower confidence — the equal-weight view. But the rule only fires if the two really ARE peers. A conflict of interest, lopsided evidence access, or a worse track record can defeat the peerhood that triggers the demand.

question: A castle steward insists 'the accounts are clean,' yet refuses to open the ledgers that would prove or disprove it — ledgers that sit on his own desk. The accounts happen to be clean. Does the steward KNOW they are clean?
answer: No — ducking evidence sitting in front of him blocks knowledge, even when the books turn out clean.
choices: No — ducking evidence sitting in front of him blocks knowledge, even when the books turn out clean.
Yes — his belief is true and trusting his own household is a reliable enough habit to count.
Yes — years of running the castle justify him, whether or not he ever opens the ledgers.
No — only an outside auditor could ever know the books are clean, never the steward himself.
context: Internalists about justification (Laurence BonJour) stress that the believer must be able to access her justifying reasons. Refusing easily-reachable evidence is willful ignorance — a failure of epistemic conscientiousness, the duty to gather evidence you could plainly check (W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief) — and it undermines the cognitive ownership that knowledge demands.

question: An oracle has never once been wrong about distant events, yet can give no reason for what she senses — no evidence, no theory, just a flawless record. She senses a far town burning, and it is. If a belief counts as knowledge whenever it comes from a reliable method, does she KNOW?
answer: Yes — a method that reliably yields truth gives knowledge, even with no reasons she can state.
choices: Yes — a method that reliably yields truth gives knowledge, even with no reasons she can state.
No — without reasons she can point to and inspect, a true belief never rises to knowledge.
No — talk of sensing distant fires is fantasy, so the case decides nothing about knowledge.
Yes — she feels sure and turns out right, and confident true belief is all that knowing takes.
context: Laurence BonJour's clairvoyance case — 'Norman' the clairvoyant (The Structure of Empirical Knowledge, 1985) — is built to pressure reliabilism (Alvin Goldman): if ANY reliable process yields knowledge regardless of access to reasons, the clairvoyant counts as a knower. Internalists balk — they hold the believer must be able to access her justifying reasons. A genuine standoff.

question: G.E. Moore answered the skeptic by raising his hand: 'I know I have hands. Having hands means I'm no brain floating in a vat. So I know I'm not a brain in a vat.' He leans on closure — knowing one thing, you know whatever it plainly entails. Granting closure, does his conclusion follow?
answer: Yes — that is just closure applied; deny his conclusion and you have to give up closure itself.
choices: Yes — that is just closure applied; deny his conclusion and you have to give up closure itself.
No — closure breaks on vat cases, since hand-belief can't reach the vat question at all.
Yes — but only from proof against the vat directly, not by passing knowledge down the chain.
No — closure never carries knowledge from one belief to another for anyone, ever.
context: G.E. Moore's 'Here is one hand' argument (1939), formalized via the closure principle: if S knows P and knows P entails Q, then S knows Q. Within the stated frame the conclusion follows. The deep fight is over closure itself — Nozick (1981) rejects it to block skepticism; Stewart Cohen and others keep closure and locate the skeptical pressure elsewhere.

question: A radio host insists: 'No moral claim can be KNOWN — cultures disagree too deeply about right and wrong.' A student notes that cultures disagree about history and science too, yet we don't toss out all of those. What's the flaw in the host's rule?
answer: His test is so strict it also erases plain calls, like torturing kids for fun is wrong.
choices: His test is so strict it also erases plain calls, like torturing kids for fun is wrong.
He treats people merely disagreeing as solid proof that nobody is actually correct.
He attacks the sort of folk who moralize instead of the moral claims they make.
He assumes whatever happens to feel obvious to him has to be true for everyone.
context: The student's move is a reductio: a standard for 'knowing' that's strict enough to kill all moral knowledge also kills history and science, since people disagree there too. Cross-cultural disagreement can't disqualify moral claims unless we let it disqualify everything — so consistency dissolves both or neither.

question: A scientist reports a drug works, but adds: 'I could be wrong — the data has a margin of error.' A critic snaps: 'Then you don't KNOW it; to know is to be certain.' Is the critic right that admitting you might be wrong means you can't know?
answer: No — knowing needs strong evidence, not total certainty; we know lots we can't prove beyond all doubt.
choices: No — knowing needs strong evidence, not total certainty; we know lots we can't prove beyond all doubt.
Yes — any chance of error at all downgrades a claim from real knowledge to mere belief.
No — but only science earns this pass; everyday knowledge really does demand certainty.
Yes — but the caveat is mere modesty, so deep down she actually knows it works anyway.
context: Fallibilism — most associated with Charles Sanders Peirce — is the standard view in philosophy of science: you can know something while admitting you might be wrong. Demanding Descartes-style certainty would erase almost all of what we ordinarily call knowledge. The live debate is how much evidence knowing takes, not whether it takes certainty.

question: A statistician finishes an analysis and it looks sound to her. A colleague then says: 'Careful — you've been awake 40 hours, and tired people make errors they can't spot from the inside.' No mistake has been found. What should she rationally do?
answer: Lower her confidence — a warning that her own judgment may be off counts even with no error found.
choices: Lower her confidence — a warning that her own judgment may be off counts even with no error found.
Keep full confidence — her actual math is the evidence, not gossip about her sleep.
Throw the whole analysis out — once fatigue is in play the result is worthless.
Keep full confidence until a fresh colleague reviews and points to a real mistake.
context: This is higher-order evidence (David Christensen, 2010): evidence not about the analysis itself, but about whether her own reasoning can be trusted right now. It rationally lowers her confidence even though it points to no specific bad step — yet it doesn't justify junking the work outright, since the analysis may well be fine.

question: A man glances at the station clock, sees 3:00, and notes the time, confident. The clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago — but by sheer coincidence it really IS 3:00 right now. Did he KNOW the time?
answer: No — his belief is true, but only by luck; the stopped clock reads 3:00 no matter the real time.
choices: No — his belief is true, but only by luck; the stopped clock reads 3:00 no matter the real time.
Yes — he had a true belief and a normally trusted instrument, which is all knowing requires.
No — a clock reading is never knowledge; only some other source could possibly count.
Yes — he was right and reasonable to trust the clock, and being right by luck is still knowing.
context: This is Russell's stopped-clock case (Human Knowledge, 1948) — an ancestor of the kind of luck case Edmund Gettier made famous in 1963. The belief is true and the man had a reason for it, yet the reason (the clock) doesn't track the truth, since it would read 3:00 whatever the real time. When being right is luck relative to your reasons, it isn't knowledge.

question: Descartes tried doubting everything that could be a trick: his senses, his memories, even 2+2=4 and the whole outside world. One thing the doubting itself could not erase. Why couldn't it be erased?
answer: Doubting is itself a kind of thinking, so for doubt to happen some thinking thing must exist.
choices: Doubting is itself a kind of thinking, so for doubt to happen some thinking thing must exist.
The outside world must be real, since the doubts have to be coming from somewhere outside.
Truths like 2+2=4 can't be faked, so no trickster could ever make the doubt land on them.
Right and wrong rest on reason, not the senses, so a deceiver could never reach them.
context: Descartes's Meditations (1641) imagines an 'evil demon' faking everything. The doubting can't erase one thing because doubting is itself a thought — so some thinker must exist. That survivor is the cogito: 'I think, therefore I am.' Whether anything else (math, the world, God) can be rebuilt from there is what Descartes spends the rest of the book contesting.

question: A chick-sexer sorts day-old chicks by sex with 99% accuracy but can give NO reason at all — she just 'sees' it. One judge says that without reasons she has no knowledge, only a knack. Which view of knowledge does that verdict rest on?
answer: Evidentialism — knowing needs evidence you can hold and give.
choices: Evidentialism — knowing needs evidence you can hold and give.
Reliabilism — a process this accurate just is knowledge, reasons or not.
Pragmatism — if her sorting reliably works, that's enough to count.
Contextualism — whether she 'knows' shifts with how strict the talk is.
context: The chick-sexer is a case widely used against externalism: bare reliability with no inner justification. Conee and Feldman's Evidentialism (2004) ties knowing to evidence the agent actually has — so the inarticulate sexer fails it. Goldman's reliabilism (1979) reads the very same case as confirming HIS view, since the process is so accurate.

question: A driver glances at a roadside barn and thinks 'a barn.' It really is one — but this stretch of road is lined with barn-fronts: fake facades propped up to look real. Had he glanced at any neighbor, he'd have been fooled. Did he KNOW it was a barn?
answer: No — he was right, but he could so easily have been wrong; one glance over would have fooled him.
choices: No — he was right, but he could so easily have been wrong; one glance over would have fooled him.
Yes — the barn he saw is real and his eyes worked fine, so what the neighbors are can't matter.
No — eyes alone never give knowledge in a tricky place; he'd need someone to confirm it for him.
No — after passing a row of fakes he can never trust his eyes on a barn again.
context: Goldman's fake-barn country (1976) is a Gettier variant: the belief is true, but only because he happened to point at the one real barn.
