Philosophers like Sosa and Pritchard added a 'safety' test — it's knowledge only if the belief couldn't easily have been false. Here it easily could have, so safety fails.

question: Holding one ticket in a huge lottery, a man believes 'mine will lose' purely from the odds. It does lose — yet a philosopher says he never KNEW it would, because he'd have believed the very same thing even in the world where his ticket won. Which test of knowledge is the philosopher using?
answer: Sensitivity — if it were false, you would NOT still believe it.
choices: Sensitivity — if it were false, you would NOT still believe it.
Reliabilism — a method this accurate already delivers knowledge.
Evidentialism — the long odds justify the belief, so it qualifies.
Virtue epistemology — reading the odds is a skill, so he knows.
context: Nozick's Philosophical Explanations (1981) defends sensitivity: you know p only if, were p false, you would not believe it. The lottery is the classic pressure — the belief is reliable and well-justified, yet insensitive, since you'd believe 'I'll lose' even as a winner. Safety (Sosa, Pritchard) was built to handle such cases differently.

question: Friday, relaxed: 'I KNOW the bank opens Saturday — I was just there.' Friday, with a check that MUST clear: same man, same memory, now says 'I don't really know it opens tomorrow.' One philosopher says the word 'know' itself just got stricter as the stakes rose. Which view is that?
answer: Contextualism — the bar for the WORD 'know' rises with the stakes.
choices: Contextualism — the bar for the WORD 'know' rises with the stakes.
Pragmatic encroachment — high stakes change what he actually knows.
Strict invariantism — one fixed bar; the casual claim simply misspoke.
Reliabilism — the memory's reliability is fixed, so he knows both times.
context: Keith DeRose's bank case ('Solving the Skeptical Problem,' 1995): 'knows' is context-sensitive, its standard rising with conversational stakes — so the same evidence underwrites 'know' when relaxed and not when it matters. Stanley (2005) and Hawthorne (2004) offer the rival diagnosis: the stakes change knowledge itself, not just the word.

question: You and a friend, both quick at arithmetic, split a dinner bill in your heads — and reach two DIFFERENT totals, each of you sure. One philosopher says you must now lower your confidence and move toward your friend: an equal's disagreement is itself evidence your own sum may have slipped. Which view of disagreement is that?
answer: Conciliationism — an equal's dissent should move you toward them.
choices: Conciliationism — an equal's dissent should move you toward them.
Steadfastness — your own reasons keep their weight; you may hold.
Permissivism — both of you may sit pat; two reasonable takes can coexist.
Justificationism — true equals are so rare this rarely applies.
context: David Christensen's 'Epistemology of Disagreement: The Good News' (2007) defends conciliationism: peer disagreement is higher-order evidence that demands real downward revision toward the peer — his own restaurant-check case is the standard illustration. Thomas Kelly (2010) defends a steadfastness-leaning reply, where first-order reasons keep their weight. The debate is genuinely unresolved.

question: The schedule says 5:14, and she reads it. Monday it's a routine meeting; she just goes. Tuesday she's testifying and can't be late, so she rechecks twice. A philosopher says on Tuesday she is NOT yet in a position to KNOW what she could know on Monday — the stakes changed her knowledge itself. Which view is that?
answer: Pragmatic encroachment — higher stakes raise the bar on KNOWING.
choices: Pragmatic encroachment — higher stakes raise the bar on KNOWING.
Contextualism — only the WORD 'know' shifts; her knowing does not.
Evidentialism — same evidence both days, so the caution is mere nerves.
Reliabilism — the schedule's reliability is fixed, so she knows both days.
context: Jason Stanley's Knowledge and Practical Interests (2005) and Hawthorne's Knowledge and Lotteries (2004) defend pragmatic encroachment: practical stakes affect what one is in a position to know — so the high-stakes day really does demand more. Critics (DeRose, Jessica Brown) say the word 'know' shifts while knowledge itself does not.

question: After years at her bow an archer looses an arrow into a gusting crosswind — and still buries it in the gold. A philosopher says this is a genuine HIT in the fullest sense, because her trained SKILL, not the lucky wind, earned the strike. Applied to knowing, which view is he using?
answer: Virtue epistemology — knowing is a success earned by the archer's own skill.
choices: Virtue epistemology — knowing is a success earned by the archer's own skill.
Reliabilism — any dependable method yields knowledge, skill or not.
Evidentialism — what counts is how well the evidence fits the belief.
Sensitivity theory — you'd have dropped the belief had it been false.
context: Ernest Sosa's A Virtue Epistemology (2007) uses exactly this archer: a shot can be accurate (it hits), adroit (skillful), and — when it hits BECAUSE of the skill — apt. 'Apt belief' is his model of knowledge: true belief that succeeds through the knower's own competence, not lucky circumstance. Linda Zagzebski's Virtues of the Mind (1996) is the other major program. The signature move: judge the knower, not just the belief.

question: A juror believes the suspect was at the scene because a witness picked him from a lineup. She then learns the lineup lights distorted faces. This doesn't show the pick was wrong — only that the lineup proves nothing. How does the news hit her belief?
answer: It cuts the support out from under it, without showing the belief itself is false.
choices: It cuts the support out from under it, without showing the belief itself is false.
It hands her fresh proof the suspect was somewhere else that whole night.
It changes nothing, since the witness still said exactly what he said.
It mostly shows she is a careless thinker who shouldn't be on a jury.
context: John Pollock (1986) named two kinds of defeater. A REBUTTING defeater shows the belief is false — an alibi would. An UNDERCUTTING defeater leaves the belief standing but kills your reason for holding it, which is exactly what the distorting lights do to the lineup ID. The distinction is standard in epistemology and AI reasoning.

question: G.E. Moore raises a hand before a room of skeptics: 'Here is one hand. I know it's a hand. I know a hand means I'm no brain in a vat fed fake hand-images. So I know I'm not such a brain.' Which principle does his proof rely on?
answer: Closure — if you know one thing, you know what it plainly entails.
choices: Closure — if you know one thing, you know what it plainly entails.
Sensitivity — a real belief would vanish if the fact were false.
Contextualism — 'know' demands more proof in some settings than others.
Reliabilism — knowing is any belief a dependable method delivers.
context: Moore's 'Proof of an External World' (1939, British Academy Hertz Lecture) makes the gesture famous; closure (know p, know p entails q, so know q) carries his ordinary knowledge of his hand to the anti-skeptical conclusion. Williamson defends closure; Nozick and Dretske reject it — their price is knowing p but not its known consequences.

question: A traveler reports he watched a dead man rise from his grave. His past reports were decent but not flawless. One scholar says: weigh the claim only as far as his record beats the odds against it — ask which is likelier, that he erred or that the dead truly rose. Which view of testimony is this?
answer: Reductionism — a report is only as good as the inductive evidence for the source.
choices: Reductionism — a report is only as good as the inductive evidence for the source.
Anti-reductionism — trust a report by default, doubting only on a red flag.
Self-reliance — accept nothing on another's word; verify it all yourself.
Deference — believe whoever holds the official rank, record aside.
context: Hume's 'Of Miracles' (Enquiry Sect. X, 1748) treats testimony as inductive and applies it to exactly this case: no report outweighs the standing improbability of a miracle unless its falsehood would be the greater wonder. Thomas Reid (1785) instead takes testimony as a basic source, trusted by default absent a defeater. C.A.J. Coady's Testimony (1992) restarted the modern debate.

question: At the zoo you see stripes and believe 'zebra.' A philosopher says you know it's a zebra rather than a painted mule — your eyes rule that out — yet you do NOT know it's a zebra rather than a mule in clever disguise. Knowing, he says, is always pinned to the rival you're ruling OUT. Which view is this?
answer: Contrastivism — you know a thing only as 'this rather than that.'
choices: Contrastivism — you know a thing only as 'this rather than that.'
Contextualism — how much proof 'know' needs shifts with the setting.
Infallibilism — you know only if you can rule out every possibility.
Reliabilism — knowing is believing truly by a dependable method.
context: Jonathan Schaffer's 'Contrastive Knowledge' (2005) makes 'knows' a three-place relation — the subject knows p rather than q, with the contrast built in, so the SAME fact can be known against one rival yet not another. It is a successor to Fred Dretske's relevant-alternatives view (the zebra-vs-disguised-mule case is Dretske's, 'Epistemic Operators,' 1970).

question: Quine claimed any theory can be saved from any experiment forever: when data threaten it, just quietly revise some background assumption instead. Two physicists fit identical instrument readings with rival theories that part only over particles no tool can see. Why can the data alone never crown a winner?
answer: You can always blame a background assumption, rather than the theory, to keep it.
choices: You can always blame a background assumption, rather than the theory, to keep it.
The two physicists secretly mean different things by the very same equations.
Whichever of the two rival theories is the simpler one must be the true one.
No explanation is ever good enough to justify believing that it is the truth.
context: This is underdetermination of theory by data, the Duhem-Quine thesis. Pierre Duhem (1906) argued theories meet evidence as whole webs, never one claim at a time; Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) sharpened it: a stubborn defender can always revise an auxiliary assumption rather than drop the theory. The wrong choices name three NEIGHBORING ideas Quine gets confused with: meaning holism, a simplicity rule for choosing theories, and van Fraassen's doubt about inference to the best explanation.

question: At the end of a 20-hour shift a forecaster finishes a careful calculation; the result looks fine to her. A colleague notes: 'Twenty hours in -- exhausted people make mistakes they can't spot from the inside.' No specific error is found. What should she rationally do?
answer: Lower her confidence, since she now has reason to doubt her own checking.
choices: Lower her confidence, since she now has reason to doubt her own checking.
Keep full confidence, since no one has pointed to an actual mistake yet.
Throw the result out entirely and fall back to having no view at all.
Keep full confidence, since the colleague is just commenting on her mood.
context: This is the standard fatigue case for higher-order evidence (David Christensen, 'Higher-Order Evidence,' 2010): evidence not about the drug or the sums, but about whether YOUR OWN reasoning can be trusted right now. It rationally defeats a first-order judgment even when no particular step is shown to be wrong -- and a defeater is not a reason to bin the work, only to hold it more loosely.

question: A philosopher says: 'I know I have hands — for were I handless I would not still believe I had them. But I do NOT know I'm not a demon-deceived mind fed fake hands — such a mind would believe it anyway. So I can know the first without the second.' Which view of knowledge allows this?
answer: Sensitivity — you know only what you'd give up believing were it false.
choices: Sensitivity — you know only what you'd give up believing were it false.
Closure — knowing a thing carries knowing whatever it entails.
Reliabilism — you know whatever a dependable method delivers.
Contextualism — 'know' sets a higher bar in some conversations.
context: Robert Nozick (Philosophical Explanations, 1981) ties knowledge to tracking the truth: you must be such that, were the claim false, you would not believe it. He accepts the striking cost — this breaks closure, so you can know you have hands yet not know you're not a deceived mind. Critics like Sosa and Williamson find the cost too high.

question: A forecaster faces one fact two ways. She can commit flat out, 'It WILL rain,' and bet the village picnic on it, or report instead, 'I'm 0.78 confident.' Same mind, same evidence. Two epistemologists watching argue not about the weather but about which of these is the REAL shape of a belief. What is their disagreement?
answer: Whether belief comes in degrees or is simply all-or-nothing.
choices: Whether belief comes in degrees or is simply all-or-nothing.
Whether her reasons sit inside her mind or out in the world.
Whether her beliefs rest on bedrock or instead hold each other up.
Whether the rain will actually fall on the village this time.
context: This is credence versus categorical belief: is the basic unit of the mind a graded probability (Bayesian credence, 0 to 1) or a flat yes/no commitment, with the other merely derived from it? The 'Lockean thesis' (believing just IS being confident enough) tries to bridge them and is contested. The wrong choices are three OTHER famous epistemology splits: internalism versus externalism, foundationalism versus coherentism, and a plain factual dispute, none of which is the one on the table.

question: In Tetlock's tournament, amateur volunteers beat intelligence analysts holding classified files. One amateur's '70% rain' days rained right at 70% of the time: her numbers meant what they said. A rival won more plain rain-or-shine calls, yet his percentages matched nothing real. What did the first have that the second lacked?
answer: Calibration: her stated odds line up with how often things actually happen.
choices: Calibration: her stated odds line up with how often things actually happen.
Accuracy: a higher share of her plain yes-or-no calls turning out right.
Coherence: her odds never contradict each other from one question to the next.
Sensitivity: her odds would have shifted if the underlying facts had differed.
context: Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting (2015) treats calibration as the master forecasting virtue: when you say 70%, it should happen 70% of the time. His Good Judgment Project amateurs beat intelligence analysts holding classified data partly this way. Calibration comes apart from raw accuracy: you can win more coin-flip calls while attaching meaningless numbers to them. Glenn Brier (1950) built the scoring math.

question: A hiker sees a white, sheep-shaped lump on a far hillside and thinks, 'There's a sheep in that field.' The lump is actually a rock -- but hidden behind it, out of sight, a real sheep is grazing. So his belief is TRUE. Did the hiker KNOW there was a sheep in the field?
answer: No -- the thing he saw isn't the thing that made his belief true, so he was right only by luck.
choices: No -- the thing he saw isn't the thing that made his belief true, so he was right only by luck.
Yes -- his belief was true and his eyes were working, which is all knowing requires.
Yes -- a sheep really was there, and being right about it is exactly what knowledge is.
No -- you can never know what's in a distant field without walking over to check.
context: Roderick Chisholm's sheep-in-the-field case (Theory of Knowledge, 1966) is a Gettier example aimed at perception: the belief is justified and true, yet the hiker's REASON (the rock) and what makes the belief true (the hidden sheep) come apart, so the truth is an accident. The same lesson drives Edmund Gettier's original 1963 cases and Goldman's fake-barn country (1976).

question: Descartes grants that one thing survives the evil-demon doubt: 'I think, therefore I am' -- a thinker must exist to be fooled. A journalist asks why this doesn't rescue ordinary beliefs too, like 'I have hands.' What's the strongest reason hand-beliefs still aren't safe?
answer: Any belief past 'I exist' leans on senses and memory -- the very things the demon controls.
choices: Any belief past 'I exist' leans on senses and memory -- the very things the demon controls.
A demon can't deceive without a real world to do it in, so the doubt cancels itself.
Each belief is only usually right, so this one might be the rare unlucky miss.
Moral and beauty judgments fall first, so factual ones must be the last to go.
context: Descartes's Meditation One (1641) raises the deceiving demon; Meditation Two recovers the cogito -- the bare fact that some thinking thing exists (its wording there is 'I am, I exist'; the famous 'cogito ergo sum' is from the earlier Discourse, 1637). But everything BEYOND that bare existence (hands, a sun, yesterday) rides on perception, memory, and inference, exactly the faculties a demon could rig -- so the doubt cannot be neatly walled off. Whether Descartes's later moves win the rest back is the founding question of modern epistemology.

question: Mia gives half her chips to a new kid sitting alone. She says, 'I want to BE the kind of person who notices and helps.' Which view of ethics fits her reason?
answer: Virtue ethics — she's choosing the kind of person she wants to be.
choices: Virtue ethics — she's choosing the kind of person she wants to be.
Consequence ethics — what's right is whatever makes the best outcome.
Rule ethics — sharing is right only if a universal rule demands it.
Care ethics — what matters is the bond with the lonely classmate.
context: Virtue ethics (rooted in Aristotle) asks 'what kind of person should I be?' Mia names a TRAIT she wants to live out — noticing and helping — rather than weighing an outcome, obeying a rule, or tending a relationship.

question: Sam tells Mom his brother broke the vase, though he promised not to. His reason: 'If she doesn't know, she'll keep buying bad glue and break more.' Which view fits Sam?
answer: Consequence ethics — telling leads to a better outcome at home.
choices: Consequence ethics — telling leads to a better outcome at home.
Virtue ethics — telling shows the honest person Sam wants to be.
Rule ethics — a no-lying rule decides it, outcomes aside.
Care ethics — what matters most is the bond with his brother.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill) judges actions by their effects. Sam's stated reason is the practical result — Mom having accurate information — not honesty as a virtue, a rule against lying, or the bond with his brother.

question: Ravi won't let his friend peek at the answers. 'Cheating is wrong, period — it doesn't matter if I'd never get caught.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: A flat rule that holds no matter what — cheating is just out.
choices: A flat rule that holds no matter what — cheating is just out.
The outcome — weighing who gets hurt or helped by it.
His character — the honest sort of person he wants to be.
The bond — protecting the tie he has with his friend.
context: Rule ethics (linked to Kant) says some rules bind in every case, whatever the results. Ravi's 'period — even if I'd never get caught' shuts the door on outcomes, so the rule itself is doing the work — not the good it brings, not his character, not the tie to his friend.

question: Ava returns a found wallet to its owner. 'If I lost mine, I'd want someone to return it — so I have to do the same.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: The swap — do for them what she'd want done for her.
choices: The swap — do for them what she'd want done for her.
A flat rule — keeping what isn't yours is just forbidden.
The outcome — the world runs better when wallets get home.
Her character — the honest sort of person she wants to be.
context: Reciprocity ethics — the Golden Rule, in Confucius's negative 'do not do what you'd hate' form and the Sermon on the Mount's positive 'do for others' form — runs one test: how would I want to be treated? Ava pictures losing her own wallet, then flips it. An honesty rule or a good outcome could also point this way, but the swap is the reason she actually gives.

question: Leo skips practice to sit with his sick friend Owen. 'Owen needs someone, and our friendship matters more than one practice.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: The bond — this friend, right now, needs him there.
choices: The bond — this friend, right now, needs him there.
The outcome — whichever choice does the most good overall.
A flat rule — friends must always show up when one is sick.
His character — the loyal sort of person he wants to be.
context: Care ethics (Nel Noddings, Carol Gilligan) puts the particular person in front of you at the heart of morality — not a rule or a head-count. Leo names the relationship and Owen's real need. Being a loyal sort of person is close, but his stated reason is the bond itself.

question: Mocked in the training yard, Ben just walks away. 'I want to be someone who keeps cool, not someone who has to win every fight.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: His character — the calm sort of person he wants to become.
choices: His character — the calm sort of person he wants to become.
The outcome — whichever choice does the most good overall.
A flat rule — you must never answer an insult with words.
The swap — treat the teaser as he'd want to be treated.
context: Virtue ethics (rooted in Aristotle) asks 'what kind of person should I be?' and treats each choice as shaping that. Ben's words — 'I want to be someone who keeps cool' — name a trait he's building, not an outcome, a rule, or the Golden-Rule swap.

question: Nina splits her ten cookies among the nine other kids and takes none. 'Nine smiles is more than one — that's just more good in the room.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: The outcome — nine happy beats one, so that's more good.
choices: The outcome — nine happy beats one, so that's more good.
A flat rule — sharing sweets in a group is simply required.
Her character — the generous sort of person she wants to be.
The bond — the friendships in the room matter most of all.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill) totals up the good across everyone affected. Nina's 'nine smiles is more than one' is exactly that sum — not a sharing rule, not the trait of generosity, not the friendships in the room.

question: A better offer lands for the night Maya promised to babysit her cousin Mia. 'A promise is a promise — I said I would, so I'll be there.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: A flat rule — a promise binds, better offer or not.
choices: A flat rule — a promise binds, better offer or not.
The outcome — whichever choice does the most good overall.
Her character — the reliable sort of person she wants to be.
The bond — her tie to her cousin Mia matters most of all.
context: Rule ethics holds a duty binding even when a better deal comes along. Maya's 'a promise is a promise' treats the promise as final — not a calculation of outcomes, not the trait of reliability, not even her tie to her cousin Mia.

question: Theo offers his swing to a smaller kid who's been waiting. 'When I was little I hated waiting for swings — so I won't make him do it.' Which kind of reason is that?
answer: The swap — give the kid what he once wished for himself.
choices: The swap — give the kid what he once wished for himself.
The outcome — more total fun when the swings get shared.
A flat rule — bigger kids must always yield to smaller ones.
His character — the kind sort of person he wants to be.
context: Reciprocity ethics — the Golden Rule — runs the 'put yourself in their shoes' test. Theo remembers his own past wish and acts on it directly. Sharing for more total fun, or just being a kind person, would be different reasons; his is the swap.

question: Cal tells his dad about a low grade Dad would never have found out about. 'I want to be honest even when nothing forces me.' Which kind of ethics fits his reason?
answer: Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
choices: Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
Reciprocity ethics — do as you would want done to you
context: Virtue ethics (rooted in Aristotle) asks what KIND of person to be. Cal names a trait — honesty — and points out nothing outside him is forcing it, so a rule or a payoff is not doing the work; the trait is.

question: Kids plan to hide the bus driver's passes as a prank. Jules objects: 'Ten kids miss school and the driver gets blamed — not worth it.' Which kind of ethics fits her reason?
answer: Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
choices: Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
Care ethics — protect the relationship you are in
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill) judges acts by their effects. Jules adds up the harm — ten missed school days, a wrongly blamed driver — and weighs it against one laugh. That tally, not a rule or a trait, is her reason.

question: Eli spots a $20 bill on the empty shop floor and walks on. 'No one would ever know, but taking it is still stealing.' Which kind of ethics fits his reason?
answer: Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
choices: Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Reciprocity ethics — do as you would want done to you
context: Rule ethics (associated with Kant) holds some rules bind no matter the outcome. Eli grants no one would ever know, then says taking it is still stealing. The rule settles it on its own, with the payoff set aside.

question: Older kids tease a new student, and Hana steps in. 'If I were being teased, I'd want someone to step in — so that's what I'm doing.' Which kind of ethics fits her reason?
answer: Reciprocity ethics — do as you would want done to you
choices: Reciprocity ethics — do as you would want done to you
Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Care ethics — protect the relationship you are in
context: Reciprocity ethics — the Golden Rule of the Sermon on the Mount — runs a swap test: how would I want this if I were on the other side? (Confucius taught the flip side: do not do to others what you would not want done to you.) Hana states the swap and acts on it.

question: Grace's grandma had a hard week, so Grace calls just to listen. 'She needs someone — that's what our relationship is for.' Which kind of ethics fits her reason?
answer: Care ethics — protect the relationship you are in
choices: Care ethics — protect the relationship you are in
Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
context: Care ethics (Nel Noddings, Carol Gilligan) centers the particular relationship and the person right in front of you. Grace names the bond itself — what our relationship is for — not a rule, a trait, or a head-count of good.

question: Theo's whole table is mocking a younger kid. He speaks up at a cost to himself: 'I'd rather be the kind of person with some backbone.' Which kind of ethics fits his reason?
answer: Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
choices: Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
Care ethics — protect the relationship you are in
context: Virtue ethics asks what KIND of person to be. Theo names the trait he wants — courage, backbone — and acts on it even at a cost to himself. The disposition he is building, not a rule or a payoff, is his reason.

question: Picking the recess game, Kira pushes for kickball: 'In tag someone always gets hurt — kickball is more total fun for everyone.' Which kind of ethics fits her reason?
answer: Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
choices: Consequence ethics — weigh the total harm against the good
Virtue ethics — act from the good trait you want to have
Rule ethics — obey the rule, whatever the result
Reciprocity ethics — do as you would want done to you
context: Consequence ethics (utilitarianism) compares expected outcomes for everyone affected. Kira weighs the predictable hurt in tag against broader fun in kickball — total fun for everyone is the aggregate, not a rule or a trait.

question: Tia's brother broke a window. Asked if she saw it, she tells the truth even though it gets him in trouble: 'Lying is wrong, full stop.' Which view matches Tia's reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics - one flat rule against lying, kept whatever it costs.
choices: Rule ethics - one flat rule against lying, kept whatever it costs.
Virtue ethics - being the honest sort of person she wants to be.
Consequence ethics - telling the truth makes things turn out better.
Care ethics - shielding someone she feels close to from harm.
context: Rule ethics (associated with Kant) holds some rules bind in every case, whatever the cost. Tia's 'full stop' is the tell: the rule decides it, not the outcome, her character, or the relationship.

question: Marco lends his notes to a kid who was out sick. Asked why, he shrugs: 'If I missed a week, I'd want help catching up. Same idea.' Which view matches Marco's reasoning?
answer: Reciprocity ethics - do for him what he'd want if the roles flipped.
choices: Reciprocity ethics - do for him what he'd want if the roles flipped.
Virtue ethics - being the generous sort of person he wants to be.
Consequence ethics - notes reaching absent kids help everyone.
Rule ethics - a flat rule to help classmates, binding every time.
context: Reciprocity ethics - the Golden Rule, found in Confucius and the Sermon on the Mount - runs the 'how would I want to be treated?' test. Marco pictures himself in the sick kid's place, then acts on the answer.

question: Nora kills a poll ranking classmates by looks: 'Kids we actually know will feel awful for days.' Which view of ethics best fits the reason Nora gives?
answer: Consequence ethics - the days of real hurt it causes are what make it wrong.
choices: Consequence ethics - the days of real hurt it causes are what make it wrong.
Virtue ethics - running the poll shows a small cruelty she won't grow.
Rule ethics - rating people like objects is just off limits, hurt or not.
Care ethics - the poll cuts across real friendships kids depend on.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill) judges an act by its effects on well-being. Nora's stated reason is the predicted harm - days of feeling awful - not character, a rule, or relationships. The other three views would oppose the poll too, but for different reasons.

question: Asked to lie to a teacher to cover a friend's missing homework, Theo refuses: 'Using someone's trust as a tool is off limits - no matter how it turns out.' Which view of ethics best fits Theo's reason?
answer: Rule ethics - some acts are off limits whatever the result they bring.
choices: Rule ethics - some acts are off limits whatever the result they bring.
Virtue ethics - he won't become the kind of person who tells such lies.
Consequence ethics - lying like this usually backfires in the long run.
Care ethics - the lie would corrode the teacher-and-student bond itself.
context: Kant's rule ethics (Groundwork, 1785) forbids using a person merely as a means - here the teacher's trust, treated as a tool. Theo's 'no matter how it turns out' is the tell: the rule binds regardless of the outcome.

question: Alone with an unwatched candy display, Maya takes nothing. Asked later, she says: 'I don't want to be someone who takes things just because no one is looking.' Which view of ethics best fits Maya's reason?
answer: Virtue ethics - she's shaping the honest kind of person she wants to be.
choices: Virtue ethics - she's shaping the honest kind of person she wants to be.
Consequence ethics - small thefts add up and the shop loses real money.
Rule ethics - a flat rule against stealing binds whether or not she's seen.
Care ethics - quiet theft slowly frays her trust with the storekeeper.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics) asks 'what kind of person should I be?' rather than 'what should I do?' Maya's reason - the sort of person she wants to be - tracks character, not an outcome, a rule, or a relationship.

question: A new student sits all alone at lunch. Priya goes and sits with her: 'She looks miserable right now and nobody else is moving. I'm not leaving her there alone.' Which view of ethics best fits Priya's reason?
answer: Care ethics - she meets the lonely person right in front of her.
choices: Care ethics - she meets the lonely person right in front of her.
Virtue ethics - she's growing into the kind, welcoming sort of person.
Consequence ethics - one less lonely kid makes the lunchroom better.
Rule ethics - a flat rule to include others binds her in every case.
context: Care ethics (Gilligan 1982; Noddings 1984) grounds morality in attending to the particular person in front of you, not abstract rules or totals. Priya answers this one girl's need right now - the care ethicist's center.

question: Asked why he sat out after fouling, Sam shrugs: 'We all agreed on the rules before we started. Going back on that wrecks the whole game.' Which view of ethics best fits Sam's reason?
answer: Contract ethics - the shared agreement is what gives the rule its force.
choices: Contract ethics - the shared agreement is what gives the rule its force.
Rule ethics - the rule binds because it's a rule, agreement or not.
Consequence ethics - keeping it makes the game run better for everyone.
Virtue ethics - sitting out shapes a fair-playing kind of person.
context: Contract ethics (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau; modernized by Rawls) grounds obligation in agreement among the affected parties. Sam's 'we all agreed' is the tell: consent generates the duty, not reason, results, or character.

question: At the harvest-fair stall, Aiden argues for low prices: 'Cheaper treats means more villagers can afford one - more smiles all round.' His reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Consequence ethics: an act is right if it produces the most overall good.
choices: Consequence ethics: an act is right if it produces the most overall good.
Virtue ethics: act as a generous person would, whatever the result.
Rule ethics: charge a fair price because a binding rule demands it.
Care ethics: price low to protect your bond with each villager.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham; Mill, Utilitarianism, 1861) judges an act purely by its effects on total well-being. Aiden counts smiles across everyone affected - the utilitarian's signature move. The other three would also like low prices, but for non-outcome reasons.

question: The whole debate club has piled onto the other side, yet Jordan keeps arguing his lone position: 'I'd rather say what I think than win by going along.' His reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Virtue ethics: act so as to build the brave, honest person you want to be.
choices: Virtue ethics: act so as to build the brave, honest person you want to be.
Consequence ethics: speak up because honest debates turn out better.
Rule ethics: never lie about your own view, because a rule forbids it.
Care ethics: speak honestly to protect the trust between your classmates.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle; revived by Anscombe, 1958) asks 'what kind of person should I be?' Jordan names the trait - courage to say what he thinks - not an outcome, a rule, or a relationship. Aristotle's andreia is exactly facing social risk for what you believe.

question: Offered a peek at the quiz answers, Lila refuses: 'If everyone cheated, the test would be pointless - so I shouldn't either.' Her reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Rule ethics: an act is wrong if its rule, made universal, defeats itself.
choices: Rule ethics: an act is wrong if its rule, made universal, defeats itself.
Consequence ethics: cheating is wrong because it harms real learning.
Virtue ethics: cheating is wrong because it makes you a dishonest person.
Care ethics: cheating is wrong because it betrays the teacher's trust.
context: Kant's Categorical Imperative (Groundwork, 1785): act only on a rule you could will for everyone. Lila runs the universalization test - 'if everyone cheated...' - which is the rule ethicist's core move, not a tally of effects or a claim about character.

question: Asked why he will not open the guild's sealed letters, Eli says: 'We all promised. A guild only works because people stick to what they agreed.' His reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Contract ethics: the promise binds because everyone in the guild agreed to it.
choices: Contract ethics: the promise binds because everyone in the guild agreed to it.
Rule ethics: a fixed rule forbids snooping in sealed mail, agreement or not.
Virtue ethics: keeping promises builds the trustworthy person you want to be.
Consequence ethics: keep the promise because trust pays off in the long run.
context: Contract ethics (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau; modernized by Rawls) grounds obligation in agreement among the affected parties. Eli's reason - 'we all promised' - tracks consent as the source of the duty. A rule ethicist would forbid the snooping whether or not anyone agreed; that contrast is the tell.

question: Caught teasing a younger kid, Marcus shrugs: 'But EVERYONE laughed when I did it.' His friend grants a crowd's reaction tells you something -- yet says this defense fails. What's the flaw in 'everyone laughed'?
answer: A crowd enjoying it doesn't make it right -- laughs track attention, not merit.
choices: A crowd enjoying it doesn't make it right -- laughs track attention, not merit.
Marcus is lying; plenty of people there clearly didn't laugh at all.
He's dodging by pointing at the kid who teased him first instead.
Teasing is fine anyway, so Marcus needed no defense to begin with.
context: This is the bandwagon fallacy (argumentum ad populum) in moral form: how many people approve of an act says nothing about whether it's right. Note what the friend concedes -- popularity CAN be evidence (of what's funny, or fashionable); it just can't settle a question of right and wrong. The three wrong choices each make a DIFFERENT mistake: denying the facts, swapping in tu quoque, and waving the wrongness away entirely.

question: Asked why she made fun of a classmate's clothes, Eva shrugs: 'She made fun of my shoes last week, so we're even.' Why does 'she did it first' fail to make Eva's mockery OK?
answer: Being wronged first settles who started it, not whether her reply is fair.
choices: Being wronged first settles who started it, not whether her reply is fair.
Her mockery is fine — being fair just means paying back what you got.
Only proof of who truly started it could settle whether Eva was right.
One teasing remark is too small a thing to count as a real wrong.
context: This is the 'two wrongs make a right' fallacy - close kin to tu quoque, but distinct: tu quoque dodges a critic, while this CLAIMS one wrong justifies another. A prior unkindness fixes who began the quarrel; it never erases the wrongness of what you choose to do back.

question: About to post a cruel joke, Olivia stops and deletes it: 'Thousands will see it and his whole weekend is wrecked - too much weight for one laugh.' Her reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Consequence ethics: weigh the harm against the good and act on the balance.
choices: Consequence ethics: weigh the harm against the good and act on the balance.
Virtue ethics: don't post cruel jokes, because that isn't who you want to be.
Rule ethics: never treat a person as mere entertainment, harm or no harm.
Care ethics: attend to the real person you are about to hurt with the post.
context: Consequence ethics weighs predicted costs against benefits across everyone affected. Olivia literally puts a wrecked weekend on one side and a laugh on the other - 'too much weight for one laugh.' The other views would also delete the post, but not by weighing outcomes.

question: Asked why he returned the wallet from the locker room, Diego shrugs: 'I want to be someone who returns wallets even when no one would ever know.' His reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Virtue ethics: do the act that builds the kind of person you want to be.
choices: Virtue ethics: do the act that builds the kind of person you want to be.
Rule ethics: return it because keeping what isn't yours is always wrong.
Consequence ethics: return it because the owner's loss outweighs your gain.
Care ethics: return it because the owner is out there needing it back.
context: 'Character is what you do when no one is watching' is a virtue-ethics commonplace; it echoes Aristotle's idea that virtue is a settled habit (hexis) shown in unwatched moments. Diego names the person he wants to become - settled honesty - not a rule, an outcome, or a relationship. That self-shaping focus is the virtue ethicist's mark.

question: Tempted to ditch his babysitting shift for a better offer, Liam says no: 'I said I'd be there. A promise that bends for a cooler plan stops being a promise.' His reason points to which view of right and wrong?
answer: Rule ethics: a promise is a duty to keep, even when a cooler plan comes along.
choices: Rule ethics: a promise is a duty to keep, even when a cooler plan comes along.
Consequence ethics: keep it because a no-show leaves the family worse off.
Virtue ethics: keep it because that builds the reliable person you want to be.
Care ethics: keep it because your bond with the family depends on showing up.
context: Kant (Groundwork, 1785): a rule of 'break promises when convenient' cannot be willed for everyone without destroying promising itself. Liam's focus on what a promise even IS - binding, not re-tradeable - tracks the rule ethicist's view, not a tally of effects.

question: The team built a turn-rotation by vote. Noah hates some picks but takes them: 'We worked this system out together. Ducking the turns I dislike breaks the deal we made.' Which view fits Noah's reason?
answer: Contract ethics — what binds is the deal the affected people agreed to.
choices: Contract ethics — what binds is the deal the affected people agreed to.
Rule ethics — what binds is a duty that holds for everyone, deal or no deal.
Consequence ethics — what binds is whatever makes the outcome go best.
Virtue ethics — what binds is becoming the fair-minded sort of person.
context: Contract ethics (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau; modernized by Rawls) grounds obligation in agreement among the affected parties. Noah's stated reason ('we worked this out together') is the contractarian move: consent generates the duty, not raw outcomes or character.

question: Aria opposes printing students' names in the discipline column: 'A named eighth-grader carries that label through every later grade. Lasting damage beats one week's gossip.' Which view fits Aria's reason?
answer: Consequence ethics — weigh the lasting harm against the short-lived gain.
choices: Consequence ethics — weigh the lasting harm against the short-lived gain.
Care ethics — attend first to this one student whose life will hurt.
Rule ethics — never use a person as mere content for readers.
Virtue ethics — refuse the careless habit such printing would build.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill) judges acts by weighing effects on everyone affected. Aria's reason explicitly trades long-run cost against short-run benefit. The other three views could also oppose naming the student, but each for a different reason than the one Aria gives.

question: Pressured to deny what she saw in the hall, Ana refuses: 'I won't be someone who covers things up to fit in. Doing it would just make me that person.' Which view fits Ana's reason?
answer: Virtue ethics — each choice shapes the kind of person you become.
choices: Virtue ethics — each choice shapes the kind of person you become.
Rule ethics — a duty not to lie binds you whatever the cost.
Consequence ethics — a cover-up makes things worse for everyone.
Care ethics — protect the people a cover-up would end up hurting.
context: Aristotle's habituation: each act shapes the next, and character is built one choice at a time. Ana's reason ('make me that person') is explicit character-formation language — the virtue ethicist's distinctive move, not duty or outcome.

question: Jay keeps 'needing' Mia to cover the homework he forgot. Her aunt warns: 'Helping every time isn't really helping — you're just training him to skip his own work.' Which view does the aunt defend?
answer: Virtue ethics — rescue him too often and you train worse habits in.
choices: Virtue ethics — rescue him too often and you train worse habits in.
Care ethics — meet his felt need and keep the friendship whole.
Consequence ethics — cover for him whenever it nets the most good.
Rule ethics — a duty to help friends binds you in every case.
context: Virtue ethics judges acts by the character they build — in both helper and helped. Its critique of indiscriminate caring: easing the moment can trade short-term comfort for long-term capacity, harming the very person it seems to serve. The aunt's worry is about the habits Jay forms.

question: An aunt gives her own niece more time than the other kids: 'She's MINE — I'm the one who shows up when no one else does. I owe her that.' A friend objects, 'That's just bias.' Which view is the aunt defending?
answer: Partial duties — a special bond you stand in creates duties to your own.
choices: Partial duties — a special bond you stand in creates duties to your own.
Impartial fairness — every child's claim is equal; favoring one is bias.
Consequence ethics — give the hours wherever they do the most good.
Rule ethics — one fair-treatment rule binds you to all kids alike.
context: John Cottingham defends agent-relative obligations: the extra weight you give your own kin is not a failure of impartial reasoning but a morally grounded feature of human life. The friend's 'just bias' charge is the impartialist position the aunt rejects.

question: A debate captain won't lie to cover for a friend. She says: 'Each lie makes the next one easier — I'd be filing down my own honesty. It's about the kind of person I become every time I choose.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — even a harmless lie corrodes the honesty you're building.
choices: Virtue ethics — even a harmless lie corrodes the honesty you're building.
Act utilitarianism — judge the lie only by who it helps or harms.
Kantian duty ethics — lying breaks a universal rule, whatever it does to you.
Contract ethics — if the friend consents to the lie, it's basically fine.
context: Virtue ethics (revived by Anscombe 1958, MacIntyre 1981) judges acts by what they do to the agent's character, not only by consequences or rules. 'Filing down my own honesty' and 'the kind of person I become' are the virtue-ethics signature — habituation — which is why her reason fits it and not the harm-counting or rule-breaking views.

question: A newspaper editor argues against a clever cheat code for a graded online quiz: 'Ask yourself — what if every student did this? The whole system collapses and grades mean nothing.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Kantian duty ethics — an act fails if everyone doing it wrecks the point.
choices: Kantian duty ethics — an act fails if everyone doing it wrecks the point.
Act utilitarianism — it's wrong because the harm outweighs the benefit.
Virtue ethics — it's wrong because cheating corrupts the cheater's character.
Care ethics — it's wrong because it betrays trust with teachers and friends.
context: Kant's Categorical Imperative (Groundwork, 1785) asks whether you could will the rule of your act to become a universal law. If everyone cheating would destroy grading itself, the act fails the test. The editor's 'what if everyone did this?' is the universalization move, not harm-summing or character talk.

question: A stranger could ruin $100 shoes wading into a pond to save a drowning child. An ethicist says he must: 'A life saved hugely outweighs the shoes. Just do whatever the trade favors.' Which view is she using?
answer: Consequences — choose the act that does the most good.
choices: Consequences — choose the act that does the most good.
Duty — you must help in distress, whatever the outcome.
Virtue — a brave person just wades in, the math aside.
Care — you owe a near, known child more than a stranger.
context: Peter Singer built this case in 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972). Act utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill) judges each act by the good its consequences produce; the appeal to 'whatever the trade favors' is its signature move.

question: A knight who swore an oath to guard the gate could slip away THIS one night to do a greater good. He stays: 'Gate-guards keeping their word protects more than one breach helps, so the oath holds.' Which view is he using?
answer: Rule consequences — keep the rule that does the most good overall.
choices: Rule consequences — keep the rule that does the most good overall.
Act consequences — break it, since this once does more good.
Duty — keep promises whatever the results, on principle.
Virtue — keep it because that is what an honest person is.
context: Rule utilitarianism (Brandt, Harsanyi) judges acts by the rule they follow, and rules by the good they do if generally kept. It splits from act utilitarianism on exactly this case — where the one-off breach would help.

question: A minstrel spends her free evening helping her own grandmother instead of a charity that would help more people. 'The bond itself matters,' she says. 'Strangers aren't substitutes for the woman who raised me.' Which view is she using?
answer: Care — duties grow from particular bonds, not equal weighing.
choices: Care — duties grow from particular bonds, not equal weighing.
Consequences — help wherever you can do the most good.
Duty — a rule of favoring kin can't be willed for everyone.
Relativism — there's no fact about what she really owes.
context: Care ethics (Gilligan 1982, Noddings 1984) answered impartial frameworks that treat every moral agent as interchangeable. Particular relationships — parent, child, friend — generate real obligations the equal-weighing view misses.

question: Before a storm, a ship's crew agrees on a lifeboat-rationing rule that could doom the very sailor who proposed it. He backs it anyway: 'No one aboard could reasonably reject it — any of us might be the one it falls on.' Which view is he using?
answer: Agreement — go by rules no one aboard could reasonably reject.
choices: Agreement — go by rules no one aboard could reasonably reject.
Consequences — the rule simply produces more good than harm.
Duty — a universal rule of fairness binds every rational agent.
Virtue — a just sailor takes the same risk as everyone else.
context: Contractualism (Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other, 1998) grounds morality in principles no one could reasonably reject. Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' (1971) is a kindred contract-based approach: rules justified by what we'd accept not knowing our own place.

question: Caught shoving a smaller kid, Marcus grins: 'Come on — EVERYONE picks on the freshmen here, it's basically tradition.' An ethics teacher pushes back. Why does 'everyone does it' fail as a moral defense?
answer: What students DO is a fact about behavior; it can't settle what they OUGHT to do.
choices: What students DO is a fact about behavior; it can't settle what they OUGHT to do.
A tradition is real only if you can prove every single student joins in.
Shoving counts as wrong only when it leaves a victim with a lasting mark.
Once a whole school treats something as normal, no rule is broken by it.
context: The is-ought gap (Hume, Treatise, 1739): claims about what people DO never by themselves entail what people SHOULD do. Calling a thing 'tradition' just dresses up the appeal to popularity - widespread practice may hint at a norm, but prevalence alone can never make an act right.

question: A school-paper columnist answers a classmate's lie with a bigger lie of his own: 'She lied to me first, so I'm justified.' An ethics teacher pushes back. Why does 'they did it first' fail here?
answer: Her earlier lie settles who started it, not whether his own lie is now wrong.
choices: Her earlier lie settles who started it, not whether his own lie is now wrong.
His lie is fine as long as it stays no bigger than the one she told him first.
Without proof she really lied first, his comeback simply cannot be judged at all.
A school paper owes no one honesty, so the columnist's lie breaks no real duty.
context: This is the 'two wrongs make a right' move applied to ethics: a prior wrong by someone else is offered as a license to do wrong back. Moral wrongs do not cancel each other out - the columnist owns his own choice fully, no matter who started it.

question: A columnist is caught printing a falsehood. Instead of answering, he shoots back at his critic: 'You lied in YOUR column last month, so who are you to judge me?' Why does 'you do it too' fail to settle the charge?
answer: A critic's own lie may make him a hypocrite, but it leaves the charge untouched.
choices: A critic's own lie may make him a hypocrite, but it leaves the charge untouched.
His falsehood is fine as long as it was no bigger than the critic's earlier one.
Until the critic's past lie is proven, the columnist's piece cannot be judged.
A school paper owes no one honesty, so printing a falsehood breaks no real duty.
context: This is the tu quoque move: rather than answer the charge, the columnist points at his critic's hypocrisy. But a critic can be a hypocrite and still be right - whether the column's claim is false stands or falls on its own, no matter who is throwing the stone.

question: A scientist is tempted to fake one data point: the paper looks better, no one will catch it, the conclusion is probably right anyway. Judge it as Kant would - by asking whether the rule behind the act could hold for everyone. Why is faking wrong?
answer: If everyone faked data when handy, data would mean nothing - the rule destroys itself.
choices: If everyone faked data when handy, data would mean nothing - the rule destroys itself.
It is fine here, since the conclusion is probably true and no one actually gets harmed.
It is fine, since one tiny point can hardly change what the full data already shows.
It is wrong because a good scientist simply would not be the type of person who cheats.
context: Kant's universalizability test (Groundwork, 1785): a maxim is wrong if it cannot be willed as a law for everyone. 'Fake data when convenient' fails - universal faking would wipe out the very practice of data the cheat depends on.

question: A debater loses a tournament she trained months for. She tells a teammate: 'The loss isn't up to me. My response is. I'll prepare differently and try again — without resenting the judges.' Which view is she using?
answer: Stoic — what is not up to you is no place for your peace.
choices: Stoic — what is not up to you is no place for your peace.
Virtue — a sore loser just needs to toughen up and stop whining.
Consequences — resenting the judges simply does no good.
Duty — there is a rule to meet setbacks with reason, not feeling.
context: Stoicism (Epictetus, Discourses, ~108 AD; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, ~170 AD) splits the world into what is and isn't 'up to us.' Externals are indifferent; the response is everything. Her exact framing — the loss isn't up to her, her response is — is the Stoic signature.

question: Five patients will die without transplants; one healthy visitor's organs could save all five. A writer says a surgeon still may NOT harvest him: 'Some basic claims a person has can't be outvoted by numbers.' Which view is she using?
answer: Rights — basic claims act as limits numbers can't override.
choices: Rights — basic claims act as limits numbers can't override.
Consequences — five saved beat one taken, so the math wins.
Virtue — a good surgeon simply wouldn't have it in her.
Care — she owes the visitor more, being right there with him.
context: The 'transplant case' (Thomson, Foot) is a classic reply to consequentialism: rights act as 'side-constraints' (Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) — limits on what may be done to a person no matter the good it would produce for others.

question: A student says of the trolley case — divert a runaway trolley to kill one, not five — 'always divert, five beats one.' Asked if he'd cut up one healthy patient for five organ recipients, he wavers. Which reply best shows the cases differ?
answer: Diverting redirects a threat already loose; the harvest starts a new one on a safe man.
choices: Diverting redirects a threat already loose; the harvest starts a new one on a safe man.
The two cases are identical, so consistency forces him to harvest the organs too.
Since the cases match, he was wrong to divert and should let the five die.
Five lives beat one however the saving happens, so the organ harvest is fine too.
context: The doing-vs-allowing distinction (Foot 1967, Thomson 1976) does real work here: diverting redirects an existing threat, while harvesting creates a new one against someone who was safe. Many philosophers accept the first and reject the second for exactly this reason.

question: A host hides a refugee soldiers mean to kill. They knock and ask where she is. A strict guest insists: 'Never lie — tell them the truth.' Which reply best answers that strict line?
answer: Killers who twist the truth forfeit any claim to an honest answer.
choices: Killers who twist the truth forfeit any claim to an honest answer.
Lying is always wrong; the death would rest on the soldiers.
Lie whenever the outcome favors it, here or anywhere else.
There's no fact about lying, so his choice can't be judged.
context: The 'murderer at the door' (Constant against Kant, 1797) is a classic stress test for absolute rules. Many philosophers separate a general duty of truthfulness from a duty owed a specific person — the latter forfeited by one who weaponizes the truth.

question: A minstrel promised to visit her grandmother this Saturday. Then a well-paid gig opens for the same day. She visits anyway: "I keep my promises — that's who I am." Whose reasoning is she using?
answer: Virtue ethics — the act expresses the honest person she is becoming.
choices: Virtue ethics — the act expresses the honest person she is becoming.
Act utility — visiting brings more total happiness than the gig.
Duty ethics — a promise is a universal rule, binding either way.
Contract ethics — she owes her grandmother a fair justification.
context: "That's who I am" is the virtue-ethics signature: the choice is judged by the character it expresses, not by consequences (utility), a universal rule (Kant), or a justification owed (contractualism). All four would keep the promise — but only her reason is about the kind of person she is.

question: A student steals answers for a test and defends it: 'I FELT like I deserved a better grade than studying alone would get me.' An ethics teacher pushes back. Why does 'I felt I deserved it' fail as a defense?
answer: Feeling he deserved a better grade is a fact about his wishes, not a reason that earns one.
choices: Feeling he deserved a better grade is a fact about his wishes, not a reason that earns one.
Cheating would be fine if only he had wanted the grade badly enough to lose sleep over it.
Whether he truly deserved it can't be known until his real ability is fairly tested.
Since grades are just numbers on a page, taking the answers is not really wrong at all.
context: Another form of the is-ought gap: feeling you deserve something is a psychological fact that entails no moral conclusion. The strength of a desire is evidence about how much you want a thing - never evidence that the thing is owed to you.

question: A student insists everyone is secretly selfish: 'Even someone who jumps on a grenade to save friends does it because it FEELS right to him — so that's selfish too.' If 'selfish' now fits self-sacrifice as well, what has gone wrong with the claim?
answer: By fitting every possible act, the word explains everything and so distinguishes nothing.
choices: By fitting every possible act, the word explains everything and so distinguishes nothing.
Nothing: it is true, and we should admit kindness is always self-serving underneath.
It is false, since plenty of people help others while hating every minute of it.
It is unprovable, since only a brain scan could ever reveal a person's real motive.
context: This is psychological egoism — the claim that every act is self-interested. Joseph Butler (Fifteen Sermons, 1726) gave the classic reply: stretching 'selfish' to cover the soldier on the grenade makes it unfalsifiable and empties the word. Feeling satisfied by a choice is not the same as choosing FOR yourself; the satisfaction can follow from caring about someone else.

question: A knight refuses to break his word even when a lie would save him: "If everyone broke promises whenever it suited them, a promise would mean nothing." In his view, where do right and wrong come from?
answer: From reason — the consistency every rational agent must will.
choices: From reason — the consistency every rational agent must will.
From God — the commands of a divine lawgiver above us.
From custom — the practices of one's own community.
From feeling — the approval that people widely share.
context: Kant grounded morality in pure practical reason (Groundwork, 1785): a moral rule must be one every rational agent could consistently will — his own example is the lying promise, which collapses if everyone made it. Rival groundings put right and wrong in divine command, in cultural custom, or in shared moral sentiment; the knight's appeal to consistency is the Kantian tell.

question: A young knight spends his own night-watch teaching a green squire to hold a shield steady. Asked why he gives up his rest, he says: 'It's just the kind of knight I mean to be.' Which ethical view is he reasoning from?
answer: Virtue ethics — do what a person of good character would do.
choices: Virtue ethics — do what a person of good character would do.
Utilitarian — pick whatever produces the most total good.
Kantian — follow a rule that must hold for everyone.
Care ethics — honor the bond to this one squire.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, ~340 BC) judges an act by the character it expresses and forms, not by its consequences or by a universal rule. The knight's reason — who he wants to BE — is the virtue-ethics signature. Care ethics would stress the bond to the squire itself; the knight instead points to his own character.

question: She would normally return a borrowed book on time, but instead drives an injured stranger to the hospital: "In each case, do whatever produces the most good. The book can wait." Whose reasoning is this?
answer: Act utility — weigh each act on its own by the good it produces.
choices: Act utility — weigh each act on its own by the good it produces.
Rule utility — follow the rule that works best overall.
Duty ethics — a ranked duty to help outranks the promise.
Care ethics — the closer human tie is the one that wins.
context: "In each case, do whatever produces the most good" is the act-utilitarian signature (Bentham, 1789): every act judged on its own consequences. Rule utility would instead defer to a good general rule; duty and care reach the same act by different routes.

question: A teacher grants an extension every time a student cries about a deadline. A colleague objects: "The pattern teaches them their tears change reality and that planning is optional." What is the colleague's worry?
answer: It trains worse work habits — the practice forms bad character.
choices: It trains worse work habits — the practice forms bad character.
Meeting real distress is itself the caring, moral act.
The welfare cost to the class outweighs the welfare gain.
Fairness is broken — criers and non-criers differ in treatment.
context: This is the virtue-ethics critique of indiscriminate caring: a practice is judged by the character it cultivates over time, and rewarding tears trains dependency. Care ethics (respond to distress), consequence-weighing, and equal-treatment fairness are the three rival readings ruled out here.

question: A donor funds soup kitchens in a town stuck in lasting crisis, never the reforms that would shrink it. An economist notes: "The soup is real care — but it makes the crisis bearable enough to last." Which view grounds his worry?
answer: Consequence ethics — relief that sustains the crisis loses on net.
choices: Consequence ethics — relief that sustains the crisis loses on net.
Care ethics — the concrete meals are themselves the moral fact.
Duty ethics — feed the hungry, whatever the wider effects may be.
Virtue ethics — steady giving forms the donor's good character.
context: The consequentialist critique of care-as-relief: helping with felt need can stabilize the very conditions that produce it, so downstream relief and upstream reform must be weighed by total outcome. Care, duty, and virtue each treat the giving as right without that weighing — which is the economist's point.

question: A profitable reality show humiliates contestants who consent, for audiences who enjoy it. A critic objects: "Repeating humiliation trains producers, viewers, and contestants into worse people — that's what the show actually IS." Whose reasoning is this?
answer: Virtue ethics — the wrong is the worse character the habit forms in everyone.
choices: Virtue ethics — the wrong is the worse character the habit forms in everyone.
Consequence ethics — wrong only if the harms outweigh the benefits.
Duty ethics — wrong because it uses people merely as a means.
Contract ethics — wrong only if fair parties would refuse to allow it.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle; MacIntyre, After Virtue, 1981) judges a practice by the character it forms. The critic's question isn't 'did anyone object?' or 'do harms outweigh benefits?' but 'what kind of person does this habit of humiliation make?' — which is why consent and enjoyment don't redeem it.

question: A writer urges shifting half the aid budget to a single antimalarial program: "It saves the most lives per dollar. Every other consideration is sentiment — the only question is which use prevents the most deaths." Whose reasoning is this?
answer: Consequence ethics — rank the options purely by total deaths prevented.
choices: Consequence ethics — rank the options purely by total deaths prevented.
Virtue ethics — judge by the donor character the giving forms.
Care ethics — give first to the people you are already tied to.
Duty ethics — respect each person as an end, not a statistic.
context: Act-consequentialism (Bentham, Mill; Singer, Famine, Affluence, and Morality, 1972) ranks acts by total expected welfare — here, deaths prevented per dollar. Critics charge it overrides duties to particular others; defenders reply those duties already track expected welfare. 'Lives per dollar' is the tell.

question: A trial would gather valuable data from refugees who would say yes. The lead researcher pulls the plug: 'They would consent only because they are desperate. Enrolling them mainly to mine their hardship uses them as a tool for our paper.' What makes the act wrong on her reasoning?
answer: It treats the refugees as a means to the study, not as people owed respect.
choices: It treats the refugees as a means to the study, not as people owed respect.
Its likely harms to the refugees outweigh the whole study's medical payoff.
It would train the research team into exploitative habits over time.
It betrays a bond of trust she already owes these refugees in her care.
context: Kant's 'humanity formulation' (Groundwork, 1785): never treat a person merely as a means, but always also as an end. Consent does not cancel the wrong when the whole point of enrolling someone is to use their desperation. The other choices are the consequentialist, virtue, and care readings of the same case.

question: A columnist sets rates from behind a veil that hides whether you will be born rich or poor: 'No one choosing blind would accept a system that left the poorest with almost nothing.' Which test of justice is she using?
answer: The veil-of-ignorance test: choose rules blind to your own place.
choices: The veil-of-ignorance test: choose rules blind to your own place.
The greatest-good test: choose whatever raises total welfare the most.
The respect-for-persons test: never use any taxpayer merely as a means.
The good-character test: choose what a fair-minded citizen would feel is right.
context: John Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) built the 'original position': choose principles behind a 'veil of ignorance' that hides your wealth and talents. Scanlon later generalized the contract idea. The other three are the utilitarian, Kantian, and virtue tests of the same plan.

question: A government analyst signed a strict nondisclosure agreement, then found proof of illegal mass surveillance. She decides to leak it: 'My duty to stay silent can't hold when keeping it lets millions be harmed.' Which ethical view is she reasoning from?
answer: Consequence ethics — the choice with the better outcome wins.
choices: Consequence ethics — the choice with the better outcome wins.
Rule ethics — a duty binds no matter what it costs.
Virtue ethics — do what an honorable person would do.
Care ethics — protect the people closest to you first.
context: When duties clash, the question is which one the speaker lets win. The analyst treats her duty of silence as conditional on its results — outweighed once the harm grows large enough. That is the consequentialist move (Bentham, Mill), even if she never names it. A rule-ethics analyst would hold the signed duty whatever the cost.

question: A sponsor offers poor volunteers a year's pay to test a risky drug. Ethicist Soren objects: 'Even if it saves more lives than it costs, paying that much to exploit their poverty is a line I won't cross.' Which ethical view is Soren reasoning from?
answer: Rule ethics — a duty can hold even when the math favors breaking it.
choices: Rule ethics — a duty can hold even when the math favors breaking it.
Consequence ethics — the choice that saves more lives wins out.
Virtue ethics — do what a decent researcher would choose to do.
Care ethics — protect each volunteer you personally know first.
context: Soren grants the welfare math — more lives saved — yet refuses to let it override the duty not to exploit. Treating human dignity as a constraint that outcomes cannot buy off is the deontological (rule-ethics) move, associated with Kant. A consequentialist would let the life-saving total settle it.

question: A man can rebuild the well his own village drinks from, or send the same gold overseas to save more strangers. He chooses the well: 'This village raised me — that's not a bias to correct away, it's a debt I owe.' Which ethical view is he reasoning from?
answer: Care ethics — a bond to particular people carries real moral weight.
choices: Care ethics — a bond to particular people carries real moral weight.
Consequence ethics — give where it will save the most lives.
Rule ethics — owe the very same duty equally to everyone.
Virtue ethics — give in the way a generous person would.
context: Care ethics treats particular relationships — to neighbors, kin, community — as genuine moral facts, not biases to be cancelled out. The man's reasoning leans on the tie to the village itself. The clash between giving close to home and giving where impact is highest is one of the sharpest care-vs-impartialist debates; both sides have serious defenders.

question: Born a slave in Rome and walking with a limp from his years in bondage, Epictetus was freed and became a famous teacher. His whole philosophy turned on one division he drilled into students. What was the line he told them to draw?
answer: Between what is up to you and what is not, and to mind only the first.
choices: Between what is up to you and what is not, and to mind only the first.
Between acts that help the most people and acts that help the fewest.
Between pleasures worth chasing and pleasures that leave you emptier.
Between duties you owe everyone and favors you owe only your friends.
context: Epictetus (~55-135 AD) opens the Enchiridion: 'Some things are in our control and others not.' By tradition lamed during his years in bondage, a man who had been owned by another located freedom in the one thing no master could seize, his own judgments and responses. The other choices are the utilitarian, Epicurean, and partiality lines.

question: A hospital bans lethal injection even for patients in agony. A chaplain's reason: 'Whatever the suffering, deliberately killing an innocent person is wrong in itself; the good you hope for afterward cannot fix what the act IS.' Which kind of reason is he giving?
answer: The act is wrong by what it directly does, whatever its results.
choices: The act is wrong by what it directly does, whatever its results.
The act is wrong because its total harm outweighs its relief.
The act is wrong because no cruel person could be a good doctor.
The act is wrong because no patient could agree to it in advance.
context: Natural-law ethics (Aquinas, Summa; Finnis, 1980) holds that some acts are wrong by their 'object', what they aim at, regardless of motive or outcome. The doctrine of double effect grows from it. The other choices are the consequentialist, virtue, and contractualist readings.

question: A billionaire's tax dodge is legal and seems to hurt no one. A columnist objects: 'It sounds like "what if everyone did it," but my worry is not a contradiction — it is that the tax base would collapse and schools and roads go unfunded.' What is the basis of her objection?
answer: The bad outcome if the rule were made general, not this one act.
choices: The bad outcome if the rule were made general, not this one act.
This single act's measurable harm to people who can be named now.
A flat duty to obey the tax law that holds whatever the results.
What the dodge reveals about the billionaire's selfish character.
context: Rule-consequentialism (Brad Hooker, Ideal Code Real World, 2000) judges acts by the welfare effects of the RULE allowing them. 'Imagine if everyone did this' looks Kantian but is really welfare-math at the rule level: the give-away is that the worry is the bad outcome, not a logical contradiction.

question: A news site writes every headline to provoke clicks. A critic grants each one is technically defensible, yet objects: 'The habit of phrasing everything to inflame slowly makes the newsroom, and its readers, worse thinkers.' On what does her objection rest?
answer: The kind of people the daily habit shapes, not any one headline.
choices: The kind of people the daily habit shapes, not any one headline.
The total harm the headlines cause readers, summed across all of them.
A duty never to manipulate, binding on every editor everywhere.
What readers would agree to if the terms were set up fairly.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle; MacIntyre, After Virtue, 1981) judges a practice by the character it forms over time. The point is not 'who got hurt by this headline?' but 'what does a workflow of provoking turn writers and readers into?' The others are the consequentialist, Kantian, and contractualist readings.

question: A merchant prepares to swear a false oath before the city magistrate to win his son a guild place. His sister stops him: 'You wouldn't want every father swearing false. A rule that can't hold for everyone isn't a duty — it's just favoritism.' Which view is the SISTER reasoning from?
answer: Rule ethics — a real duty must be a rule that holds for everyone.
choices: Rule ethics — a real duty must be a rule that holds for everyone.
Consequence ethics — weigh the harm the lie does to others.
Care ethics — a parent's bond to his child comes first.
Virtue ethics — ask what an honest father would do.
context: Kant's test (Groundwork, 1785) asks whether your reason could be willed as a law for everyone. The sister isn't denying the merchant loves his son; she's denying that love makes a duty he could hold against the universal test — 'swear false for my own child' fails it the moment every father claims it.

question: A platform debates a moderation rule. One analyst sets the bar: 'The question is not which rule gives the best speech overall; it is whether it is a rule no affected user could REASONABLY reject. That is what a platform owes the people under it.' Which standard is she using?
answer: A rule is right if no affected person could reasonably reject it.
choices: A rule is right if no affected person could reasonably reject it.
A rule is right if it produces the best total outcome for all.
A rule is right if it respects each user's dignity as an end.
A rule is right if it builds the best kind of user community.
context: Scanlon's contractualism (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998) tests rules not by 'what could everyone agree to?' but by 'what could no one reasonably REJECT?', weighing each person without summing welfare across them. The other choices are the utilitarian, Kantian, and virtue standards.

question: A reporter could break a source's confidence for a career-making scoop and never be caught. She refuses: 'A kept confidence is a good built into this craft itself. Breaking it isn't who I'm trying to become.' Whose reasoning is she using?
answer: Virtue ethics — judge the act by the character it builds
choices: Virtue ethics — judge the act by the character it builds
Consequence ethics — tally up the harms and the good
Duty ethics — obey the rule that binds every agent
Care ethics — honor your bond to a specific person
context: Her tells are 'a good built into the craft' and 'who I'm becoming' — the act is weighed by the kind of person it forms, not by results, rules, or one relationship. Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981) calls such role-duties goods internal to a practice. A consequentialist would weigh the harms; a Kantian would cite a universal rule.

question: In Mill's own century, a pamphleteer defends a man's right to attempt a dangerous mountain the town council wants outlawed: 'The state may stop you harming OTHERS — a risk you run on your own life alone is none of its business.' Which ethical view is she reasoning from?
answer: Rule ethics — a fixed line the state may not cross for any payoff.
choices: Rule ethics — a fixed line the state may not cross for any payoff.
Consequence ethics — ban it if it improves health overall.
Virtue ethics — ask what a self-governing citizen would do.
Care ethics — let those who love the person step in instead.
context: Mill's harm principle (On Liberty, 1859) says coercion is legitimate only to prevent harm to others, not to protect people from themselves.
