question: Gilbert Ryle in 1949 mocked the 'ghost in the machine.' To call a soldier brave, he said, isn't to name a hidden feeling — it just IS that he charges the fire and holds steady. Which view of mind fits Ryle?
answer: Mind is behavior — bravery just IS charging the fire; nothing hides behind it.
choices: Mind is behavior — bravery just IS charging the fire; nothing hides behind it.
Mind is the brain — bravery is the brain pattern firing as he charges.
Mind is separate — a non-physical will steers the soldier into the fire.
Mind is the pattern — anything wired to charge fire would count as brave.
context: Logical behaviorism — Gilbert Ryle, The Concept of Mind (1949). Ryle coined 'the ghost in the machine' to mock Descartes: talk of mind, he argued, is talk about behavioral dispositions, not a hidden inner stage. The hard case critics press back with: a stoic soldier who feels terror yet shows none.

question: By candlelight in 1641, Descartes writes: 'I can imagine my whole body gone — even my brain. But I cannot imagine away the I doing the imagining. So mind and body differ.' Which view fits Descartes?
answer: Mind is separate — the I outlasts imagining the body away, so the two differ.
choices: Mind is separate — the I outlasts imagining the body away, so the two differ.
Mind is the brain — the doubting I just IS the brain he imagined away.
Mind is behavior — being a thinker just IS doing thinker-ish things out loud.
Mind is the pattern — anything that ran his doubts would be a thinking thing.
context: Substance dualism — Descartes, Meditations (1641). His conceivability argument (I can doubt my body exists but not that I think) makes mind and body distinct substances. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him by letter in 1643: how can a non-physical mind push a physical hand? The interaction problem is still the standard objection.

question: A young abbess watches her newborn nephew sleep. He can't speak, yet he flinches at a crash and smiles when warmed. Her novice asks: how can she KNOW the baby truly FEELS, instead of just reacting?
answer: She can't be sure — she reads feeling from behavior, never from inside him.
choices: She can't be sure — she reads feeling from behavior, never from inside him.
She's sure — a baby that flinches must feel, since flinching just IS fear.
She's sure — every newborn feels just what a grown adult feels, from birth.
She can't be sure — only a being that can SAY it feels has feelings at all.
context: The 'other minds' problem (Bertrand Russell, Problems of Philosophy, 1912) bites hardest for beings we can't ask — babies, animals, anyone who can't tell us. We infer their inner life from behavior but can never verify it from the inside. The puzzle is genuinely open.

question: Reaching for a cookie, Aman notices something odd: he WANTED it (a thought), and his hand MOVED (a motion). He's sure the want caused the move — but how can a thought push a hand? Whose old puzzle is this?
answer: The mind-body problem — how a thought could ever cause a physical motion.
choices: The mind-body problem — how a thought could ever cause a physical motion.
The free-will problem — whether reaching was a choice truly up to him.
The other-minds problem — whether others feel wanting the way he does.
The Gettier problem — whether a lucky true belief counts as knowledge.
context: The mind-body problem (Descartes, Meditations VI, 1641): a thought FEELS like it causes an action, but how a non-physical thought could push a physical hand has never been fully explained. Free will, other minds, and Gettier are real puzzles too — but each is about something else.

question: Sara cries real tears over a sad story, then catches herself: the character was never real, yet her sadness clearly IS. A friend says she only PRETENDED to be sad. What is Sara's best reply?
answer: Her tears were real though the character wasn't — that's the real puzzle.
choices: Her tears were real though the character wasn't — that's the real puzzle.
Real sadness needs a real person to mourn, so hers was only pretend.
Sadness just IS crying, so if she cried, real sadness happened. Done.
Fiction-feelings sit in a sealed-off mind-part and never count as real.
context: The 'paradox of fiction' (Colin Radford, 1975): we have real emotions over people we know never existed. It turns on what an emotion fundamentally IS — a question at the heart of philosophy of mind, and still actively debated.

question: In bio class a snail touches salt and its nerves fire. Ben asks: does the snail FEEL the salt, the way he'd feel a hot pan? Which answer is the honest one?
answer: Nobody can tell from outside — nerves firing don't prove a feeling is there.
choices: Nobody can tell from outside — nerves firing don't prove a feeling is there.
Yes — anything with nerves feels, since nerve activity just IS feeling.
Yes — every living thing feels, snails and trees and bacteria alike.
No — only word-users feel; with no words for it, the snail feels nothing.
context: Where in the animal kingdom felt experience begins is one form of the 'hard problem' of consciousness (David Chalmers, 1995). Nerve activity and behavior alone never settle whether anything is actually FELT inside — you can't read a feeling off the wiring. Peter Godfrey-Smith ('Other Minds,' 2016) treats octopus and invertebrate minds as the live test case. The puzzle is genuinely open.

question: In 1956 U.T. Place asked a heretical question: when you feel terror, is that terror the very same thing as the brain firing — one thing, not two? Yes, he said: the firing IS the fear. Which view is this?
answer: Mind is the brain — the fear and the firing are one event, not two things linked.
choices: Mind is the brain — the fear and the firing are one event, not two things linked.
Mind is separate — the felt terror is non-physical; the firing only signals it.
Mind is behavior — terror just IS trembling and fleeing, not anything inside.
Mind is the pattern — any system firing this way would feel the same terror.
context: Mind-brain identity theory — U.T. Place (1956) and J.J.C. Smart (1959). Mental states are not caused by brain states; they ARE brain states, one thing under two descriptions. The view rose with mid-20th-century neuroscience. Critics ask whether the felt quality of terror can really just BE a firing pattern.

question: The AI tutor explains a math problem flawlessly. Sara asks: did it really UNDERSTAND the problem, the way her teacher does? Which answer is the honest one?
answer: Maybe not — a perfect explanation doesn't prove anyone home understands it.
choices: Maybe not — a perfect explanation doesn't prove anyone home understands it.
Yes — giving the right explanation just IS understanding, nothing more.
Yes — anything that can solve a problem must understand it to do so.
No — only humans can understand; a machine never can, whatever it says.
context: Searle's Chinese Room (1980): a system can shuffle symbols by rules and produce perfect answers while understanding none of it — syntax is not the same as meaning. Whether 'understanding' is anything more than flawless output is a leading open question in philosophy of mind, and far from settled.

question: Mary has read every science book about how eyes see RED, but only in a black-and-white room. She steps outside and sees a red rose. Did she LEARN something new?
answer: Yes — what red LOOKS like was a fact no book ever gave her.
choices: Yes — what red LOOKS like was a fact no book ever gave her.
No — she had every fact about red, so seeing it adds nothing.
Yes — but only because her science books left out one page.
No — seeing red and knowing about it are simply different topics.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Mary's Room' (Epiphenomenal Qualia, 1982) is the 'knowledge argument.' It targets physicalism — the view that every fact is a physical fact. If Mary, who already knew all the physics, still learns what red LOOKS like, the physical story seems to leave out how experiences feel from the inside. Physicalists reply that she gains only a new ability, not a new fact (Lewis, Nemirow) — so the case stays debated.

answer: Between what is up to us and what is not — judge only your own choices, not outcomes.
choices: Between what is up to us and what is not — judge only your own choices, not outcomes.
Between rich and poor — peace belongs only to those who own enough to feel secure.
Between pleasure and pain — chase every pleasure and flee all pain to stay content.
Between friend and rival — guard your peace by trusting allies and crushing your foes.
question: A Stoic teacher watches a student rage that a rival was praised instead of him. The teacher says the student has made himself miserable by staking his peace on a thing he never controlled. Which line did the Stoic draw to free him from that misery?
context: This is the Stoic 'dichotomy of control,' the opening teaching of Epictetus's Enchiridion (c. 125 AD): some things are 'up to us' (our judgments, desires, and choices) and some are not (our reputation, the weather, others' praise). Suffering comes from staking our peace on what we cannot control. The student's rage over another's praise hangs entirely on something outside him; the Stoic frees him by returning his attention to the one thing that is his — his own response. Marcus Aurelius and Seneca built whole works on this single distinction.

question: Footage shows an octopus working a puzzle box, flushing colors as it goes. When the lid finally pops, it brightens. The host asks: in that bright flash, is the octopus FEELING something, the way we feel a small win?
answer: Unknown — where in the animal kingdom feeling begins is an unsettled hard problem.
choices: Unknown — where in the animal kingdom feeling begins is an unsettled hard problem.
Yes — the solving behavior just IS the feeling; no inner spark is needed on top.
Yes — any nervous system feels, so even worms and bugs feel exactly as we do.
No — only mammals feel; a human-style cortex is the one thing that makes feeling.
context: Peter Godfrey-Smith's 'Other Minds' (2016) treats octopus cognition as a test case for the hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995). Clever behavior alone never settles whether there is inner experience, so the bank attributes the views to the host and audience rather than declaring a winner.

question: A debate club argues 'self-driving cars deserve moral status.' One speaker says: 'My car spotted the kid in the crosswalk, decided, and swerved — that's what minds do.' When it swerved, could the car have FELT anything?
answer: Probably not — but what it takes for any system to feel is still an open puzzle of mind.
choices: Probably not — but what it takes for any system to feel is still an open puzzle of mind.
Yes — sensing, deciding, and acting just IS feeling; no extra feeling is needed.
Yes — a machine that saves a life must care, and caring is itself a feeling.
No — only living things feel; machines are sealed out of feeling, however clever.
context: Whether function (sensing, deciding, acting) is enough for felt experience is the heart of the hard problem (Chalmers, 1995); functionalists say yes, Nagel's 'what-it's-like-ness' (1974) presses back. The question stays live, so the bank attributes the view to the debaters rather than declaring a winner.

question: Children wake from a nightmare sweating and terrified — yet the monster they fled was never real. A young monk recording this insists the fear itself was real, though nothing real caused it. Which view of feeling is the monk taking?
answer: Real-feeling view — the fear is genuine even when its object is imaginary.
choices: Real-feeling view — the fear is genuine even when its object is imaginary.
Object-required view — no fear is real unless a real threat causes it.
Body-only view — there was no fear, only sweat and a pounding heart.
Waking-only view — the feeling begins only once the sleeper wakes up.
context: The paradox of fiction (Colin Radford, 1975): we feel real emotions toward things we know aren't real — dream monsters, characters in a play. The puzzle turns on what a feeling fundamentally IS, a question at the heart of philosophy of mind. The monk takes the side that the dread is fully real even with no real object.

question: Hilary Putnam pressed a thought experiment in the 1960s: build a silicon brain that runs the SAME patterns as a human one — would it have a mind too? Yes, he argued; mind depends on what the parts DO, not what they are made of. Which view is this?
answer: Mind is the pattern — run the same patterns in silicon and a mind follows, whatever the stuff.
choices: Mind is the pattern — run the same patterns in silicon and a mind follows, whatever the stuff.
Mind is the brain — only a living brain firing is a mind; silicon could at most copy it.
Mind is separate — the mind is non-physical, so no silicon or cells could produce one.
Mind is behavior — having a mind just IS acting the part; the inner patterns do not matter.
context: Functionalism — Hilary Putnam (1960s), later Jerry Fodor. A mental state is defined by its causal role (what it does), not the stuff doing it, so a mind could in principle run on biology OR silicon — the 'multiple realizability' idea. It became central to cognitive science; the hard problem of consciousness is left as a separate puzzle.

question: A debater defends a bold claim: 'When you feel happy, that happiness is not merely caused by neurons firing — it IS that firing, the exact same thing.' A rival shoots back that a dog, an alien, even a robot might feel happy on different wiring. Which view is the debater defending?
answer: Mind is the brain — this exact feeling is one brain-state, the very same thing.
choices: Mind is the brain — this exact feeling is one brain-state, the very same thing.
Mind is the pattern — many different systems could feel it, so it is no one brain-state.
Mind is separate — the felt happiness is non-physical, only running alongside the firing.
Mind is behavior — being happy just IS smiling and bouncing, not the firing behind it.
context: Type-identity physicalism — Place, Smart, Armstrong (mid-20th century). Each type of mental state is identical to a type of brain state. The rival's jab is the multiple-realizability objection (Hilary Putnam): if a dog, an alien, or a robot can feel happy on different hardware, happiness can't be one single brain-state — which is why functionalists reject the identity.

question: Pitching his smart speaker, a founder says: 'If it acts EXACTLY like it knows you — responds, remembers, anticipates — then it really knows. Knowing just IS behaving that way.' Which view of mind is the founder defending?
answer: Mind is behavior — knowing just IS responding and anticipating, with nothing hidden behind it.
choices: Mind is behavior — knowing just IS responding and anticipating, with nothing hidden behind it.
Mind is the brain — only a living brain can know; the speaker just mimics the outward signs.
Mind is separate — real knowing takes a non-physical mind the speaker plainly does not have.
Mind is the pattern — it knows only if its inner program matches a knower's, not by its acts.
context: Logical behaviorism — Gilbert Ryle, The Concept of Mind (1949). To have a mental state just IS to behave (and be disposed to behave) the right way; there is no inner fact beyond it. The classic objection: someone who hides every outward sign of pain seems to leave the behaviorist forced to say there is no pain.

question: In 1643 Princess Elisabeth wrote Descartes a hard question: how could a mind with no size or place ever PUSH a physical arm? He held his ground — mind and body are two different kinds of thing, the mind somehow moving the body. Which view is that?
answer: Mind is separate — a non-physical mind chooses, then moves the arm; the two differ in kind.
choices: Mind is separate — a non-physical mind chooses, then moves the arm; the two differ in kind.
Mind is the brain — the choice to lift the arm just IS brain activity, not a separate mind.
Mind is behavior — deciding just IS the arm going up; no inner choice runs ahead of it.
Mind is the pattern — the choice is a program any system could run, brain or silicon.
context: Substance dualism — Descartes, Meditations VI (1641). Mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance, the mind initiating bodily action. Princess Elisabeth's 1643 challenge — the interaction problem — asks how a non-physical mind could move a physical arm at all; the puzzle has never been fully settled.

question: In 1995 the philosopher David Chalmers named the 'hard problem': mapping every wire in a brain is the EASY job, he said, but explaining why any of it comes with FELT experience inside is a separate job. Which view is he using?
answer: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a real further fact, not just the wiring.
choices: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a real further fact, not just the wiring.
Brain-state view -- the mind just IS the brain's activity, nothing more.
Pattern view -- what matters is the pattern, not the stuff; silicon could do it.
Behavior-only view -- having a mind is just acting like it; nothing felt inside.
context: Chalmers split consciousness into 'easy problems' (how perception, memory, and attention work) and the one 'hard problem' (why any of it is FELT at all). His answer is property dualism: felt experience is a real extra fact about the brain -- without adding a separate soul-substance.

question: Squires build a clockwork face that smiles when praised and frowns when mocked. It grins on cue for the crowd. One squire says it is only moving brass lips — there is no felt pleasure behind the smile. Which view of mind is that squire taking?
answer: Zombie view — behavior can run perfectly with no inner feeling behind it.
choices: Zombie view — behavior can run perfectly with no inner feeling behind it.
Behaviorist view — to act pleased simply IS to be pleased.
Functionalist view — anything this lifelike must feel along with it.
Biology-only view — only living flesh could ever feel anything.
context: The philosophical zombie (David Chalmers, 1996): a being that behaves exactly like a feeling creature yet has no inner experience at all. The squire's claim — outward smile, no felt pleasure — is the zombie intuition. Whether such beings are even possible is one of the deepest disputes in philosophy of mind.

question: A bard tells of a she-ape that keened over her dead infant — slumped, refusing food, like any grieving mother. A monk objects: we can never know the beast felt grief — we see only behavior, never the feeling within. Which view is the monk taking?
answer: Other-minds view — we see behavior but can't directly confirm the feeling.
choices: Other-minds view — we see behavior but can't directly confirm the feeling.
Behaviorist view — to grieve exactly as we do simply IS to grieve.
Same-feeling view — every beast must feel just what a human feels.
Language-only view — without words there can be no real feeling at all.
context: The problem of other minds (Bertrand Russell, 1912): each of us directly experiences only our own mind, so another's feelings must always be inferred from behavior. Animal grief makes it vivid — the keening strongly suggests sorrow, yet we cannot check from the inside. The monk presses exactly this gap.

question: Mocking what he called 'the ghost in the machine,' Gilbert Ryle argues there is no hidden inner anger: to say someone is angry just MEANS they shout, slam doors, and glare -- no extra feeling behind it. Which view of mind is he using?
answer: Behavior-only view -- a mind just IS how you act; nothing is hidden inside.
choices: Behavior-only view -- a mind just IS how you act; nothing is hidden inside.
Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
Pattern view -- mind is the pattern, not the stuff; silicon could run it too.
Brain-state view -- a mental state just IS a particular brain firing.
context: Logical behaviorism (Ryle, The Concept of Mind, 1949) treats talk of mental states as talk about behavior patterns; the anger-equals-shouting move is textbook Ryle. The classic objection: a person in real pain who hides every sign perfectly seems to have a feeling with no behavior at all.

question: An ether cloth on a wounded knight's face leaves him limp, though his chest rises and pulse beats. The apothecary cannot tell whether anything is felt, and says watching the body cannot settle it. Which view of mind fits her reasoning?
answer: Hard problem — the physical signs are all present, yet leave the felt question open.
choices: Hard problem — the physical signs are all present, yet leave the felt question open.
Identity view — experience just IS brain activity, so an active brain must feel.
Behaviourism — with no outward behaviour, there is no feeling to ask about.
Soul view — the soul does the feeling, and it has left the body for now.
context: The puzzle of why ANY brain activity is ever felt from the inside is the hard problem of consciousness (David Chalmers, 1995). Anaesthesia makes it vivid: it seems to switch experience OFF while the body runs ON. The identity view (experience IS brain activity), behaviourism, and the soul view are the rival positions the apothecary is NOT taking. The puzzle is unresolved.

question: A robot at a tech demo jokes, paints, and flinches from a pinch -- wired much like us. A guest argues: 'Even with the full wiring diagram, ONE question stays open -- is anything felt in there?' Which view of mind is the guest using?
answer: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a further fact about the same brain.
choices: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a further fact about the same brain.
Pattern view -- mind is the pattern, not the stuff; silicon could run it too.
Brain-state view -- once you know the wiring, you know all there is to know.
Behavior-only view -- a mind just IS how you act; nothing is felt inside.
context: Property dualism (Chalmers, The Conscious Mind, 1996) holds the world is physical, but felt experience is a further property the physical facts don't pin down. Unlike older 'separate soul' dualism, it adds no second thing -- just a second kind of fact about the very same brain.

question: A minstrel films her cat: when the laser dot vanishes, its whiskers flatten and it freezes. Was it let down? She figures the look is real evidence of a feeling, but that no one could ever confirm it from outside. Which view of mind is she using?
answer: Other-minds problem — behaviour is real evidence, but no outside test confirms the feeling.
choices: Other-minds problem — behaviour is real evidence, but no outside test confirms the feeling.
Behaviourism — the flattened-whisker behaviour just IS the disappointment, nothing more.
Anthropomorphism — the cat must feel exactly what a let-down child would feel.
Pure instinct — cats have no inner life, so the look is something humans read in.
context: The other-minds problem (Bertrand Russell, Problems of Philosophy, 1912) is sharpest for creatures we cannot ask: we read feeling off behaviour but can never check it from the inside. Behaviourism (the behaviour just IS the feeling), anthropomorphism (it feels exactly as we would), and the instinct-only view are the rival readings. The puzzle is genuinely open.

answer: Shuffling symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what the symbols mean.
choices: Shuffling symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what the symbols mean.
Any system that gives the right answers must, by that fact, truly understand them.
Understanding is impossible for anyone, since all of us merely follow hidden rules.
Machines already understand language exactly as well as a fluent human speaker does.
question: A philosopher imagines a man locked in a room who knows no Chinese, yet by following a giant rulebook he slides back paper answers so perfect that Chinese speakers outside are sure the room understands them. The man understands nothing. What did this scene aim to show?
context: This is John Searle's Chinese Room (1980), his argument against 'strong AI' — the claim that running the right program is sufficient for genuine understanding. The man inside manipulates Chinese symbols by syntax (formal rules) alone, producing perfect output, yet grasps no meaning (semantics). Searle's point: syntax is not sufficient for semantics, so passing a behavioral test for understanding does not establish that understanding is present. Critics offer the 'systems reply' (the whole room understands, even if the man doesn't); the debate it launched is one of the most argued in philosophy of mind.

question: A debate-club opponent argues: "A baby has no word for fear, so it cannot really HAVE fear — you need language before feeling is possible." Watching her cousin flinch at a crash and settle when held, the proposer answers. What is her best reply?
answer: Having a feeling does not require naming it — words report feelings, they do not create them.
choices: Having a feeling does not require naming it — words report feelings, they do not create them.
Only the baby itself could ever know, so the claim can be neither proved nor disproved.
A single crash is too small a test; only real pain could show that a baby truly feels.
Babies cannot feel anything at all until the day they begin to talk to themselves.
context: The opponent's claim — that feeling requires the words to label it — confuses REPORTING a feeling with HAVING one. A pre-verbal baby plainly flinches and is soothed; the feeling comes first and language describes it later, not the other way round. (Whether we can ever fully confirm a non-speaker's inner life is a separate, deeper puzzle — the other-minds problem, Russell, 1912.)

question: A mathematician argues: 'A thinking thing isn't tied to any one stuff. The SAME thinking could run on living brain cells or on silicon chips -- what makes it a mind is the JOB its parts do, not the material.' Which view is this?
answer: Pattern view -- mind is what it DOES, not what it's made of; silicon could think.
choices: Pattern view -- mind is what it DOES, not what it's made of; silicon could think.
Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
Brain-state view -- thought just IS a living brain's activity, nothing else.
Mystery view -- the wiring-to-thought link may sit past any human mind.
context: Alan Turing's 1950 paper proposed the imitation game (the Turing test); the idea later called functionalism says what makes a mind is the role its states play, not the material running them. Putnam and Fodor formalized it -- it lets minds run on biology or silicon.

question: A YouTube video sets up the philosophical-zombie puzzle: imagine a twin identical to you in every behaviour and brain state, yet with NO inner experience at all. Philosophers argue endlessly over this twin. What exactly are they arguing about?
answer: Whether such a twin is even conceivable -- and if so, what that proves.
choices: Whether such a twin is even conceivable -- and if so, what that proves.
Whether the twin would pass a lie-detector test about its feelings.
Whether a real machine could be built to behave just like the twin.
Whether the twin counts as the same person as you, or a new one.
context: David Chalmers' philosophical-zombie argument (The Conscious Mind, 1996): if a being behaviourally and physically identical to you yet lacking all inner experience is even coherently CONCEIVABLE, the purely physical story leaves consciousness out. Whether such a zombie is truly conceivable -- and what that would prove -- has been debated for decades. The puzzle is genuinely open.

question: An old bishop writes: 'I turn inward and find my thoughts doubting, wishing, and wondering by their own light -- while my body just sits here in the garden. How can these two be one kind of thing?' Which view of mind is he leaning on?
answer: Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
choices: Mind-separate view -- mind is a different kind of thing from the body.
Brain-state view -- the inner thought just IS the brain firing, nothing else.
Pattern view -- mind is the pattern, not the stuff; silicon could run it too.
Behavior-only view -- a mind just IS how you act; nothing is felt inside.
context: Augustine (Confessions, ~400 AD) felt a sharp split between mind and body that Descartes later made explicit in 1641. Physicalists reply that the brain is doing the 'turning inward' too -- so the felt separateness is misleading evidence about what mind really is.

question: In the Chinese Room, a man who knows no Chinese follows a huge rulebook to turn incoming symbols into outgoing ones. His replies look fluent, yet he understands not one word. What does a real Chinese speaker have that the rulebook never supplies?
answer: The MEANING of the symbols, not just rules for shuffling them.
choices: The MEANING of the symbols, not just rules for shuffling them.
A faster way to look up the right symbols in the book.
A rulebook large enough to cover every possible question.
A brain made of the same living cells a speaker has.
context: John Searle's 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980) aims the Chinese Room at strong AI -- the claim that running the right program is enough to understand. Searle's point: syntax (shuffling symbols by rule) is not semantics (grasping what they mean). His own positive view, biological naturalism, is the 'living cells' option; the Systems Reply is the main rebuttal.

question: Inverted-spectrum puzzle: you and a friend both call fire engines red and grass green -- but the colour YOU see in fire is the one SHE sees in grass, and vice versa. No behaviour could catch the swap. Could you two see colours differently inside?
answer: Maybe -- matching words and actions might still hide a different inner colour.
choices: Maybe -- matching words and actions might still hide a different inner colour.
No -- once the swap changes nothing you do, there is nothing left to differ.
No -- you share the same eyes, so the colours inside must match exactly.
No -- colour words mean nothing private, so the question never gets going.
context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, II.32) raised the inverted spectrum to ask whether qualia -- what experiences are LIKE inside -- can be pinned down by behaviour. Modern revivals (Shoemaker 1981, Block 1990) press it against functionalism, the view that a mental state just IS its causal-behavioural role. The verificationist reply (the second option) bites back: with no detectable difference, is there a fact at all?

question: An AI writes a poem that moves a reader to tears. On a podcast a guest argues: 'No matter how completely we map the machine's processing, we still won't know whether anything was FELT in making it. THAT gap is the real puzzle of consciousness.' Which view of mind is the guest using?
answer: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a real further fact, not just the wiring.
choices: Extra-property view -- the feeling is a real further fact, not just the wiring.
Pattern view -- if it plays the same role we do, no felt extra is left over.
Drop-the-word view -- 'felt' is a bad folk idea brain science will retire.
Brain-state view -- the full wiring story already IS the whole story.
context: Property dualism takes seriously the gap David Chalmers (1995) drew between the 'easy problems' (how processing works) and the 'hard problem' (why processing comes with feeling). It treats felt experience as a real extra fact about the brain -- without adding a separate soul-substance.

question: In Searle's Chinese Room, a man who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to answer Chinese notes perfectly, yet grasps nothing. 'He understands none of it,' says Searle. A defender of AI snaps: 'Wrong part -- no single neuron understands either, yet the whole brain does, as the whole ROOM does.' What is the defender's move?
answer: It is the SYSTEM that understands -- man, rulebook and paper together, not the lone man.
choices: It is the SYSTEM that understands -- man, rulebook and paper together, not the lone man.
Give the room a robot body with eyes and hands, and real understanding would follow.
Have the rulebook copy a Chinese speaker's brain neuron by neuron, and it would grasp the words.
We grant other people understanding from behaviour alone, so the room earns it too.
context: This is the Systems Reply, the most defended answer to Searle's Chinese Room ('Minds, Brains, and Programs', 1980): understanding belongs to the whole system, not the man inside, so noting that he alone is clueless misses the level. The others are the Robot, Brain-Simulator and Other-Minds replies; Searle rebutted all four.

question: Neuroscientist Mary has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room and learned every physical fact about colour vision -- wavelengths, cone cells, the lot. The day she steps out and sees a red rose, she gasps: 'Oh -- THIS is what red looks like.' Did Mary just learn something new?
answer: Yes -- what red LOOKS like is a fact no black-and-white book ever gave her.
choices: Yes -- what red LOOKS like is a fact no black-and-white book ever gave her.
No -- she already knew every physical fact, so nothing about red is left to learn.
Yes -- but only a new skill, recognising red, not any new fact about it.
No -- 'seeing' and 'knowing about' are different things, so the question is confused.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Mary's Room' (Epiphenomenal Qualia, 1982) is the knowledge argument against physicalism, the view that every fact is a physical fact: if Mary gains a new fact, the physical story left out what red is LIKE. The rival 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) is the 'only a new skill' answer; Jackson himself later leaned that way.

question: Chalmers argues a 'zombie' -- your exact physical twin with no inner experience -- is at least imaginable, and that alone dents physicalism. A critic answers: 'People once clearly imagined water that ISN'T H2O, and were flat wrong. Imagining a thing never proves it is really possible.' What is the critic's move?
answer: Being able to imagine zombies is no proof they are really possible.
choices: Being able to imagine zombies is no proof they are really possible.
Zombies are a flat contradiction -- act fully alive and you ARE conscious.
Concede the point: the zombie case really does sink physicalism.
Explain every brain function and nothing conscious is left to puzzle over.
context: The conceivability-does-not-entail-possibility reply (Yablo 1993; Stoljar; Dennett) is the leading physicalist answer to Chalmers's zombie argument. It leans on Saul Kripke (Naming and Necessity, 1980): water = H2O is a necessary truth we could only discover by experiment, so vividly imagining its failure proves nothing about what is really possible.

question: Two friends match perfectly: both call fire 'red' and grass 'green,' same reactions, same ratings - yet maybe one inwardly sees fire the way the other sees grass. A philosopher waves it off: 'No test could ever tell them apart, so there's nothing there to be right or wrong about.' Which view is she taking?
answer: No hidden fact - if no test could ever find a difference, none exists.
choices: No hidden fact - if no test could ever find a difference, none exists.
Same brains since birth, so the inner color-swap simply can't happen.
Matching outer behavior must lock in the very same inner colors.
The inner colors are real, and they really could differ unseen.
context: This is the verificationist or eliminative reply to inverted-spectrum cases (Daniel Dennett, 'Quining Qualia,' 1988): if no functional or behavioral test could ever discriminate the two, the supposed inner 'what-it-is-like' difference is a fiction. Inverted spectrum traces to Locke (Essay II.32); modern versions (Shoemaker 1981, Block 1990) press it against functionalism.

question: Mary knew every physical fact about color, shut in a black-and-white room. She steps out, sees a red rose, and says: 'I've just learned a real fact about the world - what red looks like - that none of my physics ever told me.' Which view is Mary defending?
answer: Knowledge argument - she gained a real fact her physics left out.
choices: Knowledge argument - she gained a real fact her physics left out.
Ability hypothesis - she gained only a new skill, not a new fact.
Old news - her complete physics already held this fact.
Confused question - a fact and a feel simply cannot mix.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) frames Mary's room as the knowledge argument against physicalism: if she learns a new fact on seeing red, complete physical knowledge was not complete knowledge. The leading rival is the ability hypothesis (Lewis, Nemirow) - she gains know-how, not a fact. Jackson himself later (1998) switched sides.

question: Ned Block asks us to picture a billion people, each working a radio, together copying the exact firing pattern of a brain. The system behaves just like a mind, he says, yet surely no single feeling glows in the crowd. What does this aim to show against functionalism?
answer: A system can copy the full functional pattern and still feel nothing inside.
choices: A system can copy the full functional pattern and still feel nothing inside.
A mind needs a non-physical soul the radios could never supply.
Talk of 'feelings' is folk theory neuroscience will one day drop.
Behavior is all there is, so the crowd simply has no inner side.
context: Ned Block's 'Troubles with Functionalism' (1978) calls this the 'China brain' or 'nation of China' case. The worry is ABSENT QUALIA: if matching the functional role can leave felt experience missing, then a mental state cannot be just its functional role.

question: Searle says only the right biology can be conscious; no mere program could. A critic fires back: 'That's vitalism reborn. People once swore only living things could make organic molecules - then chemists built them from dead matter. You grant consciousness the same magic, on no better evidence.' What is the critic's objection?
answer: It's vitalism again - 'only biology' is the dead-end bet that lost over life.
choices: It's vitalism again - 'only biology' is the dead-end bet that lost over life.
It ducks the deeper puzzle of why any matter feels at all from inside.
It mistakes one small part for the whole working system that thinks.
It clings to 'consciousness,' a folk word science may yet discard.
context: Searle's biological naturalism (The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992) holds consciousness is a feature of the right kind of brain, not a substrate-free computation. Critics from Daniel Dennett on press the neo-vitalism analogy: vitalists insisted only living matter could make 'organic' compounds until Wohler synthesized urea (1828) - why should consciousness get the same special pleading?

question: Churchland says future brain science will scrap 'belief' the way chemistry scrapped phlogiston. A critic shoots back: but to ASSERT that is to want you to BELIEVE it, so the claim leans on the very thing it tries to throw out. What kind of objection is the critic making?
answer: It is self-defeating: stating it already uses the category it says will vanish.
choices: It is self-defeating: stating it already uses the category it says will vanish.
Belief has predicted behavior for ages, so no theory beats its track record.
Belief should be reduced to brain states, not thrown out altogether.
Even if belief goes, raw felt experience would still be left unexplained.
context: This is the self-refutation objection (Lynne Rudder Baker, Saving Belief 1987; Jerry Fodor) to eliminative materialism. Churchland's reply: science will hand us a successor concept for belief-and-assertion too, just as it replaced phlogiston-talk. The dispute is still live.

question: One theory says a mental state turns conscious only when a SECOND state looks at it. A critic presses: then what makes THAT second state conscious - a third looking at it, then a fourth, with no end, like mirrors facing mirrors? Or does it just sit there, conscious yet unwatched? Which objection is the critic raising?
answer: The watching states form an endless chain that never bottoms out.
choices: The watching states form an endless chain that never bottoms out.
The theory predicts pairings the brain scans never actually show.
It still says nothing about what the conscious state FEELS like.
'Conscious' is folk theory that mature brain science will discard.
context: This is the regress objection to higher-order theories of consciousness, a standard worry pressed against them. David Rosenthal's higher-order-thought view replies that the higher-order state can itself be unconscious unless yet another state targets it; critics say that just concedes the puzzle.

question: Tononi's theory measures consciousness by a number, phi. A critic shows the math hands a giant grid of simple logic gates MORE phi than a wide-awake person, while a perfect brain simulation scores zero. He says a theory that ranks things so strangely should be doubted. Which objection is this?
answer: Its own formula credits the wrong systems and denies the obvious ones.
choices: Its own formula credits the wrong systems and denies the obvious ones.
Only living brains feel, so no number could ever capture it.
Consciousness is fixed by what a system DOES, not how it is wired.
'Consciousness' is folk theory mature brain science will replace.
context: Scott Aaronson ('Why I Am Not An Integrated Information Theorist,' 2014) showed simple grid and XOR networks score very high phi by IIT's own rules. Tononi answered by refining the theory's exclusion postulates; the objection is widely held to be still live.

question: A student sums up a theory of mind: 'There's no hidden ghost in the machine. To call someone intelligent isn't to name a secret inner thing -- it's to say they're DISPOSED to act intelligently. Hunting for a mind behind the behavior is a category mistake.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Behaviorism -- a mind just is a set of dispositions to behave; there is no inner thing behind the acts.
choices: Behaviorism -- a mind just is a set of dispositions to behave; there is no inner thing behind the acts.
Functionalism -- inner machinery is real and defined by the job each part does, not just the behavior.
Identity theory -- each mental state simply IS a particular brain state, nothing more and nothing less.
Dualism -- the mind is a non-physical thing the body merely houses and carries around.
context: Gilbert Ryle coined 'the ghost in the machine' in The Concept of Mind (1949) to mock the picture of a hidden inner self steering the body. His logical behaviorism says mental talk is really talk about how someone is disposed to act. Functionalism later displaced it by putting the inner causal machinery back in -- which is why only the first choice fits Ryle.

question: On a panel a guest argues: 'Pain does not merely come from a brain firing - pain IS that firing, the very same thing under another name, the way water just IS H2O.' Which view of mind is the guest using?
answer: Identity theory - each mental state simply IS a brain state.
choices: Identity theory - each mental state simply IS a brain state.
Functionalism - a state is what it DOES, so other stuff could feel pain.
Property dualism - the felt side is an extra fact the brain story misses.
Behaviorism - pain is just the wincing, with nothing felt inside.
context: Type physicalism, or identity theory (U.T. Place 1956; J.J.C. Smart, 'Sensations and Brain Processes,' 1959), holds each mental-state TYPE is strictly identical to a brain-state type. Multiple-realizability arguments (Putnam, Fodor) pushed many toward functionalism instead.

question: A student sums up a theory of mind: 'What makes a feeling PAIN isn't the stuff it runs on -- it's the job it does: damage sets it off, and it makes you wince and pull back. Nerves, silicon, or an alien -- anything doing that job feels pain.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Functionalism -- a mental state is defined by the job it does, on any hardware.
choices: Functionalism -- a mental state is defined by the job it does, on any hardware.
Identity theory -- pain just IS one specific brain event and nothing else.
Behaviorism -- pain is only the outward wincing, with no inner state at all.
Dualism -- pain is an extra non-physical thing beyond any brain event.
context: Hilary Putnam ('The Nature of Mental States,' 1967) launched functionalism. Its key claim is multiple realizability: the same mental state can run on very different hardware, so pain need not be one specific brain event (which is where identity theory differs). Jackson's Mary's Room and Block's China-brain are the famous objections, pressing on what the job-description leaves out.

question: In May 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes the question that would haunt dualism for centuries: how can the soul -- being only a THINKING thing, with no push or weight -- ever make the body's spirits move an arm to perform a voluntary action? What objection is she pressing?
answer: The mind-body gap -- nothing explains how a non-physical thought could push a physical body to move.
choices: The mind-body gap -- nothing explains how a non-physical thought could push a physical body to move.
The parsimony point -- two kinds of stuff is one kind too many; one would explain it more simply.
The physics point -- a moving body gets its push only from another body, never from a weightless thought.
The union point -- a soul might steer the body from outside, yet never truly be one thing with it.
context: Princess Elisabeth's letter of May 6, 1643, and the five-year exchange that followed, is the founding statement of the 'interaction problem.' Descartes's answers -- the pineal gland, calling mind-body union a 'primitive notion' -- struck most readers as unsatisfying. Her point isn't about simplicity or physics in the abstract; it asks for the missing MECHANISM, which is why the first choice fits.

question: McGinn says consciousness has a normal explanation, but human minds are simply built wrong to grasp it. A critic answers: to KNOW we are walled off from the answer, you would need the very God's-eye view you say we lack. Which objection is the critic raising?
answer: Claiming we cannot know it already claims to know too much.
choices: Claiming we cannot know it already claims to know too much.
Brain science keeps making progress, so nothing is walled off.
A real gap this deep points to a soul, not just to our limits.
It is mere defeatism - a hard problem is no proof of a wall.
context: This is the self-defeat objection to McGinn's mysterianism (Can We Solve the Mind-Body Problem? 1989), pressed by Owen Flanagan and Daniel Dennett. McGinn replies that we can know our faculties are LIMITED without mapping exactly where the limit falls - as a color-blind person knows they miss something.

question: A judge swaps text messages with two hidden chatters — one human, one machine — and cannot tell which is which. The machine has passed Alan Turing's imitation game. A skeptic shrugs: 'It chatted like a mind — but did it UNDERSTAND a word it typed?' Has passing settled that?
answer: No — flawless chat could be pure symbol-shuffling, leaving real understanding an open question.
choices: No — flawless chat could be pure symbol-shuffling, leaving real understanding an open question.
Yes — chatting just like a mind IS thinking; there is nothing more to understanding than that.
No — only a living brain can ever understand; no machine could, however well it chats.
The question is empty — 'understanding' is a vague word that picks out no real thing to settle.
context: Alan Turing's imitation game (1950) proposed conversation as a test for thought. Searle's Chinese Room (1980) is the classic pushback: a system can produce perfect, fluent output by shuffling symbols by rule while understanding none of it — so behaving like a mind does not settle whether anything is understood inside. The puzzle stays open.

question: Panpsychism says even tiny bits of matter carry a faint speck of experience. A critic asks: so how do countless specks ADD UP into the one whole feeling you have watching a sunset? No one has shown how the bits combine. Which objection is this?
answer: It never shows how the specks merge into one whole feeling.
choices: It never shows how the specks merge into one whole feeling.
There is simply no evidence that matter feels anything.
Only living brains can feel, never plain bits of matter.
'Experience' is folk theory brain science will one day drop.
context: This is the combination problem, raised by William James himself (Principles of Psychology, 1890) and sharpened by Sam Coleman (2014). Galen Strawson, Philip Goff, and Hedda Hassel Morch offer answers (constitutive panpsychism, cosmopsychism, phenomenal bonding); none is yet settled.

question: A philosopher points out: a rock is not ABOUT anything. But a belief is always about something - a friend, a storm, even a unicorn that does not exist. He calls this 'aboutness' the one feature that marks minds off from mere matter. Which feature is he pointing to?
answer: Intentionality - a mental state is always directed AT some object, the way the belief is about a unicorn.
choices: Intentionality - a mental state is always directed AT some object, the way the belief is about a unicorn.
Consciousness - a mental state always has a felt, what-it's-like quality the rock lacks.
Behavior - a mind shows itself only in how a body outwardly acts, not in any inner trait.
Brain-basis - a mental state is just neural firing, so 'aboutness' adds nothing real.
context: Franz Brentano (Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, 1874) revived the medieval term 'intentionality' for the directedness of mental states toward objects - their 'aboutness.' He argued this is the mark of the mental: physical things like rocks are not about anything; thoughts always are.

question: A thinker argues the mind feels things but causes nothing - it is mere 'steam off the engine,' a byproduct that pushes no levers. A critic shoots back: 'Then your own belief in this theory caused nothing either - so it could not have moved your hand to write the book defending it.' What is the critic's objection?
answer: It is self-undermining - if no belief can cause anything, his belief could not have caused the book he wrote.
choices: It is self-undermining - if no belief can cause anything, his belief could not have caused the book he wrote.
Evolution would not preserve a feeling that does no work, so the mind must do something useful.
It still never explains WHAT those feelings are like, only whether they push the levers at all.
Words like 'belief' are bad theory anyway and will be dropped entirely by future brain science.
context: Epiphenomenalism (T.H. Huxley, 1874; Frank Jackson, 1982, before he reversed) says mental events are caused by the brain but cause nothing. The self-stultification objection - pressed since William James - notes the theory undercuts its own defense: if belief moves nothing, it could not have moved anyone to assert the theory.

question: A climber dangles his partner on a rope. A dark wish flickers up — let go, save yourself — and the thought so unnerves him that his hand SHAKES and the rope slips from it by accident. His wish and belief did 'cause' the drop. But did the climber ACT to drop her?
answer: No — a real action needs the intention to GUIDE the movement, not just rattle him into a slip.
choices: No — a real action needs the intention to GUIDE the movement, not just rattle him into a slip.
Yes — his wish and belief produced the very drop they aimed at, so it counts as his action.
Yes — he wanted her to fall and she fell, so he did it; the inner pathway is a mere detail.
No — no movement is ever truly an 'action'; that word is just a story we tell about reflexes.
context: Donald Davidson's 'deviant causal chain' (Freedom to Act, 1973): actions are movements caused by your beliefs and desires IN THE RIGHT WAY. Here the wish does cause the drop — but by way of a panic tremor, not by being carried out — so it is not a genuine act. Saying exactly what 'the right way' is has resisted clean solution.

question: Surgeons cut the bridge between a patient's two brain halves to stop seizures. Afterward his LEFT hand (run by the right half) reaches for an object he swears, out loud, he never saw. Speech and hand seem to know different things. Which idea does the case press hardest?
answer: One self per body may be too simple — the split brain looks like two streams of awareness at once.
choices: One self per body may be too simple — the split brain looks like two streams of awareness at once.
He is plainly one person — one body lasts through it, so the odd results change nothing.
There is no self at all — the case shows the whole idea of a person is an illusion.
The mind must be non-physical — two streams in one skull prove a soul split from the brain.
context: Roger Sperry's split-brain studies (Nobel Prize, 1981) on patients whose corpus callosum was severed, with Michael Gazzaniga's analysis (The Bisected Brain, 1970), found the two halves processing independently — one hand acting on what the talking half denies seeing. The case strains the assumption of a single unified self; whether it shows two minds is still debated.

question: An AI writes a poem that moves a reader to tears. A panelist argues: 'Even a COMPLETE wiring diagram of the machine would still leave one question open - whether anything was actually FELT as it wrote. That gap is metaphysics, not engineering.' Which view of mind is the panelist defending?
answer: Felt-extra view - it is all physical, but feeling is a further fact the full wiring story leaves open.
choices: Felt-extra view - it is all physical, but feeling is a further fact the full wiring story leaves open.
Pattern view - mind is what a system DOES, so matching the role leaves no extra question.
Brain-state view - the mind just IS the wiring, so the full diagram already settles everything.
Drop-the-words view - 'felt experience' is a bad category future science will simply discard.
context: David Chalmers ('Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness,' 1995) splits the 'easy problems' (explaining brain function) from the 'hard problem' (why any of it is FELT). Property dualism takes that gap seriously: the world is physical, but felt experience is an extra property no complete physical description captures.

question: Mary has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room, where she learned every physical fact about light, eyes, and the brain's response to red. The day she steps outside and sees a real red rose, does she LEARN anything new?
answer: Yes -- what red LOOKS like is a fact no physics book ever gave her.
choices: Yes -- what red LOOKS like is a fact no physics book ever gave her.
No -- she already had every fact about red; seeing it adds only a knack, not a fact.
Yes -- but only because no one could really know ALL the physics of color.
No -- 'seeing red' and 'knowing red' are different things; the question is muddled.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Mary's Room' (Epiphenomenal Qualia, 1982) is the knowledge argument against physicalism -- the view that every fact is a physical fact. If Mary learns what red is LIKE, the physical story left something out. The 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) is the second choice; Jackson himself later leaned that way.

question: In Searle's Chinese Room, a man who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to swap Chinese symbols for symbols, passing out replies that read as perfectly fluent -- while understanding nothing. The case is built to deny one bold claim. Which one?
answer: That running the right program is enough, by itself, to understand.
choices: That running the right program is enough, by itself, to understand.
That a machine could ever fool a judge into thinking it is human.
That brains are the only things in nature that process information.
That the word 'understand' picks out anything real to argue about.
context: John Searle's 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980) aims the Chinese Room at 'strong AI' -- the claim that running the right program is by itself sufficient for understanding. His point: syntax (shuffling symbols) is not semantics (meaning). The Systems Reply, which says the whole room understands, is the leading rebuttal.

question: Imagine a being wired exactly like you, atom for atom, acting just as you do -- yet with no inner experience at all, all dark inside. A philosopher argues this 'zombie' need not be real, only clearly imaginable. If it IS imaginable, what follows?
answer: The full physical story leaves out whether anyone is home -- a problem for physicalism.
choices: The full physical story leaves out whether anyone is home -- a problem for physicalism.
Nothing -- we imagine impossible things too, like water that isn't H2O.
'Inner experience' is a bad idea we should drop, since it allows such weird cases.
Nothing -- acting exactly like you just IS being conscious, so no gap is left.
context: David Chalmers (The Conscious Mind, 1996) argues that if a 'philosophical zombie' is even coherently conceivable, the physical facts don't fix the facts about experience -- counting against physicalism. The standard reply (Dennett, Yablo) is the second choice: conceiving something is a weak guide to whether it is really possible.

question: Two people, raised side by side, both call fire engines 'red' and grass 'green.' But what one SEES looking at fire is what the other sees looking at grass — their inner colors are swapped. Every reaction matches: same word, same pulse, same favorite. No test could catch it. Which theory of mind does this threaten most?
answer: Functionalism — a state IS the job it does, yet two identical jobs feel different here.
choices: Functionalism — a state IS the job it does, yet two identical jobs feel different here.
Dualism — the mind is a wholly separate non-physical thing from the body.
Behaviorism — a feeling is nothing over and above the outward behavior.
Eliminativism — inner 'what it feels like' is not real and should be dropped.
context: The inverted-spectrum case (Locke, Essay II.32; Shoemaker 1981; Block 1990) is built to wound functionalism specifically: the two share every functional relation — internal causes, not just behavior — yet may differ in what experience is LIKE (the quale). If role doesn't fix the feel, role-based theories of mind are incomplete.

question: A bat hunts in the dark by sonar — a sense no human has. Suppose scientists map its brain completely: every neuron, every signal, the whole physical story of how the sonar works. Even with all of that on paper, what is still left out?
answer: What the sonar feels like from inside the bat — its own point of view on the world.
choices: What the sonar feels like from inside the bat — its own point of view on the world.
Nothing at all — a complete brain map just is the complete story of the bat.
A few faint signals that today's scanners are still too weak to record.
The phrase 'what it feels like' means nothing, so nothing has been left out.
context: Thomas Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974): the subjective character of experience — the 'what-it-is-like' — is not captured by any complete third-person physical account. The paper is an ancestor of Chalmers's hard problem and a cornerstone of anti-reductive views of mind.

question: A scientist argues: 'An octopus, a human, and a silicon alien could all feel pain. What makes a state pain is what it DOES - the alarm it raises, the avoiding it drives - not the stuff it runs on.' Which view of mind is she using?
answer: Pattern view - a state counts as pain by the ROLE it plays, so many different materials can run it.
choices: Pattern view - a state counts as pain by the ROLE it plays, so many different materials can run it.
Carbon-only view - only living tissue can feel, so the silicon alien is simply left out.
Brain-state view - pain just IS one human neural type, so octopus 'pain' cannot be the same.
Behavior-only view - pain is just wincing and fleeing, with no inner role doing any work.
context: Functionalism (Hilary Putnam, 'The Nature of Mental States,' 1967; Jerry Fodor, 1968) was driven by multiple realizability: the same mental state can run in different physical systems - octopus, human, or machine - because what fixes it is its causal role, not its material.

question: Summarizing Searle, a philosopher pictures a man sealed in a room, shuffling Chinese symbols by a rulebook - fluent replies slide out, yet nothing inside understands a word. REAL understanding, he says, takes REAL neurons; the same program in other stuff stays blind. Which view of mind is this?
answer: Brain-only view - real brains cause consciousness; a copy of the program in other stuff stays unconscious.
choices: Brain-only view - real brains cause consciousness; a copy of the program in other stuff stays unconscious.
Pattern view - run the right program in ANY stuff and you get the mind that goes with it.
Felt-extra view - it is all physical, but feeling is a further fact the brain story leaves open.
Drop-the-words view - 'consciousness' is a bad category future brain science will discard.
context: John Searle's Chinese Room ('Minds, Brains, and Programs,' 1980) and his biological naturalism (The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992) hold that consciousness is caused by and realized in real brain processes, not by running a program. His other analogy - a simulated rainstorm is not wet - marks his split from any functionalism that lets minds run on any substrate.

question: Summarizing Churchland, a student says: 'Belief, desire, hope, fear - these come from an old folk theory for predicting people. As brain science matures, it will DROP them entirely, the way chemistry dropped "phlogiston" - not keep them under new names.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Drop-the-words view - belief and desire are a failed theory that brain science will scrap, not relabel.
choices: Drop-the-words view - belief and desire are a failed theory that brain science will scrap, not relabel.
Reduce-the-words view - belief and desire are real and will be MATCHED to brain states, not dropped.
Useful-fiction view - belief talk predicts people well, so we keep it even if it names nothing deep.
Pattern view - belief and desire are real functional roles and survive as a higher-level science.
context: Paul Churchland ('Eliminative Materialism and the Propositional Attitudes,' 1981) argues folk psychology is itself a theory - and a poor one - that mature neuroscience will eliminate, not reduce, just as 'phlogiston' was scrapped. The rivals KEEP the categories: reductive physicalism matches them to brain states; Dennett's instrumentalism keeps them as a useful predictive stance.

question: A guest argues: 'A pain by itself is not yet conscious. It becomes conscious only when a SECOND state notices it. The moment you become aware of HAVING the headache - that awareness of it - is what lights the pain up.' Which view of consciousness is this?
answer: Watcher view - a state turns conscious only when a second, higher state represents it (you notice the headache).
choices: Watcher view - a state turns conscious only when a second, higher state represents it (you notice the headache).
Built-in view - the right state is already conscious by itself; no second state needs to notice it.
Broadcast view - a state is conscious when it is shared widely across the brain's many systems.
Drop-the-words view - 'conscious' is a bad category future brain science will simply discard.
context: Higher-order theories (David Rosenthal, 'Two Concepts of Consciousness,' 1986; Peter Carruthers) hold a state is conscious only when a distinct higher-order state represents it - you become aware of having it. First-order theorists (Dretske, Tye) disagree: the right first-order state is conscious on its own.

question: Neuroscientist Giulio Tononi defines consciousness as integrated information, a quantity he calls phi: a system is conscious to the degree its parts together hold more information than the parts apart. He grants this means even a thermostat has a faint flicker of it. Which view is Tononi defending?
answer: Integration view -- consciousness just IS integrated information, present to some degree in any system with phi.
choices: Integration view -- consciousness just IS integrated information, present to some degree in any system with phi.
Functionalism -- consciousness is the rich job a mind does, which a thermostat is far too simple to perform.
Biological view -- consciousness is a brain phenomenon, so no thermostat or chip could ever have any of it.
Higher-order view -- a state is conscious only when the mind notices it, which a thermostat can never do.
context: Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (2004; book Phi, 2012) identifies consciousness with integrated information. Its panpsychist edge -- positive phi anywhere means a flicker of consciousness -- is its most disputed feature; Scott Aaronson objects that simple grids then score absurdly high.

question: A cognitive scientist argues: 'Most of the brain runs in parallel, in the dark. One narrow stream wins the competition and gets BROADCAST to memory, planning, and speech all at once -- and that moment of wide broadcast just IS becoming conscious of it.' Which view of consciousness is this?
answer: Workspace view -- a state is conscious when it is broadcast widely to many systems at once.
choices: Workspace view -- a state is conscious when it is broadcast widely to many systems at once.
Higher-order view -- a state is conscious only when a separate thought turns to notice it.
Integration view -- a state is conscious by how tightly its parts weave information together.
Property dualism -- broadcast is just brain wiring and leaves the felt side wholly untouched.
context: Global Workspace Theory (Bernard Baars, 1988; Stanislas Dehaene, 2014) treats wide broadcast across cognitive systems as the conscious state. Critics grant it explains 'access' consciousness -- what we can report -- yet doubt it touches why the access is FELT at all.

question: A guest argues: 'Consciousness can't pop out of nothing. Either it appears by magic once matter gets complex enough, or it's already there in tiny amounts in matter's basic bits. The second is less spooky -- consciousness is fundamental and everywhere, like mass.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Panpsychism -- consciousness is fundamental and present in tiny degree throughout all matter.
choices: Panpsychism -- consciousness is fundamental and present in tiny degree throughout all matter.
Strong emergence -- consciousness appears only at high complexity; basic matter has none of it.
Eliminativism -- 'consciousness' is a bad folk category that a mature science will discard.
Functionalism -- only systems complex enough to run the right roles are conscious at all.
context: Panpsychism (William James; Bertrand Russell; revived by Galen Strawson 2006, Philip Goff) takes consciousness as fundamental rather than emergent. Its central headache is the 'combination problem': how would countless micro-experiences fuse into the single unified experience you actually have?

question: A philosopher argues: 'Consciousness is real and non-physical -- but it does no work. Your choice to lift your arm FELT like the cause, yet the brain did all the real causing. Mind is like the steam above a train: real, but not what pulls the cars.' A critic pounces: if the feeling did nothing, how did your BELIEF in this view ever move a hand to write it down? Which view is the philosopher defending?
answer: Epiphenomenalism -- experience is a real byproduct of the brain but causes nothing itself.
choices: Epiphenomenalism -- experience is a real byproduct of the brain but causes nothing itself.
Interactionism -- the non-physical mind is real and genuinely pushes the body into action.
Eliminativism -- experience isn't a real thing at all; a mature science will drop the idea.
Functionalism -- a mental state just IS a causal role, so a powerless one is a contradiction.
context: Epiphenomenalism (T.H. Huxley, 1874; Frank Jackson, 1982, before he recanted) says brain events cause mental events that in turn cause nothing. Its sharpest worry is self-stultification: if experience does no work, how could a BELIEF in epiphenomenalism have moved anyone's hand to write the book defending it?

question: A guest argues: 'The brain DOES produce consciousness -- there's a real, natural answer for how. But our minds may be the wrong shape to ever grasp it, the way a dog can't grasp calculus. The truth exists; we just can't reach it.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Mysterianism -- the answer is natural and real, but forever beyond our minds to grasp.
choices: Mysterianism -- the answer is natural and real, but forever beyond our minds to grasp.
Property dualism -- the gap is a real split in reality, not just a limit on our minds.
Eliminativism -- there's no real puzzle here; a mature science will drop the question.
Functionalism -- map the brain's machinery and nothing puzzling is left over to explain.
context: Colin McGinn ('Can We Solve the Mind-Body Problem?,' 1989) argued for what Owen Flanagan later dubbed new mysterianism: consciousness is natural, but human minds may be 'cognitively closed' to its explanation. The answer exists in nature, out of our reach.

question: Reading Donald Davidson, a student summarizes: 'Each mental event just IS some physical event -- no ghostly extra stuff. Yet no strict laws tie mental KINDS, like belief or desire, to brain kinds.' Jaegwon Kim presses: if no law links belief to any brain-kind, what work is the belief left to do? Which view is the student describing?
answer: Anomalous monism -- each mental event IS physical, but no rule ties mental KINDS to brain kinds.
choices: Anomalous monism -- each mental event IS physical, but no rule ties mental KINDS to brain kinds.
Type physicalism -- each mental KIND, like belief, reduces neatly to one specific brain-state kind.
Property dualism -- a physical event also carries extra mental properties not found in the physics.
Eliminativism -- belief and desire are a bad folk theory, so no reduction question even arises.
context: Donald Davidson's 'Mental Events' (1970) calls this anomalous monism: physical token by token, but with no psychophysical laws, so the mental stays irreducible as a kind. The balance is delicate -- Jaegwon Kim pressed that mental properties left with no lawful role risk doing no causal work.

question: Mary knew every physical fact about color from inside a black-and-white room, then saw red for the first time and learned what red is LIKE. A physicalist answers: 'Like 'Hesperus' and 'Phosphorus' both naming Venus, her old knowledge and her new sight pick out the SAME thing two ways.' On this reply, what did Mary actually gain?
answer: A new way to think about a fact she already had — a fresh concept, not a new fact.
choices: A new way to think about a fact she already had — a fresh concept, not a new fact.
A brand-new non-physical fact that her complete science had wholly left out.
A new skill at picturing red in her head, but no knowledge of any kind at all.
Nothing real at all — 'red-feel' is a confused idea that science will drop.
context: This is the phenomenal-concepts strategy (Brian Loar, 'Phenomenal States,' 1990; David Papineau, 2002), the leading physicalist reply to Frank Jackson's Mary's Room (1982). Physical and phenomenal concepts refer to one property under different cognitive modes, so the famous 'gap' is epistemic, not metaphysical.

question: When Descartes argued the mind is a non-physical, indivisible thing that could exist without the body, Princess Elisabeth shot back: how can something with no body or location PUSH a physical arm into motion? His critics still press it. Which view was Descartes defending?
answer: Substance dualism -- mind and body are two different kinds of stuff that can exist apart.
choices: Substance dualism -- mind and body are two different kinds of stuff that can exist apart.
Property dualism -- there's only physical stuff, but it carries irreducible mental properties.
Type physicalism -- the mind just IS the brain, named differently; no second substance exists.
Functionalism -- mind is a job a system does, runnable on brains or chips, not a special stuff.
context: Rene Descartes (Meditations, 1641) split reality into res cogitans (thinking stuff) and res extensa (extended stuff). Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia's 1643 letters pressed the interaction problem -- how a non-physical mind moves a physical body -- which keeps dualism a minority view today.

question: An octopus, a human, and a silicon alien can all be in pain, a thinker argues, yet each one's pain is just some physical event firing in that creature. So pain as a KIND is tied to no single brain-state, though every instance is physical. Which view is this?
answer: Token-physical -- each pain IS a brain event, but the kind 'pain' fits no one brain-state.
choices: Token-physical -- each pain IS a brain event, but the kind 'pain' fits no one brain-state.
Type-identity -- 'pain' just IS one brain-state, so octopus and human can't share it.
Two-substance -- pain is a non-physical event that no brain event could be.
No-such-state -- 'pain' is just a folk word real brain science will replace.
context: Token physicalism keeps materialism while granting that mental kinds need not carve nature at the same joints as physical kinds: every pain is a physical event, but 'pain' the type need not equal any one neural type. It is sustained by multiple-realizability arguments (Putnam, Fodor). Davidson's anomalous monism reaches the same token-identity by a different route -- the absence of strict psychophysical laws, not multiple realizability.

question: At a philosophy-of-mind seminar a guest presses the case: 'Grant that pain always fires the same brain cells. Science can map exactly what those cells DO and how they drive behavior — yet that whole story never says why any of it feels like anything from the inside.' His worry about the ache being 'lit up' fits which view?
answer: Hard problem — the felt quality is real, and the full physical story still leaves out why it's there.
choices: Hard problem — the felt quality is real, and the full physical story still leaves out why it's there.
Illusion — 'felt-ness' is just a folk idea that mature brain science will end up discarding.
Already solved — pin down what pain DOES, and nothing felt is left over to explain at all.
Mere confusion — the gap only seems real; we simply can't yet picture the physics of it.
context: Joseph Levine named the 'explanatory gap' (1983); David Chalmers (1995) sharpened it into the 'hard problem' of consciousness. The rival replies are real: eliminativists (the Churchlands) deny the felt category, functionalists dissolve it into role, and a-priori physicalists call the gap a trick of our concepts, not a fact about reality.

question: Otto, whose memory fails, writes every fact in a notebook he trusts and consults exactly as Inga trusts her memory. Andy Clark argues that when Otto reads 'the museum is on 53rd Street,' the notebook is literally PART of his belief -- mind isn't sealed inside the skull. Which view is Clark defending?
answer: Extended-mind -- a trusted notebook doing memory's job is literally part of the belief.
choices: Extended-mind -- a trusted notebook doing memory's job is literally part of the belief.
Inner-only -- real beliefs sit in the brain; the notebook is just a tool he reads.
Two-substance -- the mind is non-physical, so no object could ever be part of it.
No-belief -- 'belief' is a folk word brain science will drop, notebook or not.
context: Andy Clark and David Chalmers, 'The Extended Mind' (1998), argue the parity principle: if a process outside the head plays the same role as one inside, both count as cognition. Critics (Adams & Aizawa, Rupert) deny the parity and insist on a 'mark of the cognitive' that stops at the skin.

question: Putnam imagines a brain in a vat, wired to a computer feeding it a whole fake life. Surprisingly, he argues it could NOT truly think 'I am a brain in a vat' -- its word 'vat' was only ever caused by vat-fed images, never real vats. Which view of meaning does his reply need?
answer: Tracking -- a word means what caused it, so its 'vat' picks out the computer's vat-feed.
choices: Tracking -- a word means what caused it, so its 'vat' picks out the computer's vat-feed.
Meaning-in-head -- meaning sits wholly in the mind, so its words could reach real vats.
Convention -- a word means whatever the local community agrees to call things.
No-meaning -- 'meaning' is a folk idea cognitive science will one day drop.
context: Hilary Putnam (Reason, Truth and History, 1981) uses semantic externalism -- first defended in 'The Meaning of Meaning' (1975, Twin Earth) -- to defuse radical skepticism: if a word means whatever caused it in one's environment, the brain-in-a-vat's 'vat' only ever picks out the computer's feed, so the thought 'I am a brain in a vat' can't get a grip from inside.

question: Locke imagines a prince's whole consciousness -- every palace memory -- waking up overnight in a cobbler's body, while the cobbler's old body now thinks and remembers as the prince. Locke says the person who wakes IS the prince, in a cobbler's body. Which view of personal identity is this?
answer: Memory-link -- you persist as long as your consciousness reaches back in memory.
choices: Memory-link -- you persist as long as your consciousness reaches back in memory.
Same-body -- you persist as the same living organism, whatever you remember.
Same-soul -- you persist as one immaterial soul behind every change of body.
No-self -- no one truly endures; each is just a run of passing experiences.
context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II ch. 27, added in the 1694 second edition) uses the prince-and-cobbler case to ground personal identity in consciousness: a person is whoever can extend consciousness back to earlier experience -- gaps like sleep allowed. Derek Parfit (1984) later widened this into psychological-continuity theory and pressed the hard branching cases.

question: Two addicts crave heroin and use it. One simply wants it and shoots up with no inner protest. The other hates that he wants it — deep down he wishes the craving had no hold on him, yet it drags him along anyway. A philosopher says only the second one shows what free will really is. What sets the second addict apart?
answer: He wants not to want it — a desire ABOUT his desires, which the first addict flatly lacks.
choices: He wants not to want it — a desire ABOUT his desires, which the first addict flatly lacks.
His craving was caused by prior states, so it can't count as a real reason to act.
If any desire at all is caused, then neither addict was ever genuinely free.
His inner wish is mere brain noise that changes nothing he actually does.
context: Harry Frankfurt, 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person' (1971): a 'person' is a creature with second-order desires — desires about which first-order desires move him. The 'unwilling' addict has them; the 'wanton' does not. Critics (Watson, Wolf) ask what makes the higher wish authoritative without an endless regress.
