question: Before sailing, every sailor signed the ship's articles by hand. The bosun says the no-grog-on-watch rule binds because they all signed. Which view of authority is he using?
answer: Consent -- the rule binds because everyone signed on to it.
choices: Consent -- the rule binds because everyone signed on to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the ship has always done it.
Strength -- it binds because the captain can enforce it.
Merit -- it binds because the ablest sailor chose it.
context: Consent theory (Locke, Rousseau) holds that rules bind only those who agreed to them. A ship's articles, signed by every hand before sailing, were a real consent device on merchant and pirate crews alike: the signature is what turns a captain's order into a rule the crew owes. The bosun's tell is 'they all signed.'

question: Coach Reeves keeps the same pre-game huddle. He says: 'Every team since 1962 has done it this way -- that's what makes us this team.' Which view of authority is Coach using?
answer: Tradition -- it binds because the team has always done it.
choices: Tradition -- it binds because the team has always done it.
Consent -- it binds because the players agreed to it.
Strength -- it binds because the coach can enforce it.
Merit -- it binds because the best player chose it.
context: Tradition theory (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) grounds authority in continuity: long-standing practice carries knowledge no single person could design from scratch. Coach's tell is 'since 1962.'

question: On the playground the biggest sixth-grader announces who gets the swings. He tells Ana: 'Rules are whatever I say -- try to stop me.' Which view of authority is he using?
answer: Strength -- it binds because he can make you obey.
choices: Strength -- it binds because he can make you obey.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because it's always been done.
Anarchism -- no rule really binds anyone at all.
context: Strength theory is what Thrasymachus defends in Plato's Republic: 'justice is the advantage of the stronger.' Socrates rejects it -- force can compel, but compulsion alone does not make a rule just. The boy's tell is 'try to stop me.'

question: Navigator Priya alone sets the ship's heading by the stars. She tells them: 'I'm the one trained to read the sky -- so the heading is mine to set.' Whose reasoning fits Priya's?
answer: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
choices: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
context: Priya grounds authority in being best-qualified -- the idea behind Plato's 'philosopher-kings' in the Republic: those who know best should rule. The hard part, critics note, is agreeing on who actually knows best.

question: A sailor refuses to sign the ship's articles: 'No captain truly owns my obedience -- I haul the rope when I choose to, never because I'm bound.' Whose reasoning fits the sailor's?
answer: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
choices: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: The sailor's claim -- that no rule has real hold on you, so obeying is always a free choice -- is the anarchist view (from Greek 'anarkhia', no ruler). Tolstoy and Henry David Thoreau (Civil Disobedience) argued obedience is chosen, never owed.

question: The scout troop votes on which lake to camp by. Leon says: 'We voted, so the winning pick binds everyone -- even the kids who wanted the other lake.' Whose reasoning fits Leon's?
answer: Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
choices: Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: Leon grounds the rule in agreement: even those who lost the vote are bound, because they agreed in advance to settle it by voting. Locke called this 'tacit consent' to the rules of the game.

question: A senior knight defends the night-watch rotation: 'The company has kept it for seven generations. Custom holds knowledge no captain could write down.' Whose reasoning fits his?
answer: Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
choices: Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
context: The knight grounds authority in inherited custom -- Edmund Burke's argument (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790): long practice carries collective knowledge no single person could design from scratch.

question: Big brother Sam grabs the remote: 'Take it from me if you can -- whoever holds it picks the show. That's the only rule that actually counts here.' Whose reasoning fits Sam's?
answer: Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
choices: Strength -- it binds because the strong can enforce it.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: Sam's 'might makes right' is the view Thrasymachus defends in Plato's Republic: justice is just the advantage of the stronger. Socrates rejects it -- force can compel, but compulsion alone doesn't make a rule just.

question: As the wounded are carried in, the field surgeon decides who is treated first: 'I'm the one trained to read these wounds -- so the call is mine to make.' Whose view is she using?
answer: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
choices: Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
context: The surgeon grounds authority in expertise -- the pilot flies the plane, the navigator reads the sky. It echoes Plato's philosopher-kings; the standing challenge is how a group picks who really is the expert.

question: When the curfew bell rings, old Mara keeps her lamp lit in the window: 'No town council owns my obedience -- I keep their rules only when I please.' Whose view is Mara using?
answer: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
choices: Anarchism -- no rule truly binds; obeying is your choice.
Consent -- it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition -- it binds because the group always has done it.
Merit -- it binds because the most-qualified one decides.
context: Mara's 'I obey only when I please' is the anarchist view: genuine cooperation can't be commanded, only chosen. Kropotkin and Emma Goldman argued obedience is always a free choice, never a duty owed to an institution.

question: Before sailing, a ship's crew met and elected their captain by open vote. When a sailor resents an order, a mate reminds him: 'We all chose him — that vote is why his command binds us.' Which view of authority is the mate using?
answer: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
choices: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because crews always have.
Strength — it binds because the captain enforces it.
Merit — it binds because the captain knows the sea.
context: Consent theory grounds authority in agreement. Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau all argued the legitimate state begins with a 'social contract' — a moment, real or implied, when free people agree to be bound, turning raw power into rightful command.

question: A student tells the principal: 'Even if you vote to ban our paper, you can't — the right to read stands whether the school votes for it or not.' Which view is she using?
answer: Natural rights — some rights stand above any rule.
choices: Natural rights — some rights stand above any rule.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the school always has.
Strength — it binds because leaders enforce it.
context: Natural-rights theory (Locke, Aquinas before him) holds some rights belong to people by virtue of being human. A school or state can recognize or violate them, but cannot create or vote them out of existence.

question: A clan elder explains the standing-stones vigil: 'We keep it because our people always have. Generations of practice know what words can't capture.' Which view is she using?
answer: Tradition — it binds because the group always has.
choices: Tradition — it binds because the group always has.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Strength — it binds because the powerful enforce it.
Merit — it binds because the wisest member set it.
context: Burke argued reforms should respect what generations of practice have shown to work, even when no one can fully explain WHY it does. Long-running customs carry collective wisdom — 'the latent wisdom that prevails in them' (Reflections, 1790).

question: A newcomer never signed the village's founding oath, yet lives by its rules. When he protests one, an elder answers: 'By staying and sharing our wells, you accepted them — that's why they bind you.' Which view is the elder using?
answer: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
choices: Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the village always has.
Strength — it binds because leaders enforce it.
Anarchism — no village rule really binds you at all.
context: Locke distinguished express consent (you sign or vote) from tacit consent — the newcomer's case: by enjoying a community's roads and protection, you accept its rules even without signing. Both turn raw power into authority by tying the rule back to agreement.

question: In Plato's Republic, Thrasymachus snaps at Socrates: 'Justice is the advantage of the stronger — a rule binds only because the powerful enforce it.' Which view is he defending?
answer: Strength — it binds only because the powerful enforce it.
choices: Strength — it binds only because the powerful enforce it.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the group always has.
Merit — it binds because the wisest one decides.
context: Thrasymachus states the strength theory in Republic I (Plato, ~380 BC). Socrates replies that if might alone made right, a powerful thief would be just — an absurdity that refutes the theory. The exchange has shaped political philosophy for 2,400 years.

question: The guild raised hands to vote on how to forge the king's blade. The old master overruled them: 'I've forged swords for forty years — the one who knows the craft decides, not a show of hands.' Which view is the master using?
answer: Merit — it binds because the expert knows best.
choices: Merit — it binds because the expert knows best.
Consent — it binds because everyone agreed to it.
Tradition — it binds because the guild always has.
Strength — it binds because the king demands it.
context: Authority-by-merit (technocracy) grants decision-power to demonstrated expertise — here, the master overruling the vote. It can be efficient, but raises a hard question: who certifies the expert, and what happens when the experts disagree?

question: A monitor denies a hungry boy lunch over a lost ticket. Theo: 'Food's a basic right!' Mara: 'Feeding him is decent -- but call it his *right* and you've drafted the cook to work for free.' What distinction is Mara drawing?
answer: A liberty asks others to leave you be; a food right makes someone serve you.
choices: A liberty asks others to leave you be; a food right makes someone serve you.
A custom outranks a fresh rule whenever the two happen to collide.
A kind act and a cruel act get judged by one and the same standard.
A wise expert, not the hungry boy, should decide who gets to eat.
context: Negative rights -- speech, conscience, property, moving freely -- only ask others to LEAVE YOU ALONE. A positive 'right' to a good like food, housing, or care requires others to PROVIDE it: the cook's labor, the farmer's grain, the taxpayer's money. Locke, Bastiat, and Nozick held only the first kind are truly natural, since no one is born owing you their work; the Declaration's 'unalienable rights' are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, not a claim on the baker. Feeding the child may still be a real duty of charity -- but that is the giver's virtue, not the boy's enforceable claim. (FDR's 1944 'economic bill of rights' argued the other way; it is steel-manned in its own question.)

question: Rousseau opened his most famous book with a thunderclap: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' What did he say could ever make those chains legitimate?
answer: Consent — the free agreement of the governed
choices: Consent — the free agreement of the governed
Tradition — the long custom of the elders
Strength — the power of whoever rules now
Merit — the judgment of the wisest one
context: Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762), building on Locke (1689), argued that legitimate rule begins only when free people agree to it — not from force or inherited custom. The chains bind justly only where the governed have, in some real sense, said yes.

question: Since no one is born another's master, the printer Proudhon argued, no king or majority can set its commands above your own judgment. What did he conclude about every government?
answer: No ruler holds real authority over you
choices: No ruler holds real authority over you
Only the elected hold real authority
Only the wisest hold real authority
Only the strongest hold real authority
context: In 1840 Pierre-Joseph Proudhon became the first person to call himself an anarchist on purpose. Anarchism (later Bakunin, Kropotkin) denies that any state holds legitimate authority at all; order, it argues, should grow from free cooperation, never from a power that can command and punish you.

question: In Plato's ideal city, only those who truly KNOW the good may rule — he called them philosopher-kings. What is his basis for who should hold power?
answer: Merit — the one who truly knows should rule
choices: Merit — the one who truly knows should rule
Consent — those who agreed should rule
Tradition — those who always ruled should rule
Strength — the one who can enforce should rule
context: Authority-by-merit traces to Plato (Republic, ~375 BC): rule belongs to those with real knowledge of the good. It fits fields like medicine or piloting, but raises a hard question elsewhere — who certifies the expert, and what happens when the experts disagree?

question: A new market-fair rule passes the council of squires. Maya tells a doubter: 'Every councilor voted yes. That vote itself — not custom, not the captain — is what binds us.' Which view is Maya using?
answer: Consent — the vote itself is what binds us
choices: Consent — the vote itself is what binds us
Tradition — the council has always voted so
Merit — the ablest councilor drafted it
Strength — leaders can punish those who dodge
context: Consent theory (Locke, 1689; Rousseau, 1762) grounds authority in the agreement of the governed. Maya makes the democratic move exactly: the vote is not merely how the rule passed — the agreement itself IS the whole claim to legitimacy.

question: As revolutionary France tore down its ancient institutions in 1790, Edmund Burke wrote a famous warning against sweeping them away. Why did he say a centuries-old custom deserves the benefit of the doubt?
answer: It carries lessons learned over many lifetimes
choices: It carries lessons learned over many lifetimes
It was chosen by today's majority vote
It was designed by a single expert mind
It is backed by whoever holds power now
context: Burke (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) argued that a practice surviving many generations holds tested wisdom no lone planner can replace, so the burden falls on the reformer to justify the change. The reply to Burke: custom can also entrench injustice.

question: Plato's ideal city is ruled by philosopher-kings — those who alone truly know the good. A captain echoes him to squires: 'The master studied this for years. She knows what we don't.' Which view is he using?
answer: Merit — her hard-won expertise is what binds
choices: Merit — her hard-won expertise is what binds
Consent — the company voted the rule in
Tradition — warriors have long eaten this way
Strength — she can bench any squire she likes
context: Authority-by-merit (Plato's philosopher-kings, Republic) grounds rule in superior knowledge of the good. Critics answer that knowing best is not the same as the right to bind — even a wise doctor cannot force her diet on you without your say.

question: Without government, Hobbes warned, life is 'nasty, brutish, and short.' So people trade some freedom for safety. Sara invokes that trade to defend her guild's rules. Which view is she using?
answer: Social contract — a trade is what binds us
choices: Social contract — a trade is what binds us
Tradition — guilds have long had such rules
Merit — the sharpest member wrote them
Strength — leaders can kick out rule-breakers
context: Social contract theory (Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651; later Locke and Rousseau) says people would rationally trade some liberty for shared benefits like peace. Sara's 'trade' is that move: plain consent needs only agreement, while the contract adds the mutual gain that motivates it.

question: In Plato's Republic, Thrasymachus snaps at Socrates: 'Justice is just the advantage of the stronger — whoever can shove the rest sets the rules.' Which view of authority is he voicing?
answer: Might-makes-right — raw power to enforce is itself the authority.
choices: Might-makes-right — raw power to enforce is itself the authority.
Consent — the weaker agreed in advance to follow the stronger.
Tradition — the city has long let the strongest rule it.
Merit — the strongest has earned the right to rule the rest.
context: Thrasymachus makes this claim in Plato's Republic I (~380 BC). Socrates' reply lands the point: then a powerful thief who can enforce his will would count as 'just' — which shows that what power CAN do and what is RIGHT are not the same thing.

question: Priya tells the principal the dress code must bind every student alike, no exemptions by background: 'We're all created equal — a fair school treats us as equals.' Which idea of justice is Priya appealing to?
answer: Equal treatment — justice means no group gets favored or exempted.
choices: Equal treatment — justice means no group gets favored or exempted.
Liberty — justice means students pick their own clothes, code or not.
Greatest good — justice means whatever outcome helps the most kids.
Custom — justice means keeping the dress code the school always had.
context: Egalitarianism holds that justice requires treating people as moral equals. The line 'all men are created equal' runs from Rousseau through the American founding to Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971), which built fairness on equal standing.

question: The chess-club president wants tournaments made mandatory. Pablo refuses: 'A club can't CONSCRIPT you — it binds you only if you freely chose to join.' Which idea of authority is Pablo defending?
answer: Liberty-first — rules may not override a free choice to take part.
choices: Liberty-first — rules may not override a free choice to take part.
Equal treatment — a rule is fine so long as it binds every member alike.
Greatest good — a rule is fine if mandatory play helps the club most.
Power — the president runs the club, so she may simply require it.
context: Libertarianism (Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) makes individual liberty the primary political value: a group may not conscript your participation, and any rule that overrides a free choice needs strong justification. The clash with equal-treatment and greatest-good views runs through modern debates.

question: The captain made everyone 'agree' to extra practice by warning that anyone who refused would be benched. They all signed. Aiden says that doesn't make the rule legitimate. Why isn't 'they all signed' enough?
answer: A name signed to dodge the bench isn't free — fear produced it, not agreement.
choices: A name signed to dodge the bench isn't free — fear produced it, not agreement.
It counts — once you sign your name, you're bound no matter why you signed.
It counts — most of the players wanted the extra practice anyway.
It's fine — the captain outranks them, so her call simply settles it.
context: Consent theory requires VOLUNTARY agreement; coerced consent ('sign or be punished') fails the precondition. Locke's Second Treatise (1689) requires a real freedom to refuse — a signature given under threat doesn't supply it.

question: Eight kids vote to ban one quiet kid from the back-row bus seats. The vote was clean — eight hands up. Layla still says it is unjust. What is her sharpest point?
answer: More hands in the air cannot turn unfair treatment into fair treatment.
choices: More hands in the air cannot turn unfair treatment into fair treatment.
The vote should be run again until the quiet kid finally wins it.
Only the bus driver has the real authority to assign the seats.
A larger group is always wiser than a smaller group of kids.
context: This is the 'tyranny of the majority' worry — Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) and Mill (On Liberty, 1859) warned that a clean majority vote can still crush one person's fair treatment. A vote settles process (how many wanted it); justice is a separate question (does it treat each kid rightly).

question: The principal moves to shut the school paper. Reese answers: 'Free speech isn't the school's to GRANT — we already have it. They can recognize the right, never invent it.' Which view of rights is Reese using?
answer: Natural rights — some rights exist before any rule and are only recognized.
choices: Natural rights — some rights exist before any rule and are only recognized.
Rights-from-rules — a right is real only once a rulebook lists it.
Rights-from-custom — a right holds because the school long allowed it.
Rights-from-deal — a right comes from a bargain students struck with staff.
context: Natural-rights theory (Locke, 1689; Aquinas's natural law before him) holds some rights — life, liberty, free conscience — belong to people simply as humans, prior to any government. Legal positivism denies any rights before law writes them.

question: Asked if a right can exist before the law names it, a positivist insists: 'A right exists only when valid law creates it — so an enslaved person in 1850 had NO right to liberty.' Which view of rights is this?
answer: Rights-from-rules — a right exists only because a rulebook creates it.
choices: Rights-from-rules — a right exists only because a rulebook creates it.
Natural rights — a right exists before any rulebook and is only recognized.
Rights-from-custom — a right holds because the law long allowed it.
Rights-from-deal — a right comes from a bargain people struck with rulers.
context: Legal positivism (Bentham, 1789; H.L.A. Hart, The Concept of Law, 1961) denies natural rights: a legal right exists only because valid law creates it. The 1850 case is the classic challenge — if the slave had no right to liberty merely because the law denied one, the view seems to lose the ground from which to call that law unjust.

question: VP Adams bans phones at lunch over Mara's protest that it's her choice: 'A few lose out, but lunch ends up better for the most students — so the rule is just.' Which idea of justice is Adams using?
answer: Greatest good — a rule is just if it helps the most people on balance.
choices: Greatest good — a rule is just if it helps the most people on balance.
Liberty — a rule is just only if it leaves the phone choice to each student.
Natural rights — a rule is just only if it respects a right held beforehand.
Equal treatment — a rule is just only if it binds every student alike.
context: Utilitarian justice (Bentham, 1789; J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism, 1861) judges rules by the total good they produce — Bentham's 'greatest happiness.' Critics object that the sum can run over an individual's choice or right when the numbers favor it, exactly as it runs over Mara here.

question: Asked why the class president may set a fundraising goal, Hassan answers: 'Her authority isn't her own — we handed it to her by the vote, for a term, to serve us.' Which view of authority is this?
answer: Consent — authority comes from the vote by which people agreed.
choices: Consent — authority comes from the vote by which people agreed.
Merit — authority comes from her being the most capable leader.
Tradition — authority comes from presidents having long set goals.
Power — authority comes from the clout the office hands her.
context: Election-as-consent runs from Locke's Second Treatise (1689) through modern constitutional democracies: a vote transfers a measure of authority to the official for a fixed term, held in trust and conditional on serving the voters' interests.

question: Sasha proposes the stranded castaways' first rule: 'Each gives up the right to grab whatever he likes — and in return, none of us fears the night. That trade is what binds us.' Which view fits her reasoning?
answer: Social contract — trade some freedom for shared safety
choices: Social contract — trade some freedom for shared safety
Strength theory — the biggest castaway makes the rules
Tradition theory — islands have always had such customs
Authority-by-merit — the cleverest castaway should decide
context: Social contract theory (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651; Locke; Rousseau) stresses the TRADE — each person surrenders a little liberty so all gain a security no one had alone. Sasha's 'in return' is the contract theorist's signature move; mere agreement names no gain, and raw strength names no trade.

question: A senior posts new debate-club rules and says: 'Nobody objected, so everyone agreed.' Ben thinks that is too quick. What is his best reply?
answer: Staying quiet can mean fear, or never seeing the post — not agreement.
choices: Staying quiet can mean fear, or never seeing the post — not agreement.
A rule is never binding unless every single member has signed it.
The senior lacked the rank to post any new club rules at all.
Silence always means a person secretly disagrees with the rule.
context: Treating silence as agreement is the weak 'tacit consent' move. Locke (Second Treatise, 1689) allowed tacit consent only when people had a real chance to dissent — posting rules with no warning denies that chance, so quiet here signals confusion or fear, not a yes.

question: A craftsman earned his gold fairly — no buyer forced. A lord would seize it for the village. The craftsman objects: 'I forced no one; however unequal it looks, this gold is justly mine.' Which view fits him?
answer: Libertarian — what you fairly earn is yours to keep
choices: Libertarian — what you fairly earn is yours to keep
Egalitarian — equals should share it out evenly
Utilitarian — give it where it does the most good
Strength theory — the lord is strongest, so he decides
context: This is Robert Nozick's entitlement view (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974): if you acquired something fairly and forced no one, it is justly yours however unequal the result — and a ruler redistributing it overrides that. Rawls drew a different line, judging justice by the final pattern, not the path to it.

question: A storm splits the crew over the route. The captain ends it: 'The navigator alone can read the stars and chart our course — that is what makes her word law at sea.' Which view fits the captain?
answer: Authority-by-merit — the one who knows best decides
choices: Authority-by-merit — the one who knows best decides
Consent theory — the crew signed on under her command
Strength theory — she could have mutineers thrown overboard
Tradition theory — ships have always trusted a navigator
context: Authority-by-merit (echoing Plato's 'philosopher-kings,' Republic Book VI) grounds a ruling in superior knowledge and access — clearest in skilled roles like navigators, doctors, and pilots. Its limit: experts still err, and merely knowing best is not the same as a right to bind others.

question: A herald reads the new charter: 'Peasant and noble alike stand equal before the law — a just realm weighs every subject the same.' A baron insists rank should still decide. Which view does the charter take?
answer: Egalitarian — treat everyone as a moral equal
choices: Egalitarian — treat everyone as a moral equal
Libertarian — let each subject choose his own station
Utilitarian — do whatever pleases the most subjects
Tradition theory — keep the old order of rank and birth
context: Egalitarianism holds that justice means treating people as moral equals ('all men are created equal'; Rawls, 1971). It does not forbid ALL differences — people can genuinely need different things — but it demands a real reason for any unequal treatment, never rank or birth alone.

question: A young smith wants to scrap a guild rite overnight. The old master refuses: 'Kept and tested since the first masters — that long practice is what gives the rule its force.' Which view fits the master?
answer: Tradition theory — long-tested custom carries the weight
choices: Tradition theory — long-tested custom carries the weight
Consent theory — every smith swore an oath to the guild
Authority-by-merit — the master simply knows the craft best
Utilitarian — the old rite just gives better results
context: Edmund Burke's classic argument (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790): customs that survive generations encode tested wisdom no single planner could reproduce, so the burden falls on the reformer who would tear them down overnight. The standing reply: longevity is not proof — an old custom can also be unjust.

question: A class president pushes a rule that targets only Dani's math team. Challenged, she shrugs: 'I won the election fair and square.' Why does that not settle it?
answer: Winning grants the office, not a free pass to make any rule fair.
choices: Winning grants the office, not a free pass to make any rule fair.
She must hold a second vote before any new rule can count.
Only a teacher may decide which clubs meet on Friday afternoons.
An election winner can never pass a rule that is unfair.
context: Winning an election justifies holding the office, not every decision made from it — whether a particular rule is fair is a further question. This was Mill's concern in On Liberty (1859): an officeholder's democratic mandate doesn't immunize her policies from being judged unjust.

question: A minstrel argues free speech is a right even where no law protects it: 'The page didn't make it a right; it already was one. Burn the charter tomorrow and the right still stands.' Whose view of rights is this?
answer: Natural rights — it exists before any law, so tearing up the charter can't erase it.
choices: Natural rights — it exists before any law, so tearing up the charter can't erase it.
Legal positivism — a right is real only once some law writes it down.
Convention — a right is whatever a society currently agrees to treat as one.
Contract — a right holds because fair-minded people would all agree to it.
context: Natural-rights theory (Locke, Two Treatises 1689; Aquinas' natural law before him) holds some rights belong to people simply as humans, prior to any government. The tell here is the repeal test: a natural right survives the law that names it.

question: Jeremy Bentham mocked natural rights as 'nonsense upon stilts': no right exists, he argued, until real law creates one. Before a country writes free speech into its code, claiming the right is just wishful thinking. Whose view of rights is this?
answer: Legal positivism — no right exists until some law actually creates it.
choices: Legal positivism — no right exists until some law actually creates it.
Natural rights — the right is there already; law only recognizes it.
Convention — a right is whatever the community treats as one in practice.
Contract — a right holds because fair-minded people would all agree to it.
context: Bentham's 'nonsense upon stilts' jab comes from his Anarchical Fallacies; H.L.A. Hart (The Concept of Law, 1961) is the modern version. On this view a right is a fact created by valid law, not something true before it. Critics ask: did enslaved people in 1850 truly have NO right to liberty?

question: A debater says rights are real but man-made, like the rules of chess or the grammar of a language: they hold only while we keep playing by them, and the day people stop honoring a right, it is simply gone. Whose view of rights is this?
answer: Convention — a right is a shared agreement, real only while people keep it.
choices: Convention — a right is a shared agreement, real only while people keep it.
Natural rights — a right is built into human nature, found not agreed.
Legal positivism — a right is real only once it is written into law.
Contract — a right is what people would accept before knowing their place.
context: Conventionalism holds rights are real but socially made — like the rules of chess or a language: binding while we keep them up, gone once we stop. Hume's account of justice (Treatise, 1739) is an early version, treating justice as an 'artificial virtue' that arises from human practice, not from nature or a statute.

question: Rawls asked you to choose society's rules from behind a 'veil of ignorance' — not knowing whether you'd be born rich or poor, strong or weak. A right is legitimate, he said, only if you'd accept it blind. Whose view of rights is this?
answer: Contract — a right is what people would agree to without knowing who they'd be.
choices: Contract — a right is what people would agree to without knowing who they'd be.
Natural rights — a right is built into human nature, prior to any bargain.
Legal positivism — a right is real only once some law writes it down.
Convention — a right is whatever a community happens to honor in practice.
context: Contract theory grounds rights in what people could agree to. Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) added the 'veil of ignorance': bargain as if you don't know your place in society, and you won't rig the rules in your own favor. The blind bargain — not a vote, not a statute — is the tell.

question: MacIntyre argued a 'right' with no community behind it is like a chess move with no game to play it in: strip away the shared tradition and history that give the right its meaning, and you're left with an empty slogan. Whose view is this?
answer: Communitarian — a right draws its meaning from a lived tradition and history.
choices: Communitarian — a right draws its meaning from a lived tradition and history.
Natural rights — a right belongs to every human, no community needed.
Legal positivism — a right is real only once it is written into law.
Contract — a right is what detached, fair-minded people would agree to.
context: Communitarianism (MacIntyre, After Virtue 1981; Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice 1982) argues moral ideas get their grip from concrete communities — so a 'right' floating free of any shared tradition is empty. Note the contrast with convention: the issue is where a right gets its MEANING (tradition), not merely whether people currently honor it. The roots are Aristotelian.

question: A slave serves a gentle master who, by habit, never gives an order and lets him do as he likes. Yet the law still says the master may command him any moment he chooses. A Roman teacher insists the man is NOT free. Why?
answer: He lives at his master's whim — left alone isn't the same as un-owned.
choices: He lives at his master's whim — left alone isn't the same as un-owned.
He is left alone in fact, so he already counts as fully free.
Only a written law freeing him could possibly make him free.
Freedom is just a feeling, so how content he feels settles it.
context: This is the republican idea of liberty as non-domination (Pettit, Republicanism 1997; Roman roots in Cicero and Livy): a free citizen is one with NO master, even a kind one. It contrasts with the liberal picture of freedom as merely not being interfered with.

question: Asked how a state may rightly TAX you by force when you never signed anything, a speaker answers: 'You consented the moment you stayed and took the benefits of citizenship — that silent acceptance binds you.' Whose view of authority is this?
answer: Consent — the state's force is rightful only because the governed agreed to it.
choices: Consent — the state's force is rightful only because the governed agreed to it.
Hobbesian order — its force is rightful because it prevents a war of all on all.
Divine right — its force is rightful because a higher power granted it.
Tradition — its force is rightful because the practice is old and unbroken.
context: Consent theory (Locke, Two Treatises 1689; Rousseau, Social Contract 1762) roots state authority in the agreement of the governed. The speaker leans on 'tacit consent' — staying put and enjoying the benefits — to bind those who never literally signed. That stretch is much contested: critics ask whether merely not emigrating can really count as agreeing.

question: A war chronicler writes of a kingdom that escaped years of bandit chaos: 'A throne that holds back the slaughter has earned its right to rule, however rough its laws.' Whose view of what makes a ruler legitimate is the chronicler using?
answer: Order-first — holding people out of bloody chaos is what earns the right to rule.
choices: Order-first — holding people out of bloody chaos is what earns the right to rule.
Consent — only the agreement of the governed can make a ruler legitimate.
Tradition — a ruler is legitimate through the shared customs of the people.
No rightful rule — no throne holds any real authority over anyone at all.
context: This is Thomas Hobbes's view (Leviathan, 1651). Without a state, he argued, life is a 'war of all against all'; almost any ruler who prevents that collapse has earned at least minimal legitimacy. Locke (consent), Burke (tradition), and the anarchist deny that order alone is enough.

question: A knight argues at council: 'The crown may draw its sword to stop one subject harming another — never to force people to be holier, healthier, or wiser against their will. Past that line it turns tyrant.' Whose view of state power is this?
answer: Harm-only — the state may use force solely to stop people harming each other.
choices: Harm-only — the state may use force solely to stop people harming each other.
Shared-good — the state may force people toward goods the community holds.
Order-at-any-cost — any force that keeps the peace falls within the state's right.
Non-domination — the state may use force to keep anyone from being ruled arbitrarily.
context: This is John Stuart Mill's 'harm principle' (On Liberty, 1859), the classic classical-liberal limit on state power: force is justified only to prevent harm to others, not to improve people against their will. Communitarian, Hobbesian, and civic-republican views draw the line elsewhere.

question: A clean, fair vote of the student body bans the chess club from ever using the library. A peer admits the count was honest but still calls the rule unjust. Why doesn't "the majority voted for it" settle whether the ban is just?
answer: A vote counts how many want a thing; it can't make stripping the chess club's access fair.
choices: A vote counts how many want a thing; it can't make stripping the chess club's access fair.
If most students want the ban, that already proves it does the most good for everyone.
A clean, fairly run vote is exactly what makes any rule just; nothing more is needed.
Whoever wins the most votes holds the power, so the rule simply sticks either way.
context: This is the 'tyranny of the majority' — Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) and Mill (On Liberty, 1859) warned that a clean majority can still crush a minority's rights. A vote is a procedure that counts preferences; justice is a separate question about whether the rule treats people rightly.

question: A school paper editor grants that the principal makes fair, sensible calls case by case. She still argues every decision should run through written rules posted in advance. Why isn't "good calls by a good principal" the same as rule of law?
answer: Posted rules bind even the principal in advance and everyone can read them; his calls don't.
choices: Posted rules bind even the principal in advance and everyone can read them; his calls don't.
Rule of law just means whatever the person in charge happens to announce that day.
Rule of law is simply good outcomes, so a fair principal already delivers it in full.
Rule of law is whatever the most students vote to approve at any given time.
context: Rule of law (Dicey, 1885; Hayek, The Constitution of Liberty, 1960) requires general, public, prospective rules that bind officials themselves. Even a benevolent ruler deciding case-by-case escapes that constraint — the citizen can't read his next decision in advance the way she can read a posted rule.

question: A school's new dress code was "agreed to" by students who would have been suspended for refusing. A reader argues their agreement doesn't count as real consent at all. Why isn't "agreed to under threat of suspension" the same as "consented to"?
answer: Consent needs a real option to refuse; "agree or be suspended" leaves none — just obedience.
choices: Consent needs a real option to refuse; "agree or be suspended" leaves none — just obedience.
It would count only if the students had signed a form, so the gap is missing paperwork.
It counts as consent as long as most of the students ended up going along with it.
It counts as consent if the new dress code happens to turn out well in the end.
context: The 'highwayman objection' to tacit consent (Spooner, No Treason, 1870; Hume, Of the Original Contract, 1748): 'your money or your life' produces compliance, not consent. Genuine consent requires a real, acceptable alternative to agreeing — the freedom to refuse without being punished for it.

question: Edmund Burke, writing in 1790 against the French Revolution's sweeping reforms, argued the burden falls on the reformer, not on a practice that has survived for centuries. What principle is his argument resting on?
answer: Age is evidence: a custom that outlasts generations has been quietly tested.
choices: Age is evidence: a custom that outlasts generations has been quietly tested.
A rule binds only if the people living under it vote for it today.
A rule binds only when it protects a genuinely basic human right.
A rule binds only if every person could rationally agree to it.
context: This is tradition theory, given its classic statement in Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790): surviving customs encode practical wisdom no single planner can see. The reply: longevity is not always wisdom -- tradition can also preserve injustice.

choices: Constitutionalism: place some basic rights in a higher law that no ordinary vote can erase.
Majority rule: whatever the greatest number of people happen to vote for becomes law.
Anarchism: no vote and no written charter ever holds real authority over a free person.
Strength theory: whoever is strong enough to enforce a rule is the one who gets to make it.
answer: Constitutionalism: place some basic rights in a higher law that no ordinary vote can erase.
context: Constitutionalism (Madison, Federalist 10 and 51, 1787-88) answers the 'tyranny of the majority': put basic rights in a higher law the majority cannot rewrite by ordinary vote. Limiting the majority is what keeps a democracy from voting away the rights that make it one.
question: In 1787 James Madison feared a determined majority could vote away the rights of the minority -- so Federalist 51 argued some rights must sit in a higher law no ordinary vote can touch. Which view of authority is that?

Michael Sandel argues you are no free-floating chooser but an 'encumbered self' -- born into a people, a language, a history that hand you duties before you ever agree to anything. Which view of authority is that?
answer: Communitarianism: belonging itself creates duties no contract could list.
choices: Communitarianism: belonging itself creates duties no contract could list.
Consent theory: only an agreement you actually made can bind you.
Natural rights: a rule binds only if it secures rights you held first.
Strength theory: a ruler binds only as far as he can enforce his will.
context: Communitarianism (Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice 1982; Taylor, Sources of the Self 1989) holds we are 'encumbered selves' -- embedded in communities whose obligations precede any contract we sign. The liberal reply: duties you never chose are hard to call binding.

question: Touring America in 1835, Tocqueville warned of a new kind of despot -- not a king, but a 51% free to crush the 49% by a vote. The view he attacked holds the majority's will is the whole of legitimacy. Name it.
answer: Majoritarianism: the majority's will is the whole of legitimacy -- no court overrides it.
choices: Majoritarianism: the majority's will is the whole of legitimacy -- no court overrides it.
Constitutionalism: some rights sit above any vote the majority can take.
Non-domination: what matters is no one rules at whim, not who has more votes.
Tradition: long custom outranks whatever today's majority happens to prefer.
context: Pure majoritarianism reduces legitimacy to a count of present preferences. Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) warned this invites a 'tyranny of the majority' -- a 51% that can crush the 49% is a new kind of despot, not a guarantee of freedom.

question: A city fines anyone who feeds the homeless without a permit. The law passed by normal procedure and is enforced evenly. A reader still calls it illegitimate. Why isn't 'lawfully passed' the same as 'morally binding'?
answer: A law can be validly enacted and still be unjust; legality and rightness are two tests.
choices: A law can be validly enacted and still be unjust; legality and rightness are two tests.
It was passed correctly, so the only real question left is whether people obey it.
Most citizens never approved it, so it never truly became law in the first place.
It plainly fails to help the homeless, and a rule that misses its goal cannot bind.
context: Legal positivism splits what law IS (validly enacted) from what it OUGHT to be (morally just). H. L. A. Hart (The Concept of Law, 1961), who defended that split, still held an unjust statute is genuinely law - but whether it ought to be obeyed is a separate, moral question.

question: Locke wrote in 1689 that rulers who set out to destroy their people's rights break their trust, and the people then owe them nothing -- the argument later kings called treason and the colonists called a Declaration. Which view of authority is that?
answer: Right of resistance: authority is conditional, and betraying those rights ends it.
choices: Right of resistance: authority is conditional, and betraying those rights ends it.
Legal positivism: a validly passed law binds whether it is just or not.
Hobbesian view: any state that keeps order keeps its authority, however harsh.
Tradition theory: long custom keeps a state's authority whatever it does now.
context: The right of resistance runs through Locke's Second Treatise (1689): when rulers 'endeavour to take away and destroy the property of the people,' they forfeit their trust. Aquinas' natural-law tradition makes a parallel claim -- an unjust law fails to bind in conscience.

question: Robert Nozick fired back at Rawls in 1974: a fortune is just if every step that built it -- the earning, the trading -- was honest, however unequal the result looks. The final pattern, he said, is nobody's business. Which view of justice is that?
answer: Entitlement view: just if every step was fair -- the end pattern is irrelevant.
choices: Entitlement view: just if every step was fair -- the end pattern is irrelevant.
Rawlsian view: just only if it lifts the worst-off, whatever the steps were.
Communitarian view: just only if it fits the community's shared values.
Utilitarian view: just only if it yields the most total good overall.
context: The entitlement (procedural) theory is Nozick's, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974): if acquisition and transfer were just, the result is just however unequal it looks. Rawls (A Theory of Justice 1971) drew the opposite line, judging a distribution by its pattern of outcomes -- chiefly how the least-advantaged fare.

question: Locke argued in 1689 that a man who clears and works a patch of unowned land has 'mixed his labour' with it -- and that makes it his, a right the state only recognizes, never grants. Which view of property is that?
answer: Labor theory: mixing your work with unowned land makes it yours; the state only recognizes it.
choices: Labor theory: mixing your work with unowned land makes it yours; the state only recognizes it.
Legal positivism: it is yours only once the law says so -- no statute, no property.
Utilitarian view: ownership is allowed because it makes people produce more for all.
Communitarian view: it is yours only if your community's customs count it as owned.
context: Locke's labor theory of property (Second Treatise, ch. 5, 1689): 'Whatsoever he removes out of the state that nature hath provided... he hath mixed his labour with, and thereby makes it his property.' The famous limit Locke adds: take only so long as 'enough, and as good' is left for others.

question: Renn wants to ban plastic straws to save the oceans. Soren objects: 'Straws are under one percent of ocean plastic. Judge the ban against what would really replace it, not against a dreamed-up plastic-free sea.' What is the flaw Soren is pointing to?
answer: Banned or not, straws are a tiny slice — judge the rule by what really replaces them.
choices: Banned or not, straws are a tiny slice — judge the rule by what really replaces them.
If most students back the ban, that already settles whether it is worth doing.
Saving even one sea turtle makes any ban worth whatever it happens to cost.
Plastic harms the ocean only when it is the most common kind of litter there.
context: Thomas Sowell's 'compared to what?' (The Vision of the Anointed, 1995) is the move: a policy looks good measured against a perfect imagined world and dubious against the alternative that would really replace it. A tiny-impact ban is the classic case.

question: Halse proposes rent control to protect tenants. Pell objects: 'The lower rent you can see. The buildings never put up, the repairs never made, the flats pulled off the market — those you can't see, but they're real.' What is Pell's central point?
answer: The visible rent drop hides real costs no one sees — homes never built, repairs never made.
choices: The visible rent drop hides real costs no one sees — homes never built, repairs never made.
Landlords and tenants should be left to strike whatever deal the two of them choose.
Rent control helps tenants right now, so any later downsides don't really matter.
A landlord always knows more about a building than the tenant living in it does.
context: Frederic Bastiat's 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen' (1850) draws the seen/unseen distinction, famous in the broken-window fallacy. Honest analysis traces the invisible effects — buildings never built, repairs deferred — beside the visible one.

question: Drew proposes subsidies to keep failing factories running. Ames objects: 'The intention is saving jobs; the result is workers and machines locked in a dying trade. Judge a policy by what it does, not what it's meant to do.' What is Ames's point?
answer: What a policy means to do can't excuse what it actually does — outcomes are the test.
choices: What a policy means to do can't excuse what it actually does — outcomes are the test.
A factory that cannot survive on its own should simply be left to close down.
Good intentions on their own are enough to make a policy worth keeping around.
Spending public money to save people's jobs can never be a fair thing to do.
context: Milton Friedman's line — 'one of the great mistakes is to judge policies by their intentions rather than their results' — names the move. Related to Bastiat's seen/unseen, but distinct: this one contrasts what a policy aims at with what it brings about.

question: A columnist writes: 'We are just ASKING the wealthy to pay their fair share.' A reader replies: 'You are not asking - refuse, and your mechanism sends penalties.' Why does the word 'asking' mislead here?
answer: A real ask lets you say no; if refusing brings punishment, it is a demand in a polite word.
choices: A real ask lets you say no; if refusing brings punishment, it is a demand in a polite word.
Asking the wealthy is unfair, since they already pay more in tax than anyone else does.
The phrase fair share has no fixed meaning, so the sentence really says nothing at all.
Most voters do back the tax, so calling it an ask matches what people clearly want.
context: This is a euphemism that quietly swaps a demand for a request - the word 'ask' implies refusal is allowed, while the mechanism penalizes refusal. The reader does not say the tax is wrong; she says 'ask' misdescribes it. The voluntary-versus-compelled line is foundational in classical-liberal thought (Locke, Spencer, Nozick) and appears in left-anarchist critiques too (Chomsky).

question: A debate-club president says: 'SOCIETY decided to provide this service.' Her opponent replies: 'Society decided nothing - particular people decided, and OTHER particular people will be made to pay.' What does the word 'society' hide?
answer: An abstract crowd-word covers up which real people are forcing which other real people.
choices: An abstract crowd-word covers up which real people are forcing which other real people.
Society is not a real thing at all, so no group can ever decide anything.
The service is wasteful, so society should not be funding it in the first place.
A majority voted for it, which is all that deciding something has ever meant.
context: Methodological individualism - tracing social claims back to identifiable individual actors - is associated with Weber, Mises, Hayek, and Popper. The opponent does not deny that groups exist; she says the abstract noun 'society' masks agency, hiding which particular people are compelling which others. That is why the 'society isn't real at all' choice overshoots: the point is concealment, not denying groups.

question: A council member announces: 'WE THE PEOPLE chose this policy.' A girl who voted no answers: 'The majority chose. I lost the vote — counting that as MY choice treats a defeat as my agreement.' What distinction is she drawing?
answer: Losing a vote is not agreeing to it — majority approval isn't consent.
choices: Losing a vote is not agreeing to it — majority approval isn't consent.
The vague word 'we' hides which real people actually decided.
The state need not obey the moral rules that bind ordinary people.
Voters chase self-interest, never some neutral common good for all.
context: Consent is not the same as majority approval: a dissenter who is outvoted has been bound, not persuaded. The thread runs through Locke (Second Treatise, 1689), Mill (On Liberty, 1859), and Tocqueville on the 'tyranny of the majority' (1835). She doesn't deny majorities may rule — she flags the slide from 'the majority chose' to 'you chose.'

question: Halden writes: 'The right to worship freely is not a privilege the constitution GRANTS. It only recognizes a right that already exists from what human beings are - and a regime that strips it forfeits its own legitimacy.' On Halden's view, where does the right come from?
answer: Discovered, not granted - it exists from what humans are; law only recognizes it.
choices: Discovered, not granted - it exists from what humans are; law only recognizes it.
Granted by law - with no statute writing it down, there is no right at all.
A social custom - it holds only while a society agrees to keep it.
A fair bargain - it exists because reasonable parties would agree to it.
context: This is the natural-rights view: rights are DISCOVERED in human nature, not handed out by the state, so unjust law fails to bind. It runs from Locke (Second Treatise, 1689) through Jefferson and the American founding. The rival 'granted by law' position is legal positivism (Bentham; H. L. A. Hart): no right exists before law writes it down.

question: Mara argues for a higher top tax rate: 'Imagine you did not yet know whether you would be born rich or poor. You would never agree to a tax code that leaves the worst-off with so little. That blindfold test is the fair one, and ours fails it.' Which test is Mara using?
answer: Pick rules you would accept before knowing your own place in society.
choices: Pick rules you would accept before knowing your own place in society.
Allow any wealth that was gained through honest earning and trade.
Distrust big redistribution because no planner knows all local needs.
Defer to long-tested custom over a clever new thought-experiment.
context: Mara's 'blindfold' is Rawls's veil of ignorance (A Theory of Justice, 1971): judge the rules from behind a veil where you don't know your own station. The three rivals are real traditions, each a different test - Nozick (honest acquisition and transfer), Hayek (no planner can know everyone's local needs), and Burke (defer to inherited practice). The bank attributes the move to Mara rather than ruling who is right.

question: Two charts of who-owns-what look IDENTICAL. One arose from people freely trading and giving; the other from a king seizing goods and handing them to friends. A thinker insists one is just and the other is not. What must he believe makes a distribution just?
answer: How it came about — the history of fair steps, not the final shape.
choices: How it came about — the history of fair steps, not the final shape.
How equal the final shares turn out to be across everyone.
How much total well-being it produces, summed across everyone.
Whether the worst-off person ends up as well off as possible.
context: Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) calls his theory historical and unpatterned: two identical-looking distributions can differ in justice depending entirely on how they arose. Just acquisition and just transfer make holdings just, whatever graph results. He set it against Rawls's worst-off test and utilitarian welfare-counting.

question: A regime still holds power but has stopped protecting its people from arbitrary arrest. One school says it has thereby LOST its legitimacy; another says holding the peace is enough to keep it. Which school sets the STRICTER bar — the one that says this regime is no longer legitimate?
answer: Lockean liberalism — legitimacy lasts only while rights are protected.
choices: Lockean liberalism — legitimacy lasts only while rights are protected.
Hobbesian absolutism — any peace-keeping sovereign stays legitimate.
Weberian sociology — legitimate means whatever the people accept.
Burkean conservatism — long-standing rule keeps its legitimacy.
context: Locke's Second Treatise (1689) makes legitimacy conditional: a government that betrays its trust to protect rights dissolves it. Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) sets a far lower bar — almost any sovereign that prevents the 'war of all against all' keeps legitimacy. 'Stricter' means the view that leaves the state LESS room, which is Locke's.

choices: Go and first learn why it was ever built — your not seeing the reason is no proof there is none.
Leave every old thing standing forever, untouched — the inherited past is never to be questioned.
Tear it straight down at once, since anything whose original purpose is unclear must be useless.
Put the whole matter to a public vote, since the majority alone should decide what stays or goes.
answer: Go and first learn why it was ever built — your not seeing the reason is no proof there is none.
context: G.K. Chesterton's 'fence' parable (The Thing, 1929): if a reform's purpose is invisible to you, that is a reason to study it, not to bulldoze it. It is the vivid form of Edmund Burke's 'prescription' — that institutions surviving long stresses hold practical wisdom a fresh redesign cannot see. Neither says never change; both say understand first.
question: A reformer finds an old fence across a road, sees no reason for it, and says: tear it down. A wiser companion answers that THIS is exactly the fence he must NOT remove — not yet. What is the companion really demanding before anyone touches it?

A rich donor can quietly ruin any candidate who crosses him — though he has made no threat and broken no law. Theorist Halbe says the candidate is ALREADY unfree, just from living at the donor's mercy. What is Halbe's core claim?
answer: Living at his mercy is itself unfreedom — the standing power to ruin you makes you unfree before any threat.
choices: Living at his mercy is itself unfreedom — the standing power to ruin you makes you unfree before any threat.
No threat was made, so nothing has happened — the candidate stays free until the donor actually acts.
The donor broke no law, so the candidate keeps every right — nothing here counts as a real wrong.
He can always refuse the money, so a free choice means he was never truly under the donor's power.
context: Freedom as non-domination (Philip Pettit, Republicanism, 1997; Quentin Skinner) revives an older republican idea: being DEPENDENT on another's arbitrary power is itself a kind of unfreedom, even when that power is never used. It contrasts with the liberal view, from Hobbes through Mill, that you are free unless someone actually interferes.

question: A thinker mocks the idea that using a country's roads counts as agreeing to obey it: 'If I leave my dishes out and you happen to walk through my kitchen, you haven't agreed to wash them.' By his standard, what does it take to truly consent?
answer: An explicit, knowing yes — just using the roads or staying put can never bind you to obey.
choices: An explicit, knowing yes — just using the roads or staying put can never bind you to obey.
Simply enjoying the roads and protection — that benefit already counts as your agreement.
Whatever most people accept — if the majority obeys, the dissenter is bound along with them.
Nothing at all — the state's power holds whether anyone agrees to it or not.
context: Locke (Second Treatise, 1689) allowed "tacit consent" — enjoying a state's roads and protection counts as agreeing to obey it. Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) ridiculed this with the dishes case: passing through a room is not agreeing to wash up. He held that only an explicit, knowing yes can truly bind you, the stricter standard of the two.

question: Sandborn rejects talk of rights as something a lone, placeless chooser simply HAS: 'A right only means what it does inside a living tradition of practice. Strip away the community, and you hollow the right out.' Which view of rights is he using?
answer: Communitarian — a right's content comes from the practices of an actual community.
choices: Communitarian — a right's content comes from the practices of an actual community.
Natural-rights — the right is built into human nature, the same in every time and place.
Legal — the right exists only once a society's law writes it down and grants it.
Contractarian — the right is whatever free, equal parties would agree to up front.
context: Communitarian critics of liberal rights theory — Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981), Michael Sandel, Charles Taylor — attack the "unencumbered self," the abstract chooser stripped of any community. On their view rights still exist, but their content can only be spelled out inside a particular tradition of practice, not derived from human nature alone.

choices: Knowledge problem - the needed know-how is scattered across thousands of separate heads, so no one planner can gather it all.
Moral hazard - shielding a person from the real cost of a risky choice just makes them choose to do far more of it.
Public choice - officials in office quietly chase their own private interests, not the public good that they loudly claim.
Compared-to-what - a sweeping plan looks fine against a mere daydream, yet far worse once set against the real available options.
answer: Knowledge problem - the needed know-how is scattered across thousands of separate heads, so no one planner can gather it all.
context: Friedrich Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) names this: the information an economy needs is dispersed and tacit, known only at the point of decision. Prices pull it together; central planning cannot. Leonard Read dramatized it in 'I, Pencil' (1958).
question: No one person knows how to make a simple wooden pencil from scratch. The logger, the miner, the chemist, the shipper - each holds one scrap of the know-how, and nobody holds it all. A planner trying to direct the whole chain by decree would fail. Which reasoning move is that?

A strike is reported as a contract dispute between equal parties. Editorial writer Renzo objects: 'They are not equal. The owners hold the factory and machines; the workers hold only their labor. Call it a freely struck bargain and you miss who holds the power.' Which lens is Renzo using?
answer: Class conflict - who owns the means of production sets the real terms.
choices: Class conflict - who owns the means of production sets the real terms.
Mutual gain - both sides trade because each expects to come out ahead.
Knowledge problem - no planner can price what each shop floor knows.
Shared tradition - a workplace runs on customs both sides inherit.
context: Marx (Capital, Vol. I, 1867) reads political economy through ownership of the means of production and the class relations that follow; the 'free contract' between worker and owner is the contested ground. The question asks which TRADITION Renzo is using, not whether his prediction holds.

choices: Harm principle - the state may use force only to stop one person harming others, never to protect you from yourself.
Legal moralism - the state may rightly ban an act purely because that act has been judged to be deeply immoral.
Paternalism - the state may step in and override the private choices you make about your own life, body, and health.
Greatest good - the state should simply take whatever sweeping action happens to raise the total public welfare the most.
answer: Harm principle - the state may use force only to stop one person harming others, never to protect you from yourself.
context: John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859) sets out the harm principle as a hard limit on the state: it may coerce only to prevent harm to others, never to make a person wiser, healthier, or better for his own sake. The soda tax is exactly the paternalism Mill rules out.
question: A town debates taxing soda to make people healthier. Host Dilara objects: 'The law may stop you harming OTHERS. But a man who only harms himself is no business of the state's - whatever the health math says, force has no writ there.' Which limit on state power is Dilara invoking?

A town guard wants to fine a hermit for a habit that endangers no one but himself. One adviser says the state may act only to stop harm to OTHERS; the other says the state may do whatever keeps order, self-harm included. Whose rule leaves the guard LESS room to fine the hermit?
answer: The harm-to-others rule — purely self-regarding acts lie outside the state's reach.
choices: The harm-to-others rule — purely self-regarding acts lie outside the state's reach.
The keep-order rule — preventing any disorder, even self-harm, is fair game.
Neither — a guard may fine whatever the town's elders have always fined.
Neither — a guard may fine only what a majority of townsfolk first approve.
context: This is Mill's harm principle (On Liberty, 1859): the state may coerce only to prevent harm to OTHERS, never to police what a person does to himself — the stricter limit. The keep-order view is Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651), who lets a sovereign do nearly anything that staves off collapse, leaving far more room to act.

question: An essayist argues: 'The right to worship freely is not a gift the constitution hands out. It exists already, from what humans ARE. A regime that strips it doesn't erase the right — it forfeits its own claim to rule.' On this view, where does the right come from?
answer: It exists before government — law can only recognize it, never grant it.
choices: It exists before government — law can only recognize it, never grant it.
It exists only once written into law — before that, there is no such right.
It is a social custom — as binding as the community currently treats it.
It comes from a fair bargain — whatever rational parties would agree to.
context: This is the natural-rights view — Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration (1689): some rights belong to humans by nature, so the state can only recognize them, and a regime that violates them forfeits its authority. The legal-creation rival is legal positivism (Bentham; Hart, The Concept of Law, 1961): no right exists before the law writes it down.

question: At-will employment: this week no one has interfered with the worker at all. But her boss holds standing power to fire her tomorrow for any reason or none, and she must mind that the whole time. An op-ed writer calls her UNFREE even now. On what grounds?
answer: Living under another's arbitrary power is itself unfreedom, even unused.
choices: Living under another's arbitrary power is itself unfreedom, even unused.
She is actually free this week — no real interference has occurred yet.
Her unfreedom is really about who owns the factory, not the firing power.
Her freedom depends on whether her workplace honors its shared customs.
context: This is freedom-as-non-domination (Philip Pettit, Republicanism, 1997; Elizabeth Anderson, Private Government, 2017): being subject to another's arbitrary power is unfreedom even when that power is never used. It contrasts with the interference-only view of liberty (Hobbes through Mill), which would record no unfreedom while the boss stays his hand.

question: Two judges rate the same vast fortune, every coin of it earned through honest trade. Nozick passes it: each step was fair, so the result is just. Rawls fails it: a gap this wide is allowed only if it lifts the poorest. Whose test rejects MORE fortunes as unjust?
answer: Rawls -- a fair history isn't enough; the gap must also help the worst-off.
choices: Rawls -- a fair history isn't enough; the gap must also help the worst-off.
Nozick -- only fortunes built on force or fraud get ruled out.
Both rate it alike; honest trade and helping the poor never clash.
Neither rules out anything; any fortune people accept is just.
context: Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) lets inequality stand only when it improves the worst-off's lot -- the difference principle. Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) asks only that each step of acquisition and trade be fair. Rawls' bar is the stricter one: it rejects gaps Nozick would wave through.

question: In a crisis a governor seizes emergency powers: 'Rights matter only once order is secured. While collapse threatens, no right can bind the one holding the line. Order comes before rights.' Whose view of rights fits his?
answer: Order-first -- rights are the sovereign's gift, void until order is safe.
choices: Order-first -- rights are the sovereign's gift, void until order is safe.
Rights-first -- guarding rights is the one thing that makes a state legitimate.
Custom-first -- only long-standing tradition can make a power legitimate.
Non-domination -- you are unfree the moment one man can rule you at will.
context: This is Hobbes' Leviathan (1651): the war of all against all is the default, so any sovereign that prevents collapse earns authority, and rights follow only after. Locke (rights-first), Burke (custom-first), and Pettit's republicanism (non-domination) mark the rival answers. Schmitt later radicalized the order-first view.

question: Reformers want to scrap a two-century constitution for a sleek new design. A columnist objects: 'This old document bears the marks of every crisis it weathered -- knowledge no fresh blueprint can hold.' Which reason is she giving to keep it?
answer: It has survived crises a fresh design never faced -- that record is wisdom.
choices: It has survived crises a fresh design never faced -- that record is wisdom.
It spreads knowledge no single planner could gather in one place.
Fair people behind a veil of ignorance would all agree to it.
It guards rights that exist before any government writes them down.
context: This is Burke's prescription (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790): an institution's survival through real stresses is itself a kind of wisdom no first-principles redesign can match. The closest rival, Hayek's dispersed-knowledge case, keeps the old order for a different reason -- the local information embedded in it, not its survival record.

question: A king rescinds the people's long-standing protection against searches of their homes. A courtier defends it: 'Whatever the crown granted, the crown may withdraw. Rights are the gift of order, not a leash upon it.' On the courtier's view, where do rights come from?
answer: Hobbes — rights are the sovereign's gift, his to revoke.
choices: Hobbes — rights are the sovereign's gift, his to revoke.
Locke — rights exist before the state and limit what it may do.
Rawls — rights are what fair, impartial parties would agree to.
Pettit — rights are guards against domination by arbitrary power.
context: Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) treats rights as the sovereign's grant: what authority gives, it may take back, since the alternative is the war of all against all. Locke (Second Treatise, 1689) is the great rival - some rights exist before any government and bind it, so a ruler who strips them breaks his trust. Rawls grounds rights in fair agreement; Pettit, in protection from domination.

question: A federal directive orders every school to teach one fixed curriculum. Talia objects: 'A decision belongs at the lowest level able to make it well. Strip the local school of that, and you strip a community of the standing to govern itself.' Which principle is Talia invoking?
answer: Subsidiarity — decide at the lowest level competent to decide.
choices: Subsidiarity — decide at the lowest level competent to decide.
Self-ownership — your holdings are yours; no one may reassign them.
Non-domination — remote power over you is itself a kind of unfreedom.
Knowledge problem — distant planners cannot grasp local facts.
context: Subsidiarity - named in Catholic social teaching (Quadragesimo Anno, 1931) and echoed in American federalism - holds that a higher body should not take over what a lower, competent one can do for itself. It overlaps with Hayek's knowledge-problem and with libertarian and republican arguments, but it is its own claim: about the right LEVEL for a decision, not about property, knowledge, or domination.

question: A chancellor posts edicts whose terms shift week to week, so no merchant can read a rule and plan around it. A scribe protests: 'A command you cannot know in advance or rely on is not law at all — it is the ruler's will, renamed.' Which idea grounds the scribe's objection?
answer: Rule of law — rules must be fixed and knowable, or they are mere commands.
choices: Rule of law — rules must be fixed and knowable, or they are mere commands.
Natural rights — some rights bind the ruler whatever he decrees.
Non-domination — living under arbitrary power is unfreedom in itself.
Tradition — institutions earn authority by surviving over time.
context: This is the rule of law as predictability. Hayek (The Constitution of Liberty, 1960) and Lon Fuller (The Morality of Law, 1964) argued that real law must be general, public, and stable enough that people can plan around it; a rule that shifts unpredictably is not law but command (Hayek's nomos vs. thesis). The objection is about the FORM a rule must take, not about any particular right or freedom.

question: Halden proposes raising the minimum wage for the working poor. Critic Mara replies: 'Set a wage above what a worker's hour adds, and the employer loses money on that hire. The math of the hire predicts the result — the least-skilled priced out of work.' Which reasoning move is Mara making?
answer: Incentive structure — the payoff facing the employer predicts the result.
choices: Incentive structure — the payoff facing the employer predicts the result.
Public choice — the lawmakers who pass it are chasing their own gain.
Knowledge problem — no planner can gather the wage facts each shop knows.
Compared-to-what — judge it against real options, not an ideal world.
context: Incentive-structure analysis (a Chicago-school staple — Becker, Friedman) predicts outcomes from the payoffs a policy changes for the people it touches. Pricing labor above its marginal product makes the least-skilled hire a loss, so fewer are made. The knowledge-problem and compared-to-what moves are real tools, but apply elsewhere.

question: Iyer proposes broad student-loan forgiveness. Critic Stenz replies: 'The winners — borrowers — are few, organized, and loud. The payers — the already-paid-off, taxpayers — are many and scattered. That lopsidedness, not the merits, is why it passes.' Which reasoning move is Stenz making?
answer: Dispersed costs — organized winners outmuscle scattered payers.
choices: Dispersed costs — organized winners outmuscle scattered payers.
Public choice — the officials who pass it are chasing their own gain.
Seen vs. unseen — the visible payout hides costs no one notices.
Regulatory capture — an agency ends up serving the group it oversees.
context: Mancur Olson's The Logic of Collective Action (1965) formalized the concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs asymmetry: a small group with a large per-head stake out-organizes a huge group with a tiny per-head stake, so the policy wins politically even when it loses on the totals. Stenz's tell is the lopsided organization, not hidden effects or a captured agency.

question: Vora defends a welfare schedule paying more than an entry-level job. Critic Halse replies: 'When the job costs more in lost benefits than it pays, the schedule rewards staying out of work. The very thing it means to relieve is what it breeds more of.' Which reasoning move is Halse making?
answer: Moral hazard — shielding the cost of not working breeds more of it.
choices: Moral hazard — shielding the cost of not working breeds more of it.
Knowledge problem — no planner can gather the local facts to set it.
Public choice — the officials running it gain by expanding it.
Compared-to-what — judge it against real options, not an ideal world.
context: Moral hazard (an insurance term generalized by Arrow, 1963) names the predictable effect of shielding people from the cost of a behavior — here forgone work — which makes that behavior cheaper, so more of it occurs. It is a cousin of plain incentive analysis but is specifically about consequences-insulation.
