answer: Greater goods — the evil is real, but it secures a good that couldn't come any other way.
choices: Greater goods — the evil is real, but it secures a good that couldn't come any other way.
Free will — evil is the price of letting people make genuinely free choices.
Skeptical theism — we simply can't tell what reasons God might have at all.
Denial — the suffering only looks bad and isn't really an evil to explain.
context: The greater-goods defense (Augustine, Aquinas, and modern theodicy) holds that an apparent evil may be permitted to secure a good unobtainable without it. The tell here is a flood, not a human crime, so the free-will defense (which answers evil people CHOOSE) doesn't fit. Critics like J. L. Mackie reply it must prove the good was truly impossible otherwise — a far bolder claim than 'maybe.'

question: Blaise Pascal, the gambler-turned-believer, argued: bet on God and win, you gain everything; bet against and lose, you lose everything. So belief is the smart wager. What kind of move is this?
answer: Treating belief as a bet — choosing by the payoffs when proof runs out.
choices: Treating belief as a bet — choosing by the payoffs when proof runs out.
Demanding hard evidence before accepting any claim at all.
Claiming to perceive God directly, the way one sees a tree.
Insisting faith needs no reasons, because reasons miss the point.
context: This is Pascal's Wager (Pensees, 1670): belief framed as a decision under uncertainty with lopsided stakes. Critics raise the 'many gods' problem (bet on which God?) and ask whether a bet-driven belief is real faith at all — a strategy isn't trust.

question: Asked why a good God allows suffering, a thinker answers that the world is no finished paradise but a vale of soul-making — hardship is the very stuff courage, patience, and mercy are forged from. Which response to evil is this?
answer: Soul-making — hardship is the workshop where strong character is forged.
choices: Soul-making — hardship is the workshop where strong character is forged.
Free-will defense — real freedom must include the power to choose wrongly.
Skeptical theism — we can't see God's reasons, but that doesn't mean none exist.
Mystery move — the question is beyond us, so it should simply be set aside.
context: The phrase 'a vale of soul-making' is John Keats's (1819); the theodicy is tied to John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966), reaching back to Irenaeus. The world is not a finished paradise but a place where character is actually built.

question: Thomas Aquinas split truths in two: preambles plain reason can prove — that God exists, is one — and deeper articles only revelation reveals. The two, he held, can never clash. Which view is this?
answer: Natural theology — reason proves the basics; revelation supplies the rest.
choices: Natural theology — reason proves the basics; revelation supplies the rest.
Fideism — faith alone reaches God; asking reason to help misses the point.
Reformed epistemology — belief in God is basic and needs no proof at all.
Verificationism — only testable claims mean anything, so God-talk says nothing.
context: Aquinas (Summa Theologiae, c. 1265) split 'preambles' reason can reach (that God exists, is one) from 'articles' needing revelation (the Trinity, the Incarnation). On his view faith presupposes reason where reason can reach.

question: At a healing service, honest people swear they watched a man's illness vanish in an instant. A skeptic grants they are sincere but still won't call it a miracle. Why isn't 'sincere witnesses reported it' enough to prove a miracle happened?
answer: A misdiagnosis or quiet recovery is far likelier than an actual break in the laws of nature.
choices: A misdiagnosis or quiet recovery is far likelier than an actual break in the laws of nature.
The witnesses were surely lying to each other to make the healer at the service look good.
Only a far larger crowd of agreeing witnesses could ever be enough to prove a miracle.
Miracles are flatly impossible by definition, so no report of one could ever count at all.
context: David Hume's argument against miracles (Enquiry, 1748): no testimony suffices for a miracle unless the witnesses being wrong would be even more astonishing than the miracle itself — and a mistake or ordinary recovery rarely is. The skeptic doesn't call the witnesses liars or rule miracles out in advance; he just weighs the odds. Critics like John Earman dispute the math.

question: William Alston argued that someone who experiences God is in the same position as someone who sees a tree — a direct perception that counts as real evidence, until you have reason to doubt it. Which view is he defending?
answer: Perception model — sensing God works like seeing, so it counts as evidence.
choices: Perception model — sensing God works like seeing, so it counts as evidence.
Evidentialism — private experience proves nothing unless others can check it.
Reformed view — belief in God is basic, needing no evidence at all.
Verificationism — only testable claims mean anything, so it shows nothing.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) frames religious experience as a 'doxastic practice' on a par with ordinary sense perception: both yield prima facie evidence, and both are circular if you demand they justify themselves from outside.

question: In Plato's dialogue, Socrates traps the priest Euthyphro: is an act holy BECAUSE the gods command it, or do they command it because it is already holy? One horn says the command itself makes it right. Which view of right and wrong is that?
answer: Divine command — what is right is fixed by what God commands.
choices: Divine command — what is right is fixed by what God commands.
Natural law — what is right is fixed by how human nature is built.
Moral realism — moral facts are simply out there; God at most reveals them.
Relativism — what is right is fixed by each culture's say-so.
context: The dilemma is Plato's Euthyphro fork: is an act right because God commands it, or commanded because it is already right? Robert Adams' modified divine command theory (Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999) is a careful modern reply to the first horn.

question: A school newspaper editor hears: 'Most cultures, all through history, have believed in some god — so a god must be real.' She thinks the leap is too quick. What is the flaw in the argument?
answer: Wide belief reveals how human minds tend to work, not that the thing is real.
choices: Wide belief reveals how human minds tend to work, not that the thing is real.
A claim is false unless every culture has agreed on it without exception.
Older beliefs are always more trustworthy, so the oldest view must win.
Whatever the most people feel strongly has to be the safest thing to believe.
context: This is the consensus-gentium ('common consent') appeal, found in Cicero: because almost everyone believes it, it must be true. The catch is that wide belief tracks how human minds are built, not the truth of the object — many false beliefs were once near-universal across cultures too.

question: The monk Anselm claimed God is a being greater than which none can be thought — and since a real God beats one that exists only in the mind, God MUST exist. What does this argument reason from?
answer: From the very definition of God, using no facts about the world.
choices: From the very definition of God, using no facts about the world.
From things that begin or change, which need a first cause behind them.
From the fine-tuned constants that make a life-bearing universe possible.
From binding moral duties that only a lawgiver could ground.
context: Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion, c. 1078) reasons from the concept of God to God's existence. The monk Gaunilo mocked it with a 'perfect island' that would have to exist by the same logic; Kant objected that existing isn't a real property. Modal versions (Plantinga, 1974) revive it.

question: A friend asks a youth-group leader: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, why does evil exist?' The leader snaps: 'Don't ask that — it's disrespectful.' Which reply would actually ENGAGE the question instead of shutting it down?
answer: Wrongdoing is the price of real freedom — forced goodness is no free choice.
choices: Wrongdoing is the price of real freedom — forced goodness is no free choice.
Asking the question is disrespectful, so it should never be raised at all.
God exists anyway, so any doubt the question stirs up must simply be wrong.
Critics only raise it because they secretly want the evil to keep happening.
context: Only the first reply engages the problem of evil: it grants the premise (evil is real) and offers a candidate reason — the free-will defense (Augustine; Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974), where genuine freedom needs a real possibility of choosing wrong. The other three dodge it: silencing the asker, declaring the verdict by fiat, and impugning motives.

question: A columnist asks: 'God could have made creatures who only ever do good — so why allow evil at all?' A theologian answers: 'Goodness that was rigged, in beings who could never choose wrong, would not be real goodness.' Which response is the theologian giving?
answer: Free-will defense — real choice needs a real chance of choosing wrong.
choices: Free-will defense — real choice needs a real chance of choosing wrong.
Soul-making — hardship is what trains a soul into virtue.
Skeptical theism — our minds are too small to read God's reasons.
Greater-goods — each evil is allowed only to buy some larger good.
context: This is the free-will defense (Augustine; sharpened by Alvin Plantinga in God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974, against J. L. Mackie's logical problem of evil): a world of genuine moral agents requires the real possibility they choose wrongly, so 'rigged' goodness would not be moral agency. The tell is the theologian's appeal to free choice, not to character-growth, human limits, or a balancing good.

question: On a philosophy podcast, host Camille presses: 'Surely we can SEE that some suffering serves no good at all.' Theologian Dwight answers: 'Failing to find a reason is not the same as proving there is none.' He grants the suffering is real but blocks that leap. Which reply is Dwight giving?
answer: Sceptical theism - a small mind can't rule out reasons a vast mind may have.
choices: Sceptical theism - a small mind can't rule out reasons a vast mind may have.
Free-will defense - the evil is the price of giving creatures real choice.
Greater-goods reply - the evil buys a specific good we can point to.
Atheist conclusion - pointless evil shows that no good God is there.
context: This is sceptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, 1984; Michael Bergmann, 2001), a reply to the evidential problem of evil. It does not name a reason for the suffering; it only denies the inference from 'we see no good reason' to 'there is no good reason' - a finite mind is in no position to canvass an infinite one's reasons. Critics say it cuts too deep, undercutting our trust in God's goodness too.

question: On a philosophy podcast, Bex lays out an argument: 'The universe had a FIRST moment - it began to exist. Whatever begins to exist must have a cause. So the universe has one: a cause beyond time itself, and immensely powerful.' Which argument is this?
answer: Kalam argument - whatever began to exist had a cause, and the universe began.
choices: Kalam argument - whatever began to exist had a cause, and the universe began.
First Way - a chain of movers acting right now needs an unmoved first mover.
Ontological argument - the very idea of a greatest being entails it exists.
Fine-tuning argument - constants set so precisely for life point to design.
context: The kalam cosmological argument turns on the universe having a temporal BEGINNING. It was sharpened by medieval Islamic theologians (al-Ghazali, ~1100; 'kalam' is Arabic for theology) and revived by William Lane Craig (1979), who joins it to Big Bang cosmology. Aquinas's cousin arguments do NOT rely on a beginning - they reason from dependence here and now, which is why the contingency and First-Way options are the traps.

question: On a panel, theologian Aleksy argues: 'Every dependent thing leans on something else to exist RIGHT NOW - not just to get started. A whole stack of leaners still leans on nothing solid, so there must be a ground that depends on no one.' Which argument is this?
answer: Contingency argument - what leans on others to exist needs a ground that leans on nothing.
choices: Contingency argument - what leans on others to exist needs a ground that leans on nothing.
Kalam argument - the universe had a first moment in time, so something must have caused it.
Design argument - the ordered, purpose-like fit of nature points to a designing mind.
Moral argument - real, binding oughts point to a lawgiver who stands behind them.
context: This is the argument from contingency - Aquinas's Third Way (Summa Theologiae I.2.3), defended today by Edward Feser (Five Proofs, 2017). Its signature is dependence HERE AND NOW: it would run even if the universe had always existed, with no first moment. That is exactly what separates it from the kalam argument (the trap here), which lives or dies on the universe having a beginning in time.

question: The monk Anselm claimed he could prove God exists without ever observing the world — from the idea of God alone: 'God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and a being that exists is greater than one merely imagined.' What kind of argument is this?
answer: From the bare idea of God, without observing the world
choices: From the bare idea of God, without observing the world
From the world's needing a first cause to exist at all
From the orderly design we observe throughout nature
From the reality of binding right and wrong in our lives
context: Anselm's Proslogion (1078) is the classic ontological argument: it reasons from the concept of God alone, with no appeal to the world. Kant's famous objection is that 'existence is not a predicate.' Plantinga (1974) recast it in modal logic. It is the one classic proof that never looks outward at all.

question: A physicist notes the universe's basic constants sit in a razor-thin band: nudge gravity or the nuclear force a hair and there are no stars, no chemistry, no life. Blind chance, she argues, is a poor explanation for such finely set dials — design is the better bet. What is her clue?
answer: The cosmic constants tuned so finely that life is possible
choices: The cosmic constants tuned so finely that life is possible
The intricate working parts of a single living organism
The fact that the universe had a beginning, and so a cause
Observers can only ever find a life-friendly universe
context: The fine-tuning argument (Robin Collins, John Polkinghorne) builds on physical-constants data since the 1970s. Paley's earlier watchmaker (Natural Theology, 1802) reasoned from living organisms instead. The anthropic principle — we could only find ourselves in a life-permitting universe — is the standard rebuttal.

question: A debater argues: 'That torturing an innocent child for fun is wrong isn't merely my feeling — it is really, bindingly wrong. Yet no pile of bare facts about atoms or evolution can squeeze out an ought. Something beyond nature must ground that duty.' What is her starting clue?
answer: That some things are really, bindingly right or wrong
choices: That some things are really, bindingly right or wrong
That the universe must have had a first cause to exist
That the very idea of God already contains His existence
That belief in God is the safer bet when the stakes are huge
context: The moral argument runs from objective right and wrong to a moral lawgiver, leaning on the is/ought gap: bare natural facts don't yield duties. Kant treated God as a postulate of practical reason; C. S. Lewis (Mere Christianity, 1952) popularized it. J. L. Mackie (1977) accepts the 'if' but denies moral facts are objective.

choices: Treat it just like seeing: with no reason to doubt it, the experience is real evidence for what it shows.
Faith needs no evidence whatever to stand; even asking for any at all mistakes what genuine believing is.
Belief in God is simply properly basic, a thing rationally held with no supporting argument behind it at all.
The skeptical reporter is exactly right: a merely private inner feeling can never truly count as real evidence.
answer: Treat it just like seeing: with no reason to doubt it, the experience is real evidence for what it shows.
context: Richard Swinburne's principle of credulity (The Existence of God, 1979): absent a defeater, an experience is evidence for what it seems to be an experience of. William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) treats religious experience as a doxastic practice on a par with sense perception. Critics dispute the perception-like claim. The other three replies are fideism, reformed epistemology, and strict evidentialism.
question: At a panel, a reporter scoffs that people who sense God are just feeling things, not gathering evidence. A philosopher replies: if that experience is genuinely perception-like, give it the same benefit of the doubt we give ordinary seeing. Which reply is the philosopher making?

An evidentialist insists no belief is rational without an argument behind it, and God is no exception. A philosopher answers: you believe there was a past, and that other minds exist, with no argument for either, yet both are rational. Which reply is she making?
answer: Belief in God can be basic too, rational without argument, like the past or other minds.
choices: Belief in God can be basic too, rational without argument, like the past or other minds.
Believing pays off hugely if God is real, so the smart bet is just to believe.
Religious experience works like seeing, so it can count as evidence for God.
The evidentialist is right: with no argument, belief in God is not rational.
context: Alvin Plantinga ('Reformed Objections to Natural Theology,' 1980; Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) argues belief in God can be properly basic, like our beliefs about the past, other minds, and the external world, which we hold rationally without argument. This rejects the classical evidentialism of W. K. Clifford. The distractors are Pascal's wager, religious-experience-as-evidence, and evidentialism conceding the point.

question: Pascal's wager says: either God exists or not; believe and be right, and you win infinitely, so just believe. Aaron objects that betting on the payoff is not the same as actually believing. What is Aaron's objection?
answer: A payoff can make you want to believe, but wanting to believe is not yet believing.
choices: A payoff can make you want to believe, but wanting to believe is not yet believing.
Rival religions each promise infinite reward, so the bet cannot pick one God.
Once any option is infinite, the math gives every choice the same value.
Chasing the payoff is dishonest; never believe anything without evidence.
context: Pascal's Pensees (1670) frames the wager as practical reasoning under uncertainty. The belief-from-utility objection: a payoff at most yields the intention to acquire belief, a different mental state from belief itself, and faith is a relational stance, not a bet. The distractors are the other standard objections, the many-gods problem (William James), the infinite-utility breakdown (Alan Hajek), and the evidentialist objection.

question: Philosopher Mira lays out an argument: 'An all-good, all-powerful God could and would prevent every evil. Evil exists. So such a God cannot — the three claims STRICTLY contradict.' Which argument is Mira making?
answer: Logical problem of evil — the three claims flatly contradict, so no such God can exist.
choices: Logical problem of evil — the three claims flatly contradict, so no such God can exist.
Evidential problem of evil — evil makes such a God unlikely, but not a flat contradiction.
Free-will defense — evil is the price of giving creatures a real choice between right and wrong.
Divine hiddenness — a loving God would not leave honest seekers stuck in doubt.
context: J. L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (Mind, 1955) is the canonical statement of the LOGICAL problem of evil: it claims a strict contradiction, so the existence of any evil at all rules God out by deduction. Plantinga's free-will defense (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) is widely taken to have shown this strict version fails — it is logically possible that God could not make free creatures who never sin — after which the debate shifted to the weaker evidential version.

question: A fawn is caught in a forest fire and dies slowly over days, alone, with no person to witness it or grow from it. A writer argues: suffering this pointless is strong EVIDENCE against an all-good, all-powerful God — though not strict proof. Which argument is she making?
answer: Evidential problem of evil — pointless suffering makes such a God unlikely, short of strict proof.
choices: Evidential problem of evil — pointless suffering makes such a God unlikely, short of strict proof.
Logical problem of evil — God and any evil at all flatly contradict each other.
Soul-making theodicy — suffering is the forge where character and virtue are made.
Sceptical theism — a finite mind cannot rule out reasons an infinite mind might have.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (American Philosophical Quarterly, 1979) introduced the dying-fawn case and the EVIDENTIAL framing: apparently pointless suffering is probabilistic evidence against God, not a deductive contradiction. The fawn dies with no one to be ennobled by it, which is what blocks the soul-making reply. Standard theistic answers (Wykstra's sceptical theism; Stump's soul-making theodicy) attack the step from 'no good we can see' to 'no good there is.'

question: Told that 'appealing to mystery is weak,' a theologian replies: 'Real goods — moral growth, meaningful choice, a stable lawful world — cannot exist unless some evils are permitted. The evil is real; it is the price of those goods.' Which response is she giving?
answer: Greater-goods defense — the evil buys identifiable goods that could not come any other way.
choices: Greater-goods defense — the evil buys identifiable goods that could not come any other way.
Free-will defense — the only good at stake is the freedom to choose right or wrong.
Soul-making theodicy — the one good is the soul growing, forged through hardship.
Sceptical theism — we cannot name the good at all, only trust there is one.
context: The greater-goods defense has roots in Augustine (Confessions VII) and Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I.49) and is elaborated by Richard Swinburne (Providence and the Problem of Evil, 1998). Its signature, and the tell here, is that it NAMES a range of identifiable goods the evil secures — broader than the free-will defense (which stakes everything on choice) and John Hick's soul-making theodicy (Evil and the God of Love, 1966, staked on character), and the opposite of sceptical theism, which insists the good cannot be named at all.

question: A traveler swears under oath that he watched a dead man come back to life. The skeptic doesn't call him a liar, but still won't believe it. His rule: a report earns belief only when the witness being mistaken would be even stranger than the event itself. What standard is the skeptic using?
answer: The rarer the claim, the stronger the evidence it takes to believe it.
choices: The rarer the claim, the stronger the evidence it takes to believe it.
Anything science cannot yet explain should simply be denied outright.
A witness under oath must always be trusted over any mere doubter.
Past events can never be known from anyone's testimony at all.
context: This is David Hume's test from 'Of Miracles' (1748): no testimony is enough unless the witness being wrong would be more astonishing than the miracle itself. The skeptic isn't calling miracles impossible or trust worthless - he's weighing two improbabilities against each other. Modern Bayesian replies (John Earman, 2000) argue strong, independent multiple testimony can in principle clear that bar.

question: Two travelers each sincerely believe their own faith is the one true faith - and the two faiths flatly contradict each other. A philosopher points out that BOTH are perfectly sincere. Why does that show sincerity cannot be what makes a belief true?
answer: Sincere people believe opposite things - sincerity can't make one true.
choices: Sincere people believe opposite things - sincerity can't make one true.
A belief is true only when enough people happen to share it.
Whatever a person deeply feels simply becomes true for them.
Beliefs about faith can't be true or false in the first place.
context: Since two sincere people can hold beliefs that contradict, sincerity is 'truth-neutral' - it can attach to a false belief just as easily as a true one, so it can't be what makes either one true. This is the heart of W. K. Clifford's evidentialism ('The Ethics of Belief', 1877). William James ('The Will to Believe', 1896) gives the famous reply that some live choices may be made on more than evidence.

question: A columnist writes that faith means believing WITHOUT reasons - the opposite of real inquiry. Marlin answers: the same God is the source of both reason and revelation, so the two overlap and can never truly contradict. Which view of faith and reason is Marlin defending?
answer: Concord - faith and reason overlap and can never truly clash.
choices: Concord - faith and reason overlap and can never truly clash.
Fideism - faith stands beyond reason; asking for proof misses the point.
Evidentialism - faith is rational only if public evidence backs it.
Properly basic - faith needs no argument, like trusting your own eyes.
context: Aquinas (Summa Contra Gentiles I.7) argues that since truth cannot contradict truth, faith and reason cannot ultimately conflict - both flow from the same source. Fideism (Tertullian's 'credo quia absurdum') puts faith beyond reason; evidentialism (Clifford) demands public proof; Reformed epistemology (Plantinga) treats belief in God as properly basic, needing no argument. The relationship stays genuinely contested.

question: Phin worries: 'If God knows TODAY what I'll choose tomorrow, my choice is already fixed — how is it free?' Selene answers: 'God doesn't forecast it in advance — He sees all of time at once, the way you take in a whole painting. Knowing your free choice doesn't cause it.' Which reply is Selene giving?
answer: Timeless God — He sees all time at once, so foreknowledge isn't an advance forecast that fixes things.
choices: Timeless God — He sees all time at once, so foreknowledge isn't an advance forecast that fixes things.
Open future — even God can't know a free choice before it's made; the future isn't settled yet.
Middle knowledge — God knows what you WOULD freely do in any situation, and plans around it.
Soft determinism — foreknowledge does fix it, but you're free if you act on your own wants.
context: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (524) gives the eternalist answer: God's knowing is timeless, not earlier-in-time, so it is no more controlling than a friend watching you choose. Rivals: open theism (the future isn't there to know), Molina's middle knowledge, and theological compatibilism.

question: Cale argues: 'A loving God wouldn't leave honest seekers unable to believe. Honest seekers exist. So no such God exists.' Riva replies: 'Real love may need room to grow — and overwhelming proof of God might crush the very freedom love requires.' Which reply is Riva giving?
answer: Epistemic distance — love needs room overwhelming divine presence would crush, so hiddenness can fit love.
choices: Epistemic distance — love needs room overwhelming divine presence would crush, so hiddenness can fit love.
Skeptical theism — our small minds can't judge what reasons an infinite God might have for hiding.
Free-will defense — overwhelming proof would force belief, so hiddenness protects free faith.
Damaged sense — seekers DO have the evidence; they miss it because their God-sense is broken.
context: J. L. Schellenberg's Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (1993) is the modern hiddenness argument. The epistemic-distance reply traces to John Hick: a relationship of love may require cognitive 'space' that overwhelming presence would foreclose.

question: Reza writes: 'So many sincere people disagree about religion — so no tradition can claim it has the truth.' Tova replies: 'Sincere people disagree about ethics and politics too. That shows the questions are HARD, not that no answer is right.' Which reply is Tova giving?
answer: Disagreement-is-hard — sincere clashes happen everywhere and don't prove that no view is right.
choices: Disagreement-is-hard — sincere clashes happen everywhere and don't prove that no view is right.
Pluralism — every great tradition is a valid path to the same hidden transcendent reality.
Inclusivism — one faith is true, but sincere outsiders share in its truth unknowingly.
Skeptical theism — our minds can't judge God's reasons for allowing so much disagreement.
context: Religious pluralism (John Hick, 1989) treats traditions as equally valid responses to one reality. Tova's exclusivist reply (Plantinga, 'Pluralism: A Defense of Religious Exclusivism,' 1995): sincere disagreement marks every hard domain, so it can't by itself refute one tradition.

question: Maren defends a theodicy: 'This world is a place for SOUL-MAKING. Courage and compassion can only grow where there is real danger and need — a frictionless paradise couldn't shape the creatures we are meant to become.' Which reply is she giving?
answer: Soul-making — hardship is the needed forge for virtues that couldn't form in an easy paradise.
choices: Soul-making — hardship is the needed forge for virtues that couldn't form in an easy paradise.
Free-will defense — evil is the price of making creatures truly free to choose good or ill.
Greater goods — an evil is allowed only when it buys a specific good, like stable natural law.
Skeptical theism — we can't see the reasons an infinite mind has for allowing a given evil.
context: John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops the soul-making (Irenaean) theodicy against the Augustinian 'perfect-then-fallen' frame: a world with real trials is the necessary forge for moral and spiritual growth.

question: A philosopher argues: 'IF it is even POSSIBLE that a greatest-conceivable being exists, then by the logic of necessity it must exist in every possible world — including ours. Grant the bare possibility, and the conclusion follows.' Which argument is this?
answer: Modal ontological — if a maximally great being is even possible, it exists necessarily, in every world.
choices: Modal ontological — if a maximally great being is even possible, it exists necessarily, in every world.
Kalam cosmological — whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so it has one.
Anselm's classic — a being than which none greater can be conceived must exist in reality, not just thought.
Fine-tuning — the constants are too precisely set for life to be chance, pointing to a designer.
context: Alvin Plantinga's modal ontological argument (The Nature of Necessity, 1974) recasts Anselm in modal logic: if a maximally great being is possible in any world, necessity carries it into every world. Critics grant the logic but challenge the loaded possibility premise.

question: The medieval Islamic theologian al-Ghazali sharpened an argument his tradition called kalam, "speech." Revived by William Lane Craig in 1979, it rests on one bold claim: the universe BEGAN to exist, so it has a cause beyond itself. Several God arguments exist; which one rests on the universe having a BEGINNING?
answer: Kalam argument: the universe began, and whatever begins to exist must have a cause.
choices: Kalam argument: the universe began, and whatever begins to exist must have a cause.
Contingency argument: things that could fail to exist need a necessary being to ground them.
Fine-tuning argument: the constants are set so precisely for life that design beats chance.
Ontological argument: the very idea of a greatest possible being implies it must exist.
context: Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) was the great critic of the falasifa, and advanced the kalam in that fight; the temporal premise, that the universe has a finite past, is its distinctive feature. The contingency, design, and ontological arguments do not use a beginning. Standard rival: a beginningless universe on some cosmological models.

question: Aquinas argued each thing might never have existed, so a world of only such things would explain nothing -- something that CANNOT fail to exist must ground them. Aldo counters that the universe BEGAN, and whatever begins needs a cause. Whose reasoning is the contingency argument?
answer: Aquinas's, since it runs from things that might not have existed, not from a beginning in time.
choices: Aquinas's, since it runs from things that might not have existed, not from a beginning in time.
Aldo's, since it turns on the universe having a first moment when it began to exist.
Both, since each one reasons purely from the order and design found in nature.
Neither, since both only define a perfect being into existence from its concept.
context: Aquinas's line is the contingency argument (here in Leibniz's 'sufficient reason' form, the move his Third Way is famous for): from beings that could fail to exist, to one whose existence cannot. Aldo gives the Kalam argument (al-Ghazali, revived by William Lane Craig), which turns instead on the universe BEGINNING in time. Both differ from the design and ontological arguments.

question: An atheist argues evil makes an all-good, all-powerful God not just unlikely but logically IMPOSSIBLE. A theist replies that he need not explain why God permits evil — only show it is possible that free creatures who can choose evil are a good worth the risk. Which reply is this?
answer: Free-will defense — evil is the possible price of creatures free to choose.
choices: Free-will defense — evil is the possible price of creatures free to choose.
Soul-making — hardship is the furnace where courage and compassion are forged.
Skeptical theism — our minds are too small to read an infinite God's reasons.
Privation theory — evil is just the absence of good, not a real thing itself.
context: J. L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955) framed the LOGICAL problem of evil: any evil at all, he claimed, is incompatible with such a God. Alvin Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) answered with the free-will defense, which need only show that God's permitting moral evil is POSSIBLE, given the good of free creatures, to defeat the charge of contradiction. Most philosophers treat the logical problem as defused; the evidential version remains live.

question: A theologian argues that virtues like courage and compassion can only form in a world with real danger and need — a frictionless paradise would leave us shallow. The hardship, he says, is the furnace that shapes the very souls we are meant to become. Which view is this?
answer: Soul-making — hardship is the furnace where courage and compassion are forged.
choices: Soul-making — hardship is the furnace where courage and compassion are forged.
Free-will defense — evil is the possible price of creatures free to choose.
Skeptical theism — our minds are too small to read an infinite God's reasons.
Privation theory — evil is just the absence of good, not a real thing itself.
context: John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops the soul-making (Irenaean) theodicy, named for the second-century bishop Irenaeus rather than Augustine. The Augustinian story blames a past Fall; Hick's treats this hard world as an environment designed to grow mature moral character. Critics such as William Rowe press that some horrors are far too severe for soul-making to plausibly explain.

question: An atheist points to a fawn dying slowly, unseen, in a forest fire: he can find no good that would justify it, so he concludes there IS none — evidence against God. A theist answers that 'I see no reason' proves 'there is no reason' only if we would surely spot God's reasons, and our minds may be too small. Which reply is this?
answer: Skeptical theism — our minds are too small to read an infinite God's reasons.
choices: Skeptical theism — our minds are too small to read an infinite God's reasons.
Free-will defense — evil is the possible price of creatures free to choose.
Soul-making — hardship is the furnace where courage and compassion are forged.
Privation theory — evil is just the absence of good, not a real thing itself.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979) built the evidential problem around exactly this fawn, dying unseen in a forest fire. The reply is skeptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, Michael Bergmann): the step from 'we see no justifying good' to 'there is none' assumes we would spot God's reasons if they were there — a 'noseeum' inference our limited minds do not license.

question: A philosopher says belief in God can be reasonable even if you never argue your way to it from evidence, the way you reasonably believe other people have minds, or that the world did not pop into being five minutes ago. You don't prove those; they are starting points. Which claim is she making about belief in God?
answer: It can be a rational starting point, not a conclusion you must infer from arguments.
choices: It can be a rational starting point, not a conclusion you must infer from arguments.
It must be built up from a cumulative case of evidence, design, and experience.
It rests entirely on religious experience counting as a kind of evidence.
It lies beyond reason itself, so asking for reasons just misses the point.
context: This is Alvin Plantinga's reformed epistemology (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000): belief in God can be 'properly basic', warranted directly, like belief in other minds, not derived from arguments. He distinguishes it from natural theology (which infers), from Alston's experience-as-evidence, and from fideism (which abandons warrant).

question: A thinker presses an objector: 'You trust your eyes that a tree is there, yet you cannot prove your eyes are reliable without already using them. Perceiving God works the same way.' If the parallel holds, what follows for the doubter?
answer: Then doubting the God-experience needs its own reason, not just the lack of outside proof.
choices: Then doubting the God-experience needs its own reason, not just the lack of outside proof.
Belief in God is a basic starting point, so no perception is even needed here.
Nothing is really known by perception, so the tree case collapses the same way.
Only shared, repeatable evidence counts, so the experience by itself proves nothing.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991): 'Christian mystical practice' is a doxastic practice on a par with ordinary sense perception, both circular if you demand outside proof, so neither can fault the other. Perception is innocent until shown guilty, which shifts the burden onto the doubter. This differs from Plantinga's basicality route, which needs no perception; Swinburne's 'principle of credulity' is kin.

question: A physicist on a panel argues: 'Tweak the cosmological constant by a hair and you get a dead universe — no stars, no life. That life-permitting band is absurdly narrow. Blind chance landing inside it would be a staggering fluke; a designer would not.' What kind of reasoning is the physicist using?
answer: Inference to the best explanation — the narrow band is far less of a fluke if designed than if left to chance.
choices: Inference to the best explanation — the narrow band is far less of a fluke if designed than if left to chance.
A strict deduction — the fine-tuned constants logically force a designer, leaving no room for doubt.
A head-count — the more finely-tuned the constants are, the more designers it must have taken.
An appeal to mystery — since no one can explain the constants, a designer must be the answer.
context: This is the fine-tuning argument (Robin Collins, John Leslie, William Lane Craig). It is probabilistic, not a proof: it weighs how expected the life-permitting constants are under design versus under chance, and argues design wins. The leading rival reply is the multiverse — countless universes make even a staggering fluke likely to turn up somewhere.

choices: It dissolves both horns: God's own loving character settles goodness, so commands are neither arbitrary nor outside-ruled.
It simply takes the first horn here: whatever God happens to command thereby becomes fully right, even an order to be cruel.
It simply takes the second horn here: goodness fully exists on its very own, and God merely reports that standard to us.
It drops God from the matter altogether: goodness instead comes from human nature aiming steadily at its own proper ends.
answer: It dissolves both horns: God's own loving character settles goodness, so commands are neither arbitrary nor outside-ruled.
context: This is the Euthyphro dilemma (Plato, Euthyphro 10a). Robert Adams's modified divine command theory (Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999): wrongness is being contrary to a loving God's commands, while goodness is grounded in God's character, so the two horns are dissolved, not chosen between. Natural-law theory (Aquinas) is the human-nature rival.
question: Socrates' puzzle: is a good act good BECAUSE God commands it (so God could command cruelty), or does God command it because it is ALREADY good (so goodness outranks God)? A philosopher answers: 'Neither. God commands it because it flows from God's loving character, which just IS goodness.' What does his move do to the puzzle?

A scholar says every religion is like blind men touching one elephant -- each grabs a different part of one Reality that lies beyond all human concepts, so none is simply right and none simply wrong. Which view of religious difference is this?
answer: Pluralism: all are partial cultural views of one reality beyond concepts, none uniquely right.
choices: Pluralism: all are partial cultural views of one reality beyond concepts, none uniquely right.
Exclusivism: one tradition is right where they conflict, the rest mistaken.
Inclusivism: one tradition holds the fullest truth, others a partial share of it.
Naturalism: there is no reality behind the experiences; it is all human psychology.
context: The blind-men-and-elephant image is the classic picture of John Hick's pluralism (An Interpretation of Religion, 1989), which borrows Kant's noumenon/phenomenon split: the religions are culturally-shaped responses to one 'Real' that none grasps as it is in itself. Plantinga and Alston defend exclusivism against it; Karl Rahner is the leading inclusivist.

question: A believer says her religion's central claims are true, so the conflicting claims of other faiths are false. 'How arrogant to think only you are right,' a classmate scoffs. 'But saying every religion is equally valid is itself a claim the rest got wrong,' she answers. Which is her defense?
answer: Calling any claim true already treats whatever contradicts it as false; that is normal, not arrogant.
choices: Calling any claim true already treats whatever contradicts it as false; that is normal, not arrogant.
She cannot be blamed at all, because no one can really know which religion is right.
Each religion is only a different window on one same reality, so in truth no one is wrong.
Her certainty is just a private feeling, so it owes no defense or explanation to anyone.
context: Alvin Plantinga, 'A Defense of Religious Exclusivism' (1995): holding substantive claims about reality just does commit you to thinking incompatible claims false, no more arrogant than any other belief. His sharpest turn, the one the believer throws back here: pluralism is itself an exclusive claim about religious truth, so it cannot escape the charge it presses.

question: Blaise Pascal helped invent the mathematics of probability — how to bet wisely when the outcome is uncertain. Late in life he aimed that very tool at God: granting that reason cannot settle whether God exists, he asked which way it is smarter to bet. On what basis does Pascal say to believe?
answer: On the payoff: if God exists the gain is infinite and the loss small, so the bet favors belief.
choices: On the payoff: if God exists the gain is infinite and the loss small, so the bet favors belief.
On the evidence: the order and design of nature already prove a maker arranged it all.
On logic: the very idea of a perfect God already implies that such a God must exist.
On feeling: faith is a leap into the dark that reason can never reach or judge at all.
context: This is Pascal's Wager, from the Pensees (1670). Having co-founded probability theory with Fermat, Pascal applied expected-value reasoning to faith: he set aside the evidence for or against God and weighed the stakes of each bet instead. Famous objections: which God do you bet on, and can belief even be chosen for a payoff?

question: Kierkegaard pointed to Abraham, the knife raised over his own son Isaac on God's command -- obeying with no proof and no calculation, only a passionate leap held in total uncertainty, reaching what reason and odds cannot. What picture of faith is this?
answer: Faith as a leap beyond reason, embraced in uncertainty, not reached by argument.
choices: Faith as a leap beyond reason, embraced in uncertainty, not reached by argument.
Faith as a smart bet: believe because the possible payoff is huge.
Faith as a basic belief: a rational starting point needing no argument.
Faith as a conclusion: the reasonable end of weighing the evidence.
context: Soren Kierkegaard built Fear and Trembling (1843) around Abraham at Mount Moriah; the Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846) names faith a passionate inwardness held in objective uncertainty, the 'leap.' He sets it apart from Pascal's wager (a calculation), Plantinga's basic belief, and natural theology's evidence, though critics press whether a leap can still be told apart from arbitrary belief.

question: On a panel, a thinker defends belief in God like this: 'No single argument proves it. But the universe existing, its fine-tuned order, minds that can know it, and reports of religious experience each nudge the odds up a little, and stacked together they tip the balance.' What is the SHAPE of her case?
answer: A cumulative case: many small clues that add up to more than any one.
choices: A cumulative case: many small clues that add up to more than any one.
A single knockdown proof meant to settle the whole matter by itself.
A leap past reason, made where evidence runs out and cannot reach.
A basic trust in God that holds firm with no argument behind it at all.
context: This is the cumulative-case strategy of Richard Swinburne (The Existence of God, 1979), built with Bayesian probability: cosmological, design, moral, and experiential arguments each raise the probability of God a little, and he argues the joint result passes one-half. It contrasts with a single deductive proof, Kierkegaard's leap of faith, and Plantinga's properly-basic belief.

question: The mathematician W.K. Clifford asked you to picture a shipowner who sends an old, leaky vessel to sea full of emigrants. He talks himself into trusting it without inspecting it; it sinks, and all aboard drown. Clifford says he is guilty of their deaths. What broader rule did Clifford draw from this?
answer: It is always wrong to believe anything on evidence you have not honestly checked.
choices: It is always wrong to believe anything on evidence you have not honestly checked.
He is guilty only because the ship happened to sink, not for believing it.
Believing whatever helps you act is fine, since hesitation costs lives too.
Owners answer for ships, but ordinary beliefs carry no such duty of care.
context: Clifford's 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877) uses the shipowner parable to argue that believing on insufficient evidence is itself a moral fault, even when things happen to turn out fine. William James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) is the classic reply: some choices we must make before the evidence is in.

question: An atheist argues: 'Some suffering an all-good, all-powerful God could prevent serves no greater good. So PROBABLY no such God exists — not that it's impossible, just unlikely given all this needless pain.' Which form of the argument from evil is this?
answer: Evidential — needless suffering makes God improbable, not outright impossible.
choices: Evidential — needless suffering makes God improbable, not outright impossible.
Logical — any evil at all is flatly incompatible with such a God.
Natural-evil — only suffering from nature, not human wrong, tells against God.
Evidentialist duty — believing without enough evidence is itself wrong.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979) gave this its canonical form — the fawn dying unseen in a forest fire — arguing apparently pointless suffering makes theism improbable (inductive), not impossible. That contrasts with Mackie's 1955 LOGICAL problem (any evil is incompatible with God), which Plantinga's free-will defense answered. Theists reply with skeptical theism: we may not see the goods that justify a given evil.

question: The Jesuit Karl Rahner startled fellow theologians with a phrase: a sincere Hindu who never heard the gospel might still be saved as an "anonymous Christian." He wants one faith to be uniquely true AND its grace to reach sincere outsiders. Which move lets him hold both?
answer: Truth can be fully present in one faith, yet its grace still reach those who never met it.
choices: Truth can be fully present in one faith, yet its grace still reach those who never met it.
Outsiders cannot share that grace at all, so only the visible faithful are ever saved.
No faith is uniquely true; each is one equal window onto the same divine reality.
Talk of salvation names nothing real, since religion is only a human invention.
context: This resolution is inclusivism. Karl Rahner coined 'anonymous Christian' in the 1960s (Theological Investigations) and helped shape the Second Vatican Council (Lumen Gentium, Nostra Aetate). It sits between exclusivism (deny outsiders share the grace — Plantinga) and pluralism (deny any one faith is uniquely true — Hick), keeping one tradition central while extending its reach.

question: Augustine, who once believed evil was a dark force at war with good, later changed his mind. He pointed to blindness: it is not some object added to the eye, but simply sight that is — missing where it ought to be. On his new view, what is evil?
answer: Not a thing at all — it is the absence or spoiling of a good that ought to be there.
choices: Not a thing at all — it is the absence or spoiling of a good that ought to be there.
A real force of darkness, equal to good and locked with it in unending war.
An illusion — nothing is truly bad; we only judge things good or evil by habit.
Whatever a community forbids — evil is just the rules a given culture lays down.
context: Augustine spent his early years a Manichaean, holding evil to be a positive substance; after his conversion he argued instead for privation (Confessions VII; Enchiridion, 421): evil has no being of its own, only the corruption of a created good. Aquinas carried the view into medieval thought.

question: You have never been to Antarctica, yet you know it is there — you trust reliable reports handed down to you. The philosopher C.A.J. Coady argues a Christian believes the same way: on testimony from scripture, church, and centuries of community. What is his claim about where that belief gets its warrant?
answer: From trusting reliable testimony — the everyday route by which we know most of what we know.
choices: From trusting reliable testimony — the everyday route by which we know most of what we know.
From an argument each believer must work out alone before being entitled to hold it.
From a private inner experience that no outside report could ever stand in for.
From a built-in instinct for God that needs no reasons and no reports at all.
context: C.A.J. Coady (Testimony, 1992) showed that testimony is a basic source of knowledge in general: most of what anyone knows rests on trusting others. Mavrodes and Plantinga extend this to religious belief — scripture and tradition can justify belief without each person re-deriving every argument.

question: Galileo argues the Earth moves, but nearly every scholar of 1610 agrees the Sun circles a still Earth. 'Everyone holds the old view, so the matter is closed.' He is near-friendless, yet objects. His best reply?
answer: How many hold a view is no evidence it is true; whole ages have been wrong.
choices: The old view must be right, since so few now dare defend the new one.
How many hold a view is no evidence it is true; whole ages have been wrong.
No claim is ever settled, so 'the matter is closed' is always a mistake.
Only the loudest scholar present, not the crowd, can decide who is right.
context: This is the bandwagon fallacy (appeal to popularity): a head-count is treated as proof. Agreement can track fashion or pressure rather than truth. For centuries nearly everyone agreed the Earth sat motionless at the center of the cosmos — and they were wrong.

question: Urging a yes vote, a speaker says: 'Be on the right side of history — the future will see we were right.' A councillor wants the plan but distrusts that reason. What is her best objection?
answer: What later ages think is no evidence the plan is right now; the future errs too.
choices: Whatever wins out in the end is right, so the speaker simply cannot be doubted.
What later ages think is no evidence the plan is right now; the future errs too.
No one can foresee the future, so every plan is exactly as good as any other.
Only tonight's vote, never history, can make a plan right or wrong at all.
context: This is appeal to novelty (and to posterity): 'the right side of history' treats the future's supposed verdict as proof now. But later ages also held views we reject, so their imagined agreement settles nothing today.

question: A petitioner warns a wavering signer: 'If you will not sign with us, you stand with the harm.' The signer backs the cause but doubts the petition will work. What is his best objection?
answer: Sharing the goal while doubting one tactic is not the same as siding with harm.
choices: Since so many have signed already, refusing now is clearly the wrong call.
A lone signature could never matter, so 'complicit' makes no sense here.
Sharing the goal while doubting one tactic is not the same as siding with harm.
No one is ever to blame for harm they merely allowed and did not cause.
context: This is a false dilemma: 'sign or you stand with the harm' offers two boxes, ally or enemy, erasing everyone who shares the aim but questions the method. The honest middle (back the goal, doubt the tactic) is the option it hides.

question: Vienna, 1847: Semmelweis shows hand-washing stops doctors killing mothers with fever. 'No respected physician believes it, so we drop it.' A colleague grants the idea is unpopular, yet objects. His best reply?
answer: A view having few believers is not the same as the view being shown false.
choices: A view having few believers is not the same as the view being shown false.
Since most physicians reject it, dropping the idea is clearly the safe course.
An idea is true only while unpopular, so dropping it proves it was right.
Ideas can never be judged at all, so the doctors have no ground to drop any.
context: This is the bandwagon fallacy in reverse (appeal to the majority): a view shedding believers is treated as a refutation. But popularity tracks mood, not truth — Semmelweis was mocked in his lifetime and vindicated long after.

question: An apprentice shipwright scorns the old hull: 'That shape is old-fashioned; ours is the modern one, so ours is the better ship.' A boatwright likes the new hull but distrusts that reason. Her best reply?
answer: Newer does not mean better; a design's age says nothing about whether it floats.
choices: The older hull must be stronger, since it has stayed afloat far longer.
No two designs can really be compared, so picking either is just arbitrary.
Newer does not mean better; a design's age says nothing about whether it floats.
Only what most shipwrights favor this season can decide which hull is best.
context: This is appeal to novelty: treating 'newer' as 'better.' Novelty and merit are independent — the real question is whether the design works, not when it was drawn. Its mirror image, 'older is wiser,' is the appeal to tradition.

question: An activist tells a student who wrote a harsh op-ed: 'Words are violence — your essay assaulted us as surely as a fist would.' The student agrees words can wound, but says this goes too far. Her best objection?
answer: A blow removes your choice; a sentence only tries to change your mind — force is not offense.
choices: A blow removes your choice; a sentence only tries to change your mind — force is not offense.
Only a count of who was hurt could settle this, never a person's heated wording now.
One short op-ed has no real reach at all, so the charge cannot stick to it here.
Words can never carry any harm whatever, so the whole worry here is simply hollow.
context: The slogan equivocates on 'violence,' sliding from a physical attack to speech that offends. The line it blurs is force versus persuasion: a punch removes your choice, an argument appeals to it. Even people who think cruel words can be wrong resist 'violence,' since it would let any offended listener claim self-defense.

question: A campaigner tells a man who skipped a charity drive: 'Not giving is the same as killing — every coin you kept let a child die.' He grants giving is good, but says the charge overreaches. His best reply?
answer: Letting a child die is not the same as taking a life — it collapses omission into murder.
choices: Letting a child die is not the same as taking a life — it collapses omission into murder.
Only a tally of who survived could ever settle this, not some stranger's guilt-trip.
One man's few spare coins are far too small to save anyone, so it cannot apply here.
Skipping a single drive can carry no blame whatever, so the whole charge is empty.
context: The slogan equivocates on 'killing,' sliding from causing a death to merely not preventing one — the act/omission distinction. Peter Singer presses this hard; most ethicists still hold that killing and letting-die differ in kind, even if both can be wrong, since otherwise everyone alive is a murderer.

question: A councillor warns: 'Ban one violent book and you may as well burn the library — soon every novel that offends someone will be gone.' A clerk grants the risk is real but says the leap is too fast. Her best objection?
answer: One narrow ban need not trigger the rest — the end is asserted, never shown to follow.
choices: One narrow ban need not trigger the rest — the end is asserted, never shown to follow.
Only a count of books actually pulled could settle this, not a vivid warning.
One small council has no power to empty a library, so the fear cannot apply.
Banning a book can never do any harm at all, so the whole worry is hollow.
context: This is the slippery-slope fallacy: a small first step is treated as if it must slide to a disastrous end, with no reason given for why each link pulls the next. The dread does the work the missing argument should. A slope is only valid if each step genuinely forces the following one.

question: A knight argues: 'Let the king tax us one copper and he will not stop — next half our gold, then our very lands.' A scribe agrees taxes can grow but says the chain is assumed, not earned. His best reply?
answer: A small tax need not lead to seizing everything — the ruin is feared, never shown to follow.
choices: A small tax need not lead to seizing everything — the ruin is feared, never shown to follow.
Only a ledger of what the king took could settle this, not a grim prophecy.
One knight's lone copper is far too little to matter, so the fear cannot apply.
A small tax can never cause any harm whatever, so the whole worry is hollow.
context: This is the slippery-slope fallacy: each step is presumed to drag the next toward catastrophe, with no mechanism given for why it must. A real chain argument has to show each link forces the following one; here only the dread of the ending supplies the push.

question: Challenged that her budget numbers don't add up, a leader fires back: 'How dare you nitpick when children are starving?' — then moves on without fixing the math. A page sees the dodge. His best objection?
answer: Starving children are real, but they don't make the budget add up — she swapped the question.
choices: Starving children are real, but they don't make the budget add up — she swapped the question.
Only her own staff's word could settle the figures, never an outsider's doubt.
One page's small objection has no weight at all, so the math need not be met.
Budget numbers can never truly be checked, so the whole challenge is pointless.
context: This is the red herring: a stirring but irrelevant point (starving children) is dropped in to pull attention off the live question (do the numbers work?). The emotion is genuine; it is simply not an answer. The repair is to set the distraction aside and return to the claim actually under fire.

question: A columnist defends a sweeping new mandate: 'It's just being kind to people who are suffering.' Pressed on whether the mandate actually helps or only feels good, he repeats, 'It's about kindness — who could be against that?' and moves on. Why is this a bad argument?
answer: He defends a mood nobody attacks (kindness) to avoid defending the mandate itself.
choices: He defends a mood nobody attacks (kindness) to avoid defending the mandate itself.
He treats his own good intentions as proof his actual policy must work.
He assumes one small kind act must scale up to every situation alike.
He counts the mandate's popularity as if being liked proved it worked.
context: A motte-and-bailey hides a contested claim (the 'bailey' — this mandate works) behind an unassailable one (the 'motte' — kindness is good), sliding to the safe claim when challenged. Nicholas Shackel named the move in 2005. The tell: the disputed policy is never argued for, only relabeled as kindness.

question: A dean defends hiring targets tied to applicants' ancestry. Asked how that squares with judging each person on merit, she says, 'Diversity just means everyone belongs here — surely you want that?' and returns to the targets. Why is this a weak argument?
answer: She retreats to a slogan all sides accept to avoid defending the ancestry targets.
choices: She retreats to a slogan all sides accept to avoid defending the ancestry targets.
She assumes her own good aim guarantees the targets produce fair results.
She takes one campus case as settling how every workplace ought to hire.
She paints the questioner as against belonging rather than truly answering.
context: Motte-and-bailey (Nicholas Shackel, 2005): an easy, agreeable claim (the 'motte' — everyone belongs) shields a contested one (the 'bailey' — ancestry-based targets), and the speaker swaps them under fire. 'Diversity' carries both meanings, so the disputed claim rides along untested.

question: A guest closes the debate: 'Ninety-seven percent of experts agree, so the question is closed — stop asking.' Even granting the ninety-seven percent, why does this fail as an argument?
answer: How many experts agree isn't the same as why they're right, and inquiry doesn't close on a head-count.
choices: How many experts agree isn't the same as why they're right, and inquiry doesn't close on a head-count.
It assumes the experts are concealing every study that happens to point the other way.
It treats just two possible positions as the only ones a careful person could take.
It brands the lone doubter dishonest rather than ever meeting the doubt being raised.
context: Appeal to authority. Consensus is real evidence, but a tally of who agrees is not the reasons behind the claim — and 'stop asking' inverts how knowledge grows, since open questions are re-examined, not sealed by vote. The error is mistaking a count of agreers for the argument.

question: On air, an anchor waves off every rival network: 'Any reasonable viewer can SEE we're the only honest one — that's just what being reasonable means.' A guest presses him for proof. Why does his argument fail?
answer: His one reason, that reasonable people agree, is built so any disagreement makes you unreasonable.
choices: His one reason, that reasonable people agree, is built so any disagreement makes you unreasonable.
He leans on his own network's fame as though being popular proved it always told the truth.
He offers only two possible camps, his one honest network and every other dishonest one.
He attacks the doubters as secretly biased instead of facing the actual point they raised.
context: Begging the question (petitio principii): the conclusion is smuggled into the premise. 'Reasonable people agree with us' defines anyone who disagrees as unreasonable, so the claim can never lose — and an argument that no one could possibly counter proves nothing. The circularity is self-sealing: the premise is rigged to include the conclusion.

choices: It calls the decree fair only by quietly assuming the decree is fair, so its reason just restates the claim.
It leans on the lawmaker's high and lofty office, as if sheer rank alone could somehow make a decree fair.
It allows only two harsh verdicts in the end: a perfectly and flawlessly just law, or an utterly worthless one.
It brands anyone who dares object a mere lawbreaker, instead of ever bothering to offer a real reasoned reply.
answer: It calls the decree fair only by quietly assuming the decree is fair, so its reason just restates the claim.
context: Circular reasoning: the premise and the conclusion are the same claim in different words, so the argument never moves forward. Whether THIS decree is truly just is exactly what was in question, and the motto settles it only by helping itself to the answer.
question: A herald nails a fresh decree to the city gate, its motto carved beneath: 'This law is just, because it is the law -- and the law is what is just.' A scribe is ordered to copy it as proof the decree is fair. Why is the motto empty as an argument?

Shown that the communes she championed left behind roughly 100 million dead -- by famine, purge, and gulag -- a thinker replies: 'Those were never REAL socialism; true socialism has not yet been tried.' She grants the record is grim. Why does this rescue fail as an argument?
answer: It rules out every actual case in advance, so no result could ever count against the idea.
choices: It rules out every actual case in advance, so no result could ever count against the idea.
It blames the failures on the leaders rather than on the system they installed.
It assumes anything that failed before is fated to fail in every future as well.
It leans on how noble the dream feels instead of on what the record shows.
context: The no-true-Scotsman move (named by Antony Flew, 1975) saves a claim by redefining its terms so no counterexample can ever count. A belief that no possible evidence could refute is not invincible -- it is empty. The death toll cited: roughly 65-100 million (Black Book of Communism).

question: A guru teaches that a hidden field guides all events. A student notes that nothing ever seems to disprove it. 'Exactly,' the guru beams, 'doubters just prove the field is testing their faith.' Why does turning every objection into support weaken the claim?
answer: If both proof and doubt are counted as evidence for it, no observation could ever show it false.
choices: If both proof and doubt are counted as evidence for it, no observation could ever show it false.
The guru attacks the doubters' sincerity rather than answering the point they raise.
The guru assumes a claim is true simply because no rival has yet disproved it.
The guru leans on his standing as a teacher instead of on any actual finding.
context: A claim is only meaningful, Karl Popper argued (1934), if some possible observation could refute it -- this is falsifiability. When a theory absorbs every result, including its own apparent failures, it explains everything and therefore predicts nothing.

question: A columnist demands triple-blind trials before believing crime rose under her favored policy, yet cites one neighbor's story as proof crime fell under it. Pressed, she says, 'I just hold claims to a high standard.' Why does this defense fail?
answer: The hard bar is aimed only at the claim she dislikes, so it tracks her side, not the truth.
choices: The hard bar is aimed only at the claim she dislikes, so it tracks her side, not the truth.
She rejects the trials over who funded them rather than on anything in their method.
She treats two rival studies as equal when their methods differ sharply in quality.
She points only to the figures that flatter her policy and buries all the rest.
context: Scott Alexander named the isolated demand for rigor (2014): one side faces a near-impossible bar while the other passes on a whisper. The tell is asymmetry -- the bar shifts with the conclusion, not with the question, so skepticism becomes a weapon rather than a discipline.

question: At a town hall, a speaker recounts the night her shop burned, then concludes: 'I lived through it, so my account of WHO set the fire cannot be questioned.' A listener grieves the loss but balks at the leap. What is the listener's sharpest objection?
answer: That the fire truly happened to her does not place her theory of who lit it beyond challenge.
choices: That the fire truly happened to her does not place her theory of who lit it beyond challenge.
Her single case is far too small a sample to support any sweeping conclusion.
Only a controlled study, never a personal account, can reveal what is really true.
Strong feeling about an event has no bearing at all on what we should believe.
context: This slides from a report of experience (which has real authority) to an interpretation of it (which does not get the same immunity) -- the testimony/inference distinction. Honoring someone's account of WHAT happened is not the same as accepting their theory of WHY, which is open to evidence like any other.

question: Defending a sweeping speech code, an organizer says: 'All we mean by violence is anything that makes a person feel unsafe.' Challenged that words then equal assault, she repeats the wide definition. Why does this redefinition mislead?
answer: Stretching 'violence' to cover discomfort lets a grave word smuggle in harm that was never shown.
choices: Stretching 'violence' to cover discomfort lets a grave word smuggle in harm that was never shown.
She retreats to a mild claim whenever she is pressed, then advances the bold one again later.
She assumes only two options exist here: a feeling of total safety or open cruelty to others.
She treats the intentions of her own side as plainly purer than the intentions of her critics.
context: This is a loaded redefinition (a persuasive definition, named by C. L. Stevenson, 1938): a word's emotional charge is kept while its meaning is quietly widened, so feelings owed to real violence transfer to things that are not. The fix is to ask whether the new sense still earns the old word's weight.

question: Thales, the first Greek philosopher, walked along gazing up at the stars. Lost in thought, he tumbled straight into a well. A servant girl burst out laughing. Why?
answer: He was so set on the sky that he missed the hole at his own feet.
choices: He was so set on the sky that he missed the hole at his own feet.
He had foretold the weather, yet failed to predict his own fall.
He claimed to know the gods, yet they let him stumble anyway.
He was the richest man in town, brought low into the mud.
context: Plato's Theaetetus (~369 BC) tells it: a Thracian maid mocked Thales for chasing knowledge of the heavens while blind to what lay right before him. The jab became the model joke about thinkers lost in abstraction.

question: In broad daylight, the philosopher Diogenes walked the crowded Athens market holding up a lit lamp, peering into every face. Asked what he sought, what did he say?
answer: An honest man — and he had yet to find a single one.
choices: An honest man — and he had yet to find a single one.
A thief who had just stolen the lamp from his hand.
The road back to his home, long after dark had come.
The richest man in Athens, to beg a coin from him.
context: Diogenes Laertius records the Cynic Diogenes (~4th c. BC) carrying a lamp by day, saying he sought a true human being (anthropon) — popularly retold as a search for one honest man. Searching at noon was living theater: as if integrity were so rare you needed a light to find it in daylight. The Cynics taught by such stunts, not lectures.

question: Diogenes owned almost nothing but a wooden cup for drinking. One day he saw a boy scoop water to his mouth with bare cupped hands. Diogenes threw his own cup away. Why?
answer: The boy showed he could live with even less than he had.
choices: The boy showed he could live with even less than he had.
The cup had cracked, so it could hold no water at all.
He wished to hand the cup to the thirsty boy as a gift.
He feared the boy would steal the cup if he kept it.
context: Diogenes the Cynic (~4th c. BC) taught that true freedom is needing as little as possible. A child outdoing him in simplicity was a lesson, not a loss — so the cup had to go.

question: The philosopher Heraclitus stood by a flowing river and said you can never step into the same river twice. The water looks the same to the eye. What did he mean it was not?
answer: The water is always new, so it is never the very same river.
choices: The water is always new, so it is never the very same river.
A river is too wide for one person to ever cross it twice.
Stepping in once makes the water dirty for the next time.
Only the gods may step into the same sacred river twice.
context: Heraclitus of Ephesus (~500 BC) taught that everything flows — the world is constant change. The water you stepped in a moment ago has already swept past; fresh water has taken its place, so it is never quite the same river.

question: On trial for his life, the philosopher Socrates was told he could go free if he simply stopped asking his probing questions in the streets of Athens. He refused. Why?
answer: An unexamined life, with no questions asked, was to him not worth living.
choices: An unexamined life, with no questions asked, was to him not worth living.
He was sure the jury would never truly dare to vote for his death.
He had sworn an oath to the gods never to fall silent while alive.
He thought exile from Athens would be a fate far worse than death.
context: Plato's Apology (~399 BC) records Socrates' defiance: offered acquittal if he gave up philosophy, he answered that 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' and chose the hemlock over a silent old age.

question: As his weeping friends looked on, the condemned philosopher Socrates calmly drank the cup of hemlock poison. He told them their grief was misplaced. Why did he not fear death?
answer: To fear death is to act sure it is bad — but no living person knows that.
choices: To fear death is to act sure it is bad — but no living person knows that.
The poison would be painless, so there was simply nothing left to dread.
A famous man's death is remembered, and such fame outlasts the body.
His accusers, not he, would carry the guilt for the killing forever.
context: In Plato's Apology and Phaedo (~399 BC), Socrates argues that to fear death is to presume you know it is an evil, when no living person knows what death holds — so dread mistakes ignorance for knowledge. He drank the hemlock calmly while his friends wept.

question: Aristotle tutored the teenage Alexander, drilling him in Homer's Iliad. Marching across Asia years later, Alexander kept the poem under his pillow and called it his guide to war. Why would a conqueror treat an old war poem that way?
answer: Its heroes model how to lead and hold honor under pressure -- a rehearsal for command.
choices: Its heroes model how to lead and hold honor under pressure -- a rehearsal for command.
It listed the exact routes and supply lines an army would need to cross into Asia.
Reciting old verse each night was thought to keep a soldier safe from harm in war.
A famous tutor's gift was a charm whose worth lay in who gave it, not in its words.
context: Plutarch reports Alexander carried Aristotle's edited 'casket copy' of the Iliad under his pillow with his dagger, calling Homer a guide to the art of war. The deeper move: great literature works as a rehearsal for conduct, letting a reader practice courage and judgment before the real test.

question: To defend his teacher Parmenides, who claimed motion is illusion, Zeno set a trap: swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise given a head start, since he must first reach where it WAS, by which time it has crept on. What kind of argument is this?
answer: A reductio: assume motion is real, derive an impossibility, conclude the assumption is false.
choices: A reductio: assume motion is real, derive an impossibility, conclude the assumption is false.
An appeal to the senses: what we plainly see in a footrace must be how the world truly is.
A generalization: because one slow tortoise wins, every race must work the same way.
An analogy: a footrace resembles a flying arrow, so both must obey one shared rule.
context: Zeno of Elea (~450 BC) defended Parmenides with paradoxes built as reductio ad absurdum -- proof by contradiction. Calculus later showed an infinite sum of shrinking gaps can total a finite distance, but the puzzle about completing infinitely many steps is still debated.

question: In Plato's tale, a prisoner chained to face a cave wall is freed, climbs to the surface, and sees the sun. He goes back down to tell the others the shadows they watch are not real. Plato warns the returning man is in danger. Why?
answer: The shadows are the only world they trust, so the man unsettling it seems a threat, not help.
choices: The shadows are the only world they trust, so the man unsettling it seems a threat, not help.
His eyes, still adjusting to the dark, leave him too blind to defend himself below.
The keepers of the cave fear him most and move first to silence the freed prisoner.
The others would simply ignore him, too absorbed in the passing shadows to listen.
context: Plato's cave (Republic VII, ~375 BC) ends in a warning: at 517a the prisoners would kill anyone trying to drag them up, since they take the shadows for the whole of reality. Plato, whose teacher Socrates was executed by Athens, knew that those who report a larger reality are often resented, not thanked.

question: Condemned to death and writing in his cell, Boethius pictures Lady Philosophy scolding him for grieving his lost honors and wealth. She points to Fortune's turning wheel. What is her core consolation to a man about to die?
answer: Goods that Fortune can spin away were never truly his, so losing them takes nothing real.
choices: Goods that Fortune can spin away were never truly his, so losing them takes nothing real.
