A total demolition — proving every past philosophy false in order to clear the ground for his own.
A retreat to one creed — rejecting all sources but Scripture as worthless pagan error.
A denial of all truth — arguing that no tradition knows anything and inquiry is hopeless.
question: Pico della Mirandola, at 23, proposed to defend 900 theses drawing on Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, and Christian sources, convinced that scattered traditions held fragments of one deep truth. The Church condemned some of his theses. What was the bold philosophical ambition behind his project?
context: Pico (1463-1494) embodied Renaissance ambition: he offered to defend 900 theses in Rome, drawing on Plato, Aristotle, the Hebrew Kabbalah, Islamic philosophy, Hermetic texts, and Christian theology, believing a hidden 'concord' (concordia) united the great traditions. His prefatory 'Oration on the Dignity of Man' became the Renaissance manifesto. The Church found thirteen theses suspect and the disputation was banned, but his syncretic vision — that truth speaks in many tongues and can be harmonized — captures the humanist confidence of the age.

answer: Reality is absolute and reason can know it, so wishes cannot reshape facts to suit us.
choices: Reality is absolute and reason can know it, so wishes cannot reshape facts to suit us.
Reality is unknowable, so each person must invent his own private truth as he pleases.
Reality bends to belief, so a strong enough faith can literally remake the world's facts.
Reality does not exist at all, so the only thing real is the flow of one's own ideas.
question: Ayn Rand built her philosophy on a starting point she borrowed from Aristotle and made a slogan: 'A is A,' existence exists, and a thing is itself. She held this was not a dry logic rule but the foundation of a whole way of living. What did Rand draw FROM this principle?
context: Rand named the three axioms of her metaphysics: existence exists, consciousness is awareness of existence, and the law of identity — A is A (a thing is what it is), taken from Aristotle. From this she drew her whole stance: reality is objective and absolute; facts are not subject to anyone's wishes, feelings, or decrees ('You can avoid reality, but you cannot avoid the consequences of avoiding reality'). Reason, the faculty that identifies and integrates what exists, is therefore man's basic tool of survival. The grand claims built on 'A is A' are precisely what her critics contest.

answer: He reframed tradition as he transmitted it, claiming continuity while quietly reinventing it.
choices: He reframed tradition as he transmitted it, claiming continuity while quietly reinventing it.
He was simply lying, since he knew full well he had invented every one of his teachings.
He truly added nothing, so the tradition he passed on was wholly unchanged by his hand.
He rejected the whole past entirely, openly declaring all earlier custom worthless and discarded.
question: Confucius said he 'transmitted but did not innovate,' presenting himself as a humble carrier of ancient wisdom — yet he transformed nearly everything he touched, redefining nobility, ritual, and rulership. Scholars debate what his self-description reveals. What is the most defensible reading of this paradox?
context: Analects 7.1: 'I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love the ancients.' Yet Confucius redefined the junzi from a hereditary noble to a man of virtue, reread ritual as character-formation, and made the moral cultivation of rulers central. The scholarly resolution: his conservatism was genuine in spirit but transformative in effect — he located his radical ethics in an idealized antiquity (the sage-kings, the Duke of Zhou), giving innovation the authority of inheritance. This 'transmission' is itself a sophisticated move; appealing to a golden past to license reform recurs across the history of thought, from the Renaissance to the American founders.

answer: Dirty hands — when right political action seems to require doing something genuinely wrong.
choices: Dirty hands — when right political action seems to require doing something genuinely wrong.
False dilemma — when only two options are offered as if no other choices actually existed.
Moral luck — when factors entirely beyond our control change how blameworthy an action is.
Weakness of will — when a person clearly knows the good yet still fails to act on what they know.
question: Machiavelli forced a problem that ethics still cannot dissolve: he held that a good ruler may have to do genuinely evil things — break faith, shed blood — for the survival of the state, and that to refuse is itself a kind of failure. Philosophers call this the problem of what?
context: Machiavelli's claim that a prince must 'learn how not to be good' poses what later philosophers (notably Michael Walzer, in his 1973 essay 'Political Action: The Problem of Dirty Hands') named the dirty hands problem: the possibility that doing the right thing in politics sometimes requires committing a real moral wrong — and that the leader is genuinely guilty even when he chose rightly. It refuses the comforting view that morality and political necessity never truly collide. The deepest reading of Machiavelli is not that he denied morality, but that he saw, unflinchingly, this tragic conflict within it.

answer: He gains by political pull, not by trade, using force through the state rather than earning it.
choices: He gains by political pull, not by trade, using force through the state rather than earning it.
He earns by honest free trade, so Rand actually praised him as the truest of all her great heroes.
He produces nothing physical at all, and Rand counted only hard manual labor as genuinely moral.
He simply grew too wealthy, and Rand held that great riches were corrupting in and of themselves.
question: Ayn Rand condemned both the bandit who steals at gunpoint AND the man who lives off government handouts taken from producers — yet she also condemned the businessman who lobbies politicians for special favors and protections. She lumped that last figure with the looters. What was Rand's reasoning?
context: Rand drew her central line not between rich and poor but between those who gain by voluntary trade and those who gain by force or political pull. In 'Atlas Shrugged' her villains include 'aristocrats of pull' — businessmen who get rich not by producing value but by lobbying for subsidies, tariffs, and favors that loot competitors and consumers through the power of the state. She named this 'the aristocracy of pull,' close kin to what economists call rent-seeking or crony capitalism. For Rand, such a man is no capitalist hero but a looter in a fine suit, since he substitutes political force for honest trade — a distinction that cuts sharply against a lazy reading of her as a mere apologist for the wealthy.

answer: A lie violates the rational basis of all trust, which no good outcome can be allowed to override.
choices: A lie violates the rational basis of all trust, which no good outcome can be allowed to override.
Kant secretly enjoyed cruelty and wanted the friend to be caught, hiding it all behind cold logic.
Kant thought the friend's life was worthless, so protecting it could not justify any lie at all.
Kant believed lying never has bad effects, so there was no real cost to telling the truth here.
question: Kant claimed the moral law forbids lying ABSOLUTELY — even, in a notorious essay, to a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding. Most people recoil; many philosophers think Kant erred. Yet a sympathetic reading explains why a man so humane held so rigid a line. What drove Kant's position?
context: In 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' (1797), Kant argues you may not lie even to a would-be murderer asking where your friend is, because the duty of truthfulness is unconditional — a lie wrongs humanity in general by undermining the very trust that makes language and contracts possible, and one is not responsible for the murderer's free choices but is responsible for one's own lie. Most readers, and many Kantians, judge this a reductio of strict rule-absolutism; defenders argue Kant is making a subtle point about not taking responsibility for others' wrongdoing onto oneself. The case is the classic stress-test of deontology against consequences — steel-manned here rather than mocked.

answer: It changes the role of ritual and authority, since one gardens innate good and one reshapes raw nature.
choices: It changes the role of ritual and authority, since one gardens innate good and one reshapes raw nature.
It changes nothing at all, since both men in the end recommended the exact same whole way of life.
It changes who may be taught, since Mencius firmly barred the wicked from any moral teaching at all.
It changes only the word choice, since 'good' and 'bad' here both mean precisely the same single condition.
question: Mencius and the later Confucian Xunzi both wanted people to become good, but disagreed at the root: Mencius said nature is good and virtue is cultivated FROM it, Xunzi said nature is bad and virtue is constructed AGAINST it. The dispute has a surprising practical edge. Why does the difference actually matter?
context: The Mencius-Xunzi split is not idle: it shapes how you teach virtue and how much external constraint people need. If nature is good (Mencius), education chiefly nourishes and protects inborn sprouts — a gentler, more optimistic vision that trusts the self. If nature is bad (Xunzi), virtue must be deliberately imposed through rigorous ritual, teachers, and authority that bend a crooked nature straight — a sterner vision giving more weight to institutions and discipline. The same fork reappears across the world's thought (Rousseau's naturally good man versus Hobbes's and the doctrine of original sin), and it quietly drives real disagreements about education, law, and how much we should trust people left to themselves.

answer: Philosophy shapes history — the abstract ideas a culture holds drive its course over centuries.
choices: Philosophy shapes history — the abstract ideas a culture holds drive its course over centuries.
Philosophy is useless — only material forces move history, while ideas are powerless froth.
Philosophy is private — abstract ideas touch the lone thinker but never affect whole societies.
Philosophy is dangerous — all systematic thought should be discouraged in favor of pure instinct.
question: Ayn Rand made a claim that unsettles even admirers: she held that to live morally requires a single integrated philosophy, and that most people's unexamined mix of inherited ideas leaves them at the mercy of contradictions they never named. She tied this to how cultures rise and fall. What was her sweeping claim?
context: Rand argued that philosophy is not an ivory-tower luxury but the deepest mover of human life and history: the fundamental ideas a culture absorbs — about reason, reality, and the good — determine, over time, whether it flourishes or collapses. In 'Philosophy: Who Needs It,' she warns that the person who never examines his premises does not escape philosophy but merely holds a jumble of inherited, contradictory ideas that rule him unawares. She read history as driven by such fundamental ideas (crediting Aristotle's rediscovery for the Renaissance, blaming Kant for modern collapse). The grand thesis — that abstract philosophy steers civilizations — is exactly what makes her both influential and fiercely contested, set here as her position for the player to weigh.

answer: Natural law — a moral rule of reason binding on everyone, above any human command.
choices: Natural law — a moral rule of reason binding on everyone, above any human command.
Royal will — whatever the king decrees becomes right simply because he commands it.
Local custom — each city's own traditions, with no rule reaching across them at all.
Brute force — the rule that the strongest may take whatever their power lets them seize.
question: Renaissance scholars rediscovered a Roman writer, Cicero, who argued there is a true law above any king's decree — a law of right reason, the same in Rome and Athens, that no ruler may rightly cancel. What did Cicero claim this higher law was?
context: Cicero (106-43 BC), recovered and revered by Renaissance humanists, gave the classic statement of natural law in 'On the Republic': 'True law is right reason in agreement with nature... it is not allowed to alter this law, nor to repeal any part of it.' The idea — that there is a moral standard above the state, knowable by reason and binding on rulers — runs through Aquinas to Locke and into the natural-rights tradition behind the American founding.

answer: Integrity — holding to one's own rational judgment even at great personal cost.
choices: Integrity — holding to one's own rational judgment even at great personal cost.
Obedience — bending one's work to whatever those in authority happen to demand.
Popularity — shaping one's work to win the approval of as many people as possible.
Humility — assuming one's own judgment is worth less than the crowd's combined view.
question: Ayn Rand told of a gifted architect who designs buildings exactly as he judges right and refuses every commission that demands he compromise his vision to please a committee, even when refusing costs him everything. Rand held him up as a moral hero. What virtue was she dramatizing?
context: The architect is Howard Roark, hero of Rand's novel 'The Fountainhead' (1943). For Rand, integrity means loyalty to one's own reasoned convictions — refusing to fake reality or surrender one's judgment to others, whatever the pressure. Roark dynamites his own building rather than let it be altered against the agreement he was promised. The virtue is not stubbornness but the refusal to betray one's mind; whether Rand's heroes model this nobly or rigidly is itself debated.

answer: Empiricism — trusting careful observation and experience over inherited book-authority.
choices: Empiricism — trusting careful observation and experience over inherited book-authority.
Traditionalism — settling every question by what the ancient masters had already written.
Mysticism — gaining truth through visions and revelation rather than the senses at all.
Skepticism — denying that we can ever really know anything about the natural world.
question: The Renaissance painter and inventor Leonardo da Vinci filled notebooks insisting that real knowledge of nature comes not from quoting old authorities but from looking closely, measuring, and testing for yourself. He called experience the one reliable teacher. What outlook was Leonardo championing?
context: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) called himself 'a man without letters' and insisted that 'experience is the mother of all certainty.' Against the bookish scholasticism of his day, which settled questions by citing Aristotle, he urged direct observation, dissection, and measurement. His notebooks brim with this method, anticipating the experimental spirit that Galileo and Bacon would soon make the engine of modern science.

answer: Doubt your own certainty — the loudest convictions are often the least examined ones.
choices: Doubt your own certainty — the loudest convictions are often the least examined ones.
Trust your strongest feelings — the more sure you feel, the more likely you are right.
Defer to the crowd always — truth is simply whatever the most people firmly believe.
Abandon all judgment — since nothing can be known, never hold any view about anything.
question: The essayist Montaigne lived through France's savage religious wars and grew suspicious of anyone certain enough to kill over their beliefs. He noticed that fierce conviction often rests on flimsy ground. What lesson did Montaigne draw about strong certainty?
context: Montaigne's 'Essays,' written amid the French Wars of Religion, are soaked in a humane skepticism: 'Nothing is so firmly believed as that which we least know.' Watching fanatics slaughter each other over doctrine, he prized intellectual humility and tolerance. His skepticism was not despair but a brake on arrogance — a reminder that our certainties are often habit dressed as truth, and that this awareness should make us gentler with those who differ.

answer: Emotions follow from your premises, so to change what you feel, examine the ideas beneath them.
choices: Emotions follow from your premises, so to change what you feel, examine the ideas beneath them.
Emotions reveal truth directly, so a strong enough feeling is itself proof that a belief is correct.
Emotions should be crushed entirely, since a fully rational person feels nothing whatsoever.
Emotions come from nowhere at all, random surges with no link to anything a person thinks.
question: Ayn Rand made an unusual claim about emotions: she did not say to suppress them, but argued that feelings are not tools of knowledge — they are automatic reactions flowing from ideas you have already accepted, consciously or not. What followed, on her view, from this account of emotion?
context: Rand held that 'emotions are not tools of cognition' — they tell you how something relates to your values, but not whether a belief is true. Crucially, she did not preach repression: emotions, she argued, are produced by one's value-judgments and premises, many absorbed unawares. So persistent feelings that clash with one's conscious convictions signal hidden contradictory premises worth uncovering. Reason and emotion need not war if one's premises are made consistent — a subtler position than the 'cold rationalist' caricature suggests.

answer: Reason applied to the facts of human life, which yields objective values without God or the crowd.
choices: Reason applied to the facts of human life, which yields objective values without God or the crowd.
Pure personal whim, where each person simply decrees his own values with no standard at all.
The will of the strongest, where whoever holds the most power thereby defines what is good.
Inherited tradition alone, where a practice is counted right merely because ancestors once long followed it.
question: Ayn Rand rejected the idea that morality must rest on God's commands OR on society's approval. A critic objects that without one of those, 'good' and 'evil' are just personal opinion. Rand answered that this misses a third option entirely. What was her alternative grounding for ethics?
context: Rand's metaethics aimed at a third path between divine-command theory and subjectivism: she argued that ethics can be grounded objectively in facts — specifically, the requirements of human survival and flourishing as discovered by reason. Just as medicine derives objective standards of health from facts about the body, she held, ethics derives objective standards of the good from facts about what a rational being's life requires. Whether values can truly be derived from facts this way (recall Hume's is-ought gap) is the central philosophical challenge to her project — presented here as her contested claim.

answer: The many judge better than one — a free people corrects errors a lone ruler cannot.
choices: The many judge better than one — a free people corrects errors a lone ruler cannot.
The crowd is always foolish — so a wise single prince must decide everything alone.
Rulers are chosen by heaven — so whoever holds the throne is right by divine decree.
Politics cannot be judged — so no form of government is any better than any other.
question: The Renaissance thinker Machiavelli, in his 'Discourses,' praised the ancient Roman Republic over any kingdom and argued that a people governing themselves will, over time, choose more wisely than a single prince. On what did he base this defense of republican self-rule?
context: The 'Discourses on Livy' show the republican Machiavelli, admirer of Roman liberty. Against the common view that crowds are fickle, he argued that 'a people is more prudent, more stable, and of better judgment than a prince' — a self-governing citizenry, debating openly and able to remove bad leaders, corrects its mistakes better than a single ruler answerable to no one. This republicanism, prizing liberty and popular participation, is the side of Machiavelli that influenced the founders of modern republics, far from the scheming 'Prince' of legend.

answer: Whose life is the standard — your own, or others', for whom you are to be sacrificed?
choices: Whose life is the standard — your own, or others', for whom you are to be sacrificed?
Which pleasures feel best — so that the most enjoyable life becomes the only moral aim?
What did tradition decree — so that the oldest custom automatically settles every case?
How can conflict be avoided — so that keeping the peace outweighs all other concerns?
question: Ayn Rand identified what she considered the deepest divide in ethics — not between specific rules, but in how a moral code answers one prior question. She said every ethics rests on an answer to it, usually unexamined. What did Rand say that foundational question was?
context: Rand framed the basic ethical alternative not as a clash of particular rules but as a question of beneficiary: for whose sake should a person act? She charged that most moral codes assume, without arguing it, that the answer is 'others' — that self-sacrifice is the essence of virtue (altruism). Her own answer was that each person's own life is properly the moral standard, neither sacrificing himself to others nor others to himself (rational egoism). Sharpening 'who is the beneficiary?' into the root question of ethics is a distinctive and much-disputed move — laid out here as her position to weigh, not a verdict.
